## popup-enter

**2026-10-31 · popup-enter: a popup's contents play their `enter` at every open, and
that stays.** A popup's contents mount each time it opens, written under an `if` or
not, so their poses replay. A stagger on open relies on it. The cost is a popup that
starts out looking like something already on screen: its copy plays `enter` over the
original and flickers. To skip the pose, leave it out, or decide it by a value:
`enter: still ? none : fade`, or `enter { x: still ? 50 : 200 }` with the node's own
`x` (50) when `still`; either way, with `still` true as the popup opens, it shows at
rest from its first frame. No new syntax. Proof, a throwaway run with a card in a
popup opened twice: `enter { x: 200 }` 14 frames at each open; `enter: none`, and each
form above with `still` true, 1 frame; with `still` false 14 and 15 frames.

## gpu-memory

**2026-10-31 · gpu-memory: the warm device asks wgpu for small allocator blocks;
its memory is measured in fdinfo, not PSS.** The docs' "+21 to +23 MB" for the
warm device on Intel is PSS, which leaves out device memory: `drm-total-gtt` was
292,956 KiB, and `GPUActive` in `/proc/meminfo` shows those pages are real. Of
that, 182 MiB was room wgpu's default `MemoryHints::Performance` reserved and
nothing used, in a device kept for the session (gpu-first), whatever the outputs.
`MemoryHints::MemoryUsage` brings it to 129,116 KiB with no frame-time difference
beyond noise on the hardware bench; a 4K target's own allocation costs about 1 ms
once per size. Speed beats size, but here size was free. Left as they are: the
4096² image atlas (64 MiB), which the warm frame makes by drawing an image, so
that an animation's first image does not pay for it (about 2 ms for the texture;
a warm frame without the image is 63,580 KiB, its first-frame cost unmeasured);
and the warm device itself, which an owner ruling keeps. Numbers: benchmarks.md
"GPU memory of the warm device". Proof:
`a_warm_device_reserves_little_beyond_what_it_uses`, which fails on the default

## presented-quiet

**2026-10-31 · presented-quiet: a paint on a presented surface that sends nothing
still does what follows a paint.** wave-cost made a presented surface send no frame
when a paint draws nothing, and a sent frame was the only thing that ran the frame's
reaction, set its regions, or woke the loop for the next one (its `Presented`). So
such a paint left a time signal stopped, an ended exit and a shrink queued, and a
changed region unsent, each until something unrelated drew; gpu-stay makes that path
permanent once a surface is promoted, and `eval-hooks` builds, which draw every frame,
never reach it. `GpuHost::present` now tells the two cases apart: on no frame it runs
`Host::painted` and `sync_presented` as a CPU's empty paint does, and where a CPU's
empty paint would send a bare commit (`State::take_owed_commit`, set when a region
changed) it asks for `GpuRequest::Commit`, a present of the last frame, since only a
present commits this surface. The same goes for what the manager itself leaves pending
with no frame to follow: a layer's new config (`reconfigure`, so `refit_layers_on`), a
popup's reposition, a keyboard mode. Sending a whole new frame for it was rejected: nothing
was drawn, and the commit already exists for a held size. No hand back to the CPU
(gpu-stay). Proof: `crates/strand/tests/presented_quiet.rs`, run alone in CI, not under
`--workspace`, whose `eval-hooks` hides the path; its `proved` asserts a paint did send
nothing. Each test was seen failing without its fix.

## gpu-pace

**2026-10-31 · gpu-pace: a presented surface's next frame waits for its last
present's frame callback, on the main thread, not in Mesa on the GPU thread.**
Asked why first acquires took about 52 ms and buffers about 40 ms, on real Intel
hardware the first acquire measured at most 0.12 ms on Ubuntu's sway 1.9, Arch's
sway 1.12 with explicit sync, and labwc, and no slow acquire appeared at all. Those
figures were not reproduced, since no compositor here offers `wp_fifo_manager_v1`
as Hyprland does, and they remain unexplained. What the same trace did show was
Strand's: `Presented` paced a surface, so its next frame was sent at once and
Mesa's `queue_present` blocked in the one GPU thread until the last frame's
callback. Every other surface's frames queued behind that wait (15 ms in the
queue), a 120 Hz output animating beside 60 Hz ones ran at 61 frames/s, and an
output turned off stopped all of them for good, since Mesa's wait has no timeout.
Since gpu-stay more surfaces stay on that thread. Now the host asks for a frame
callback as pending state before it sends a frame (`ask_present_callback`) and
sends the next once it has come (`present_due`). The thread does not wait, the
120 Hz output runs at 121 frames/s, and on a compositor without
`wp_fifo_manager_v1` the output's own surface alone stops while it is off (with it,
see the give-up below). A callback still owed when a surface is handed off counts as
stale: taken for the newest, it put every later present a frame early, back into
Mesa's wait, in two of three runs on Arch's sway before that was fixed; so does one a
CPU surface gave up on, or replaced for a new size, in `draw`, which once only cleared
it. The give-up a CPU
surface has is kept only with `wp_fifo_manager_v1`, where Mesa does not wait for
callbacks and a lost one should not stop the surface. Each present it lets go still
waits in the compositor's FIFO, though, and Hyprland lets one go per monitor present, so
the wait doubles for each present still unanswered, up to 64 s, and the callbacks' coming
starts it again: at a flat second a sleeping output's surface added a buffer a second
(dmabuf fds 24 to 321 in 300 s, drained over 4 to 6 s at the wake) and held the GPU thread
each time the images ran out (wgpu's 1 s acquire timeout), so the other output's panel
ran at 31 to 58 frames/s, with a hidden workspace's window as well as a powered-off output. Without it, a frame sent
after a give-up stops every surface, as measured: all four at 1 s of `power off`.
Without `wp_fifo_manager_v1` a `Commit` is paced as a frame is: it asks for the callback,
stays in flight until the thread answers `Committed`, and forgets the callback if it
presented nothing (with the protocol Mesa does not wait, and pacing it made things
worse: on nested Hyprland a panel's next size after a stall stayed at 0 to 1 frames/s
where the frame going along with its `Commit` gave 60, 5 runs of 5). As first written it waited for the callback and asked for none, so a frame after it waited in
Mesa for that present's own callback: with an idle panel on a powered-off output, a
region change and then a frame stopped every surface until the output came back, and for
good if it was unplugged (Arch's sway, the other panel 62 frames/s to 0; 12 s after the
unplug it had not come back, and the surface was never released). The compositor gets about one more wake per frame (the
request reaches it apart from the commit), while Strand's own about halve. Left alone:
a promotion's attach (up to about 20 ms, once per surface since gpu-stay). The 52 ms
was not seen again. Hyprland's FIFO path, measured since on a real Hyprland (nested,
`scripts/container/hyprland-nested.sh`), is why gpu-mailbox replaced it. Where a driver
has `Mailbox` Mesa never waits for a callback, so all of the above about Mesa's wait now
holds only on a driver with `Fifo` alone. Proof:
`a_presented_frame_waits_for_its_callback_or_gives_up` for the manager's half, which
fails if the stale count, the wait or the FIFO rule goes;
`a_give_up_doubles_while_presents_stay_unanswered` if the back-off goes from either the
due check or the timer; `a_given_up_shm_callback_does_not_answer_the_present` for
`draw`'s;
`a_commit_on_a_powered_off_output_stops_no_other_surface` on sway, under lavapipe, for
a `Commit`, seen failing without it; the rest of the host's wiring only shows on a
presenting GPU, so benchmarks.md "Presenting on one GPU thread" is its proof.

## gpu-idle-wakes

**2026-10-31 · gpu-idle-wakes: an idle promoted surface wakes no more than the CPU
path; the 175 wakes a second were the bench's forcing, gone since gpu-stay.** Bead's
benchmark of 2026-10-30 had an idle surface forced to the GPU at 175 wakes a second
against 8. That binary, run again, measured 178 to 188, and with a debug log it
releases and attaches its surfaces over and over (27 attaches in one short run, in
turn on each surface): its patch, which was not kept, promotes, and gpu-first's
settling, then still there, demotes the idle surface again, so each cycle rebuilds a
swapchain and draws. Those are also the swapchain rebuilds gpu-stay noted and did not
see. With gpu-stay nothing demotes it: today's forced build and a
surface promoted by opening and closing the island both measure 8.1 to 8.7 against
8.1 to 8.3 on the CPU, no Vulkan or wgpu thread woke at all, and nothing changes in
the code. Sway only, without `wp_fifo_manager_v1`, so Hyprland's figure is unmeasured. Numbers: benchmarks.md "An idle promoted
surface's wakes".

## gpu-mailbox

2026-10-31. A presented surface uses `Mailbox` where the driver has it, not `Fifo`. On a
real Hyprland 0.57, an animated panel changing size with nothing else drawing on its
monitor froze: 0 to 1 frames/s until something else made that monitor draw (a screenshot
freed it), in 8 runs of 15 under a burst of sizes. Mesa's `Fifo` sets a
`wp_fifo_v1` barrier with each commit; a commit behind one waits for the monitor to present,
and an otherwise idle monitor has nothing to present. It was there before gpu-pace's fixes
and it would have been a Hyprland report, but the rule is to fix it here
(fix-in-strand). Since gpu-pace the host sends one frame per frame callback, so `Fifo`'s
queue paces nothing, and `Mailbox` sets no barrier: the same burst runs at 60 frames/s, 8
runs of 8, with no screenshot. It also ends gpu-pace's other Hyprland cost: a present to an
output nobody draws replaces the last one rather than queuing behind it, so with one output
asleep for 200 s the other's panel keeps 60 to 62 frames/s where `Fifo` dipped to 31 and 32,
Hyprland's dmabuf fds stay flat, and no acquire times out. There is no tearing, as a
compositor shows whole buffers, and no frame is drawn to be thrown away, as the callback
paces them. The price is about one more buffer in a surface's swapchain: 2 MiB of GPU memory
for one 800×500 panel on each of two outputs. Frame rates at 60 and 120 Hz and wakes are
unchanged. `Fifo` stays for a driver without `Mailbox`, with gpu-pace's rules for Mesa's wait
(they are kept as they are on `Mailbox` too, where they cost nothing: without the protocol a
lost callback still stops only its own surface); `STRAND_GPU_FIFO=1` forces it, for its
tests and as an escape hatch. These are headless Hyprland monitors, not DRM, so a real
monitor's behaviour is the owner's session to confirm. Numbers: benchmarks.md "Presenting on
Hyprland". Proof: `mailbox_is_taken_where_the_driver_has_it`;
`a_commit_on_a_powered_off_output_stops_no_other_surface_on_fifo` keeps the fallback tested;
the freeze only shows on Hyprland, which no repo test reaches.

## read-before-line

2026-10-31. A `let`, `state` or `fn` read before its own line is checked at that read, and its
line then asks for it again through `take_done`. `force_now` swapped the state to `Checking`
before looking at it, so a declaration already `Done` stayed `Checking` for good, and each read
after that got `Ty::Error` from `def_ty`, whose cycle report says nothing when the declaration
is not on the stack. An error type reports nothing further, so `let b = base.alpha(0.3)` after
`let a = base.alpha(0.7)` and a default `c: color = a` lowered `b` to null: nothing drawn and 0
errors from `strand check`. A default was only the commonest way in, since signatures are checked
before any line: an earlier `let` reading a later one does the same. `force_now` now leaves
anything but `Pending` alone. Proof: `a_declaration_read_before_its_line_keeps_its_type`, five
ways in, all seen failing without the fix.

## palette-value

2026-10-31. `palette(…)` is a third way to make a palette, beside `material` and `import`: any
role as a colour or null, plus `from` and `dark`. A config reading colours from a file had two
paths that did not meet: `import` only reads set formats, and a `from file` service feeds no token,
so Strand's widgets, the fill-in table, the contrast guard and sprung swaps were out of reach. A new
import format would have put one file shape and its names in Strand, and copying colours with `set
{ }` skips the table and the guard. This adds no concept: a palette is already a value, the source
is any service, and the names meet the roles in a line of the config. Two overloads, as with `from`
it is never null (`Palette`) and without it null when given nothing (`Palette?`), so `use palette`
makes the fallback explicit. A given role re-derives what `Partial::fill`'s table derives from it
(`derived_from`), so `accent` brings `on_accent`; secondary, tertiary and the hues only start from
the accent and a scheme's own stay. Unknown names stay check errors, not extras: custom colours belong
in `tokens`. A token as a colour is a runtime error, since tokens are worked out from the palette.
Run with a `from file` service on headless sway under lavapipe: rewriting the file sprang the
surface and accent over about 8 captures, a broken or missing file sprang to `from`,
and 7 restarts showed the file's colours on the first frame drawn, with no fallback frame, so nothing
was added for startup. Proof: the five `palette` tests in `tests/theme.rs`.

## keyboard

(2026-10-31) Anything a pointer can do, a key can do, and the config says what each key means. Strand
knows nothing of menus, levels or modes: a shell builds those from `state`. Today a key handler can't
stop a default, a `list`'s selection can't be moved from code, only `input` and `list` hold focus, a
`scroll` can't be scrolled from code, and fuzzy search covers only apps. Run on nested Hyprland 0.57
before designing: keys reach a panel, every key sent 10 ms or more after `strand set` returned arrived
(39 of 48 with none), and `keyboard:` changes while a surface is open, both ways.

Five pieces, built in this order, each documented in spec.md and the reference as it lands:

1. **A pattern claims a key.** `on key "ctrl+n", "down" { … }` runs for those keys and stops the
   default and every other handler; `on key(k)` stays, and only observes, so it no longer takes Tab
   (gap 6). Logic runs on another thread and can't answer "handled" in time, so claims are not handler
   code: the compiler sets the active patterns as a prop of the node and the router matches them, from
   the focused node outward, the innermost first, before any default. Handlers may now sit in `when`,
   which lifts a rule rather than adding a syntax: `when view != home { on key "escape" { view = home } }`
   lets Escape reach the default at the top level. A condition is therefore reactive, as any prop is,
   and a key in the same tick as a change is judged by the old value. Patterns use the name a key has
   or its Latin fallback, so they work on non-Latin layouts, and are checked by `strand check`. `Key`
   gains `repeat`, and `on key_release(k)` is delivered, since `KeyInput` has both.
2. **Selection.** `results.next()`, `.prev()`, `.first()`, `.last()`, `.select(i)`, `.activate()`, and
   `wrap:` on `list`. `axis:` and `columns:` make one `list` a strip or a grid with arrows read from the
   layout, so there is no second selection concept. Selection stays apart from focus: it is an index,
   since virtualised rows beyond the window have no node to focus.
3. **Search.** `xs.fuzzy(query, x => x.name)` over any list, giving each item with its score and match
   ranges, beside the list methods. Frecency is a stored history, not an argument, so it is not in this.
4. **Focus and scroll.** `focus:` on any node, `node.focus()`, arrows moving focus by geometry where a
   container asks, Return activating, arrows changing a `slider`; a `scroll`'s position read and written.
5. **Text.** Compose and dead keys in `input`, which `seat.rs` doesn't do. An input method
   (`text-input-v3`) is later and is not designed here.

Not built: a menu or back-stack system; global key grabs, which stay the compositor's; a leader or
vim engine, which a `state` and `when` give. `strand toggle x value` and `strand call` on a config's
own actions were proposed and dropped: m5-owner Q13 ruled the second out, and an exported `bool` per
shortcut with `on change` already gives "this key opens that view, again closes it". Secret flow
(`check::secrets`) treats a claim that takes `(k)` as hearing keys; one without it hears nothing.

(2026-10-31, piece 1) Four things the shape above left open. A claim of a key that types, around a
`type: password` input or any `input` in a `lock`, is a check error (`check::claim_around_password`)
and not a warning, even in a `when`, which can't be proved to exclude the field: a lock whose letters
are eaten can't be left, and giving the claim a modifier or moving it off the field's path is always
possible. A claim whose `when` is false by the time its body starts doesn't run: the sentence above
judges the key by the old value, and the router does, so its default stays stopped, but several keys
queued while logic is busy (a held Escape counting a depth down) would otherwise run a handler past
the condition that spec.md 6.3 says it runs under; the key is spent. A drag's Escape stays the drag's,
so a gesture always has a way out. And a claim in an `if`, `for` or `match` body is a check error,
since those bodies mount with no element and an element's handler there has never run; a `when` is
the way to turn one on and off.

(2026-10-31, piece 1's review) An element's handler directly in an `if`, `for` or `match` body checked
clean and never ran, so every such handler is now a check error, as a claim there was. The Latin fallback
applies only to a pattern holding Ctrl, Alt or Super, as an input's shortcuts do: a plain `on key "j"`
around an `input` was eating the Cyrillic letter on that key under `ru`, so plain patterns match the name
alone, which narrows the sentence above. `check::claim_around_password` counts a component a `lock` calls
as in the lock, and what calls give a `slot` as around; it follows the calls rather than calling every
`slot` a field, since a shell's `j` and `k` around a slot of plain rows is a real pattern and the walk has
every call. Named keys are a table for checking typos, with `XF86*` and `dead_*` taken as written because
those families are open; a typo there goes unreported. A character pattern with an explicit `shift` is an
error rather than ignoring it: `"shift+1"` used to claim plain `1`.

(2026-11-01, piece 2) What the shape above left open for `axis:` and `columns:`. In an `input` with `nav:`,
Left and Right stay the caret's on a strip and a grid alike: taking them would make a field's text uneditable
by the arrows the moment its list changed shape, and a claim gives them to the list in one line. A grid has no
submenu key, since its four arrows all move it. A cell or strip row with no height of its own fills its line or
the list, as `grid`'s cells and a column's rows do, so a selected row's background is even; that costs a second
layout of a short row only. A horizontal list with no height of its own is as tall as its tallest row laid out,
since rows past the window can't be measured, so it may grow as taller ones scroll in. A drop's `at` on a grid
still comes from one axis (`drop_index`) and is not exact across lines; a grid that is reordered by dragging is
later work.

(2026-10-31, piece 3) `xs.fuzzy(query, x => x.name)` gives `[Match<T>]`. Records have no type
parameters, and a record with `item: any` would leave `m.item.name` unchecked, so the checker makes one
record per item type, the schema's `Match` with `item: T`, named `Match<Pin>`: fields, hover, reloads and
`for` keys then need nothing new, and a keyed item keys it by `item.<key>`, as `Hit` is by `app.id`. It is
writable as a type, as `Async<T>` is, since a component can't take a row otherwise and the name is what
errors print; this adds one reserved generic name and no grammar, and a config's own `type Match` keeps
the name. The VM has no static types, so the lowering passes the record as a last argument the source
doesn't write. The matcher moves to a new leaf crate, `strand-fuzzy`, used by the compiler and
`strand-services`: `strand-core` is the reactive graph and has no business with a matcher, and neither of
the two can depend on the other. It links nucleo-matcher 0.3 rather than nucleo 0.5, whose only other
parts are the worker pool and item stream that neither caller uses and that a wasm build can't run; the
matcher is the same code, so `apps.search` ranks as before. `by` returns one text: several (name and
keywords) would need `Match` to say which text its `ranges` are of, which `apps.search` answers by dropping
the ranges of a keyword match, and nothing here needs it yet; a selector can join them.

(2026-10-31, piece 3, the review) A query has no operators, in `xs.fuzzy` and `apps.search` alike: a box
someone types into must mean what it says, and nucleo's `Pattern::parse` read `!fire` as "not fire" and
`don't` as `don` plus a substring `t`. Every whitespace-separated word is a fuzzy atom, built with
`Atom::new` and no whitespace escape, since `Pattern::new` would still read `\ ` as an escape and split on
spaces only; plain words score as they did. A known limit: text with decomposed accents (`e` + U+0301)
doesn't match a precomposed query (`é`), since a cluster is matched by its first character.

(2026-11-01, piece 4) What the shape above left open for focus and scroll. A press focuses an `input`, `list` or node
with a written `focus:` under it, and a `button`, `slider` or `segmented` only when no `input` or `list` has focus and
none of those is under it too: a launcher's button beside its field must not take the typing, a menu's row of buttons
must not take a focused list's arrows, and a config that wants otherwise writes `focus:` on the button. A press moves
no `scroll`, though focus by anything else reveals, since what was pressed must stay under the pointer for its release.
`wrap: true` from the sketch became `arrows: focus_wrap`, since `wrap:` on `row` and `col` already means running children
on, and a strip of tiles wanting round arrows would have had its layout changed. Nesting seals both ways: arrows don't
leave the nearest `arrows:` nor enter another inside it, as a way in with no way out is worse than Tab. `SceneDiff`'s
`list_asks` became `asks`, of `NodeAsk`, since order across lists, focus and scrolls is what the asks are for. Return
or space goes to logic as one event (`NodeEvent::Press`), since only logic knows whether a node has an active `on
activate`; a repeat fires nothing, as a held key is not many clicks; a node in a list's row also selects and activates
the row, as a pointer does. A focused `list` keeps its own keys, and space pages it (below). `scroll_to` and
`scroll_by` take `y` and `x` by name or place, a lone `y` going along x on a scroll that runs only that way, which is
how the wheel reads it and saves a third pair of names. A position or a reveal waits for the layout of the diff that
asked, as what it reads may be what that diff mounted; a size still springing there is not waited for, so reveal
what was mounted rather than what grows. No focus ring is drawn by default: `when focused` is the config's look, and a
ring after every press would change how a mouse-only shell looks.

(2026-11-01, piece 5) The shape above says `seat.rs` doesn't do compose, but SCTK already did: its `KeyEvent::utf8`
comes from a compose state of its own, read from the same locale variables. What was missing is that the state is
private, so nothing could reset it, and a dead key pressed in one panel finished in the next
(`dead_keys_and_compose_type_the_composed_text_under_real_names` fails so with Strand's own table off). There is no way
to turn SCTK's off, so `manager/compose.rs` keeps per keyboard its own xkb state and compose state, and SCTK's text is
used only where no table loaded or a keymap didn't compile, which is what typing was. That costs a second keymap state
per keyboard and a second table. SCTK's `init_compose` parses its table for every `wl_keyboard` it is given, focused or
not, so a bar that never holds the keyboard still pays for SCTK's; only Strand's copy waits until a keyboard first reaches a
surface. Parsing `en_US.UTF-8`'s table took 6.1 ms and 384 KiB of resident memory in a release build in the container, once
each for SCTK and Strand on a focused shell (`C`'s: 3.1 ms, 148 KiB). A held key repeats what its press typed, not the key fed again: holding the last key of a
sequence gives `ééé`, not `éee`, a held dead key is one key of its sequence, and a key whose press cancelled a sequence
repeats nothing. A pointer press also ends a sequence, since a click can move focus to another `input` and the seat
can't see focus inside a surface; focus moved from code within one surface doesn't end one, and the next key finishes
it there. Passwords: the seat holds a press's text only in `Zeroizing` strings, wiped when the repeat stops. Copies it
can't wipe are SCTK's event, the `xkbcommon` crate's stack buffer and each `KeyInput.text` past the seat, which are the
same copies a plain typed key makes, and a composed character is a table entry and no more secret than one. The pending
sequence itself sits inside libxkbcommon's `xkb_compose_state` as a position in the table, which can be reset but not
wiped. Strand's is reset whenever a sequence ends and when a focused surface is destroyed, with or without a `leave`
(`destroy_surface`), so a lock or a `type: password` field going away needs no knowledge of what it held. SCTK's own
state can't be reached at all: it keeps its position until the next key press moves it, whatever Strand has reset. A
compositor's own repeats (`wl_keyboard` version 10) reach `repeat_key` with no text from SCTK, composed or not, as
they did, which this leaves alone.

(2026-11-01, piece 5, the review) A press with Ctrl, Alt or Super held is a shortcut: it isn't fed to compose, it ends a
pending sequence, and it has its ordinary text, so Ctrl+N after a dead key doesn't compose or continue anything. AltGr is
not one of them (it is Mod5, Alt is Mod1), since it types. This goes by the modifiers the seat last reported, as `KeyInput`
does. An Escape that ends a pending sequence is consumed: neither its press nor its release reaches the host, so cancelling
a mistyped dead key doesn't also close a launcher or clear a lock field, and no claim hears it. An Escape with nothing
pending, after a finished or cancelled sequence included, is an ordinary key. This replaces "whatever xkb's state says" for
Escape only. Swapping the depressed, latched and locked masks can't be seen in a key's text, since xkb reads their
effective sum, so `levels_layouts_and_chords_type_as_ever_with_a_table_loaded` catches masks put in the wrong place
against the layout (seen failing with the depressed mask and the group swapped).

(2026-11-01, piece 4's review) What the review of focus decided. Focus on a node no longer shown or hittable moves as Tab
would next, or to the surface when it is closing or nothing else can take it, and `focused` clears, for `input` and `list`
as for the rest. It moves when the diff applies and not at the next key, so `when focused` follows at once and a key finds
the new place; a Return right after a button hides itself therefore presses the node focus landed on, which shows as
focused, the same as after a Tab. The move reveals nothing, since a fade is no reason to scroll. The router remembers the
node and gives focus back when it shows again, unless focus moved on meanwhile: without that a launcher opened again
mid-fade would stop typing, its `focus: true` having never turned. A `list` is one Tab stop and what is in its rows is one
only with `focus:` written, an `input` in a row included, so a list of 50 row buttons no longer stands between two fields.
A press on a `button`, `slider` or `segmented` before the keyboard comes does not beat `focus: true` when it does; focus
held with the keyboard, back from a popup that grabbed it, still stays. Return on a focused row is what a pointer's click
there is, its click and then one `Activate`, the list's handler included. A scroll move waiting for a layout is held as the
last per node and kind, so a `scroll_by` waiting on a closed popup holds its last and not their sum, with 64 per surface.
Up and Down are always a focused `scroll`'s own, as `scroll_key` takes them. Space and Shift+space page a focused `scroll`
or `list`, whether or not there is anywhere to go, so space never falls through to a click around it. A known limit: a
slider or segmented key write that logic rejects sends no answer, so `ValueFlight` keeps the unshown value until
`EDIT_IN_FLIGHT` (500 ms) and further keys build on it. No diff can stand in for an answer, since one already on its way when
the write was sent looks the same, and clearing on it would lose the queued keys the flight is for. It takes an
acknowledgement from logic to render that does not exist; a typed `input` has the same limit.

## ci-speed-2

(2026-11-01) Run 41310281111 on de671192, medians over 60 runs: 27.6 min of wall time, with every job of a superseded
branch push running to its end. `ci.yml` now has a workflow-level concurrency group that cancels a run only on a push to a
branch other than main and on a pull request. Those use `ci-<ref>`; main, tags, schedule and dispatch use `ci-run-<run id>`,
so each is alone in its group. One shared group with `cancel-in-progress: false` would not do for main: GitHub runs a group
one at a time and keeps only the newest pending run, so a third push would cancel the second and main would queue. A
workflow-level cancel cannot reach deploy or release, whose `if` keeps them to main and tags, the runs that are alone in
their group; their own groups (`railway-deploy`, `release-<ref>`, both `cancel-in-progress: false`) still decide among
themselves as they did. A branch push and its pull request have different refs, so they don't cancel each other.

(2026-11-01) The package job took 21.4 min on every branch push, 15 of them release builds, for an archive only main and tags
publish. It now runs on a branch push or a pull request only when its inputs changed, with the shape of lock-vm's Decide step.
The inputs, from reading package.sh, smoke.sh, test-install.sh and test-publish.sh, first listed only the front files of what
test-install.sh runs in the installed tree; a later paragraph here widens them to all source, because "caught on main" is too
late when main moves on the branch's run. The skip can't reach deploy and release: the filter step's `if` leaves out
main, tags and dispatch, Decide skips only when the filter ran and answered false, and deploy and release run only on main and
tags. No check is dropped from what reaches main. test-publish.sh goes with it, and `run.sh ci` still runs it in lint.

(2026-11-01) The package job declared `cache-key: release` and never read that cache: its log says `No cache found` for
`v0-rust-release-Linux-x64-bb1eb2fe-b4987f66`, against the `63ec8b6c` that budgets saves. rust-cache hashes every variable named
`CARGO*` into the key, and `CARGO_ABOUT_VERSION` was one, so each of its builds compiled all 494 crates cold (7 min 55 s and
6 min 11 s in that run). It is `ABOUT_VERSION` now, leaving the job with the same environment as budgets. This reads a cache
and merges nothing: cargo's unit hash covers the compiler, flags, features and profile, and rust-cache drops the workspace's
own crates, so a dependency is reused only where the inputs agree. A tag reads main's cache, which only main can write.

(2026-11-01) The lock-vm filter named two paths that match nothing, `crates/strand/src/lock.rs` and
`crates/strand/src/services/auth*`, left from before the code moved to `run/lock.rs` and strand-services' `auth.rs`, both
listed; a file moved the same way would stop the VM running for it with no sign. `scripts/container/check-path-filters.sh`
now fails lint when an entry in any `filters:` block of ci.yml matches no tracked file, globs as well as literal paths, since
a dead glob fails as quietly, and it refuses braces and negation rather than guessing at them. Reading the lock code by
`Role::Lock` and the session lock manager found four files missing, now added: `manager/pose.rs`, `selection.rs`, `caps.rs`
and `lock_fallback/font.rs`, the last missed because `*lock_fallback*` stops at the directory's name. The job's own definition
and the setup action are in too, so a ci.yml edit runs the VM, as the job's comment ("the lock code or the harness") promised.

(2026-11-01) The Actions cache held 10.35 GB against its 10 GB limit, and two generations of each rust-cache key. A key is
`v0-rust-<name>-<env hash>-<lock hash>`. The last hash covers Cargo.lock, every manifest and `.cargo/config.toml`, so an edit to
any Cargo.toml saves a new key beside the old one, here `b4987f66` beside `f61c49c3`. A run restores by exact key, then the
newest under the name and env hash, so an older generation is read only by a branch still on it, and everything evicts by
least recent use: at de671192 the compositors job found no earlier generation of its own cache (`No cache found`, 6 min 00 s
of building) and no nightly key is listed at all, which the limit explains though the listing can't prove it. A new `prune-caches` job on the schedule deletes all but the newest of each name, the only job
with `actions: write`. Names are compared within one ref, since a newer cache on a branch must not take main's, which every
branch reads. `--dry-run` against today's cache names 7 entries, 4,647 MiB, leaving 5.1 GiB. A branch still on an older
lock falls back to the newest generation and rebuilds what differs, as any new branch does.

(2026-11-01) Whether keys could share a cache. lock-vm passed `cache-save: false` under its own job's key, so nothing ever wrote
what it reads: `No cache found`, and 13 min 37 s of its 24 building. It now reads `test` without saving, the same debug profile
and environment, and the key string `v0-rust-test-...` that the test job already writes. That merges no saved cache, so the
test job's content does not change, and cargo rebuilds a unit whose features differ. Merging the keys that save stays out:
lint, test, timing, release, wasm, eval and site differ by profile, target or workspace, so one key would hold the sum, restore
it into every job, and be written by whichever job finished first with only its own units. compositors could read `test`
the same way, but it saves a cache of its own, which pruning should now leave in place, so it stays as it is until a run shows
otherwise. The 10 GB limit is unchanged.

(2026-11-01) Measured on this branch, run 41326056081 at 4dc65029, all jobs green in 22 min, against de671192's run. Package
restored `v0-rust-release-Linux-x64-63ec8b6c-b4987f66` and compiled 167 crates, not 494: its two release builds went from
14 min 6 s to 10 min 21 s and the job from 19 to 14 min, and smoke.sh passed on the result; that time did not hold on the image, as "package on the image" below records. lock-vm restored the test key and

(2026-11-01) One image for GitHub and the laptop. The reason is one pinned environment, not time. GitHub's jobs installed apt packages on the runner, fresh each run, while the laptop ran the Dockerfile's image, frozen until the file changes, so pixel references could break on one side only. The Dockerfile's base is pinned by digest, and CI publishes it at `ghcr.io/jakeb-grant/strand-ci:<hash of the Dockerfile>` the first time a run needs it. `image` looks with no registry login; `image-publish`, the only job with `packages: write`, always runs so later jobs need no status-function `if` (a skipped ancestor would skip deploy and release by default). A registry error during its check fails rather than guessing absence; GHCR's `denied` for a package that doesn't exist yet counts as absent, since a token that truly can't write fails at the push and overwrites nothing. A fork's pull request skips publishing, and `run.sh` builds locally when the registry says the tag is absent, so a fork's own Dockerfile should still work with no write access, though no pull request has run yet ("What has not run on GitHub" below). Jobs run through `run.sh` rather than `container:`, which is what the laptop proves daily: the same mounts and env, though not the same uid (1001 on the runner, 1000 here, the difference e7f52558 had to fix).

## docs-sweep

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: the Start, Help, home and playground claims quote what they cite, and three sentences change.** Every `path:line` source for these pages becomes a snippet, chosen by reading the page sentence against the code, and proofs that named a test which did not test the sentence now name one that does: "save all" is `save_all_is_one_batch`, not the reload fuzz. Edge: `publish.sh` publishes nothing when `main` has moved on, so "every push that passes CI replaces it" was too strong, and the page now says a newer push wins. Root: `--force` also lets the script run as root, which "will not run as root" left out, so the page says so; the code stands. Hyprland: Lua is Hyprland's only kind of config from 0.57, not 0.56 as laptop-resilience (2026-10-09) wrote; hyprlang is deprecated in the 0.56 wiki and 0.56.2 still has the legacy parser (`keyword can't work with non-legacy parsers`), and the matrix image's 0.57.0 binary holds no `hyprland.conf`.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: `on activate` is documented as what it does.** The reference said it runs when "clicked", and a pointer's click fires `Activate` only on a `list`'s row (`Router::button`); spec.md 6.7 never promised otherwise, so the code stands and the schema, keys.md and guide level 4 say so. `a_pointers_click_runs_no_activate_off_a_list_row` holds it. Hyprland's versions: its Lua config is 0.55 and later (running.md) and its only config from 0.57 (see the claims migration below); `strand compositor-rules` prints 0.56's `hl.layer_rule`, the version it was tested on, and stands. README's bar keeps `pad: 0, 12`: it is design.md's hello bar word for word and the picture's source (`eval/scenarios/docs/hello.scn`), while `strand new`'s template is the guide's first step, so the difference is meant. performance.md's sentence on budgets moves into repo-only, the page's place for what the project holds itself to.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: a claim's source can quote what it cites.** `site/claims.toml` held about 526 `file:line` sources and the build checked only that the line was in range, so a sampled 108 showed nearly every `docs/spec.md` and `builtin.schema` citation landing on unrelated text. `path "snippet"` fails the build, naming the claim, when the words are not in the file. It is a string like every other source, not a table, so `source` keeps one shape and removes no form that works; a TOML literal string (`'path "snippet"'`) spares the escaping. The path ends at the first ` "`, and the check runs before the `#` and `:line` forms, so a snippet can hold quotes, `#` and `:12`. Whitespace runs count as one space, as they do for `text`, so rewrapping a paragraph doesn't fail a citation. A snippet needs 8 characters because a shorter one turns up by chance and would rot as quietly as a line number. Uniqueness isn't asked: the snippet has to be there, which is what the problem needs, and a reader searches for the rest. `path:line` passes while the migration runs page by page, and `LINE_SOURCES` in `claims.rs` turns it into an error once no entry uses it; the tests hold both settings, so flipping it touches only the constant. (Superseded in 2026-11-01: docs-sweep, "the build rejects a `path:line` source", on `path:line` and `LINE_SOURCES` only.)

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: the Concepts and Tools claims quote what they cite, and one sentence changes.** Every `path:line` source for `site/concepts/**` and `site/tools/**` becomes a snippet, chosen by reading the page sentence against the code, and a proof that said only "read" names the test that holds the sentence where there is one: "keeps running the last good version" is `a_broken_file_is_held_back_and_the_last_good_tree_stays`, not the reload fuzz. `layout.md` called `ch` the width of a character in the node's font; `dim` takes `1ch` as `CH_EM`, 0.6 of the font size, with nothing measured, so the page says that and the code stands. Four claims keep a plain path, since no text in the repository says them: that it ships no editor plugin (`git ls-files`), the two Helix and Neovim configs (run in Arch, 2026-10-26), and the 28 services, a count of the reference's sections. Arch's `helix` binary is an outside fact, rerun 2026-11-01, cited to the Arch image it ran on.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: the how-to claims quote what they cite, and one sentence changes.** Every source for `site/how-to/**` becomes a snippet, chosen by reading the page sentence against the code, so a citation of the site's own page or of a whole file goes. A proof saying only "read", or naming a test beside the point, now names the test that holds the sentence where there is one: a search keeping its last result is `coalesce_covers_a_pending_async`, not `await_waits_for_a_pending_load`, and the last written claim winning is `the_last_written_active_claim_wins`. `calendar-popup.md` said the guide's clock had one `when` added; it also has `id: cal`, which that `when` reads, so the page says both.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: the build rejects a `path:line` source.** The migration left no `path:line` or `path:first-last` in `site/claims.toml`, so `check_source` now fails on either form, naming the claim and asking for a quote, even when the line is in range or the file is gone. `LINE_SOURCES` is removed, not left `false`: a switch nothing can turn back on is one more thing to read. A snippet or heading holding `:12` still passes, and so does a path with a colon before its `#heading`. This commit also takes the how-to migration's ledger hunks and `calendar-popup.md`'s sentence, because the switch can't land over the 79 `path:line` sources the how-to pages and `surfaces.md` still had at its parent. The lock row's claim keeps the page's present words and takes the quote the uncommitted `screens:` rewording uses. The 42 claims for page text not yet committed stay out, with those pages.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: design.md's memory table is an estimate, and CI's gates are what is held.** It called the table's totals, 29–34 and 59–64 MB, the targets CI warns above, and CI warns at 42 and 76 MB (`COLD_PSS_TARGET_KB`, `COLD_FULL_SHELL_TARGET_KB`), so "about 30 MB" in its summary was a figure nothing held. The cold bar measures 41,269 kB (benchmarks.md), and speed beats size: these gates catch regressions, so nothing is re-based down to meet the old estimate. So the summary states the measurement, the paragraph states the gates as tripwires, and the table stays, labelled, for where the memory goes. Reason for amending design.md: no behaviour changes; it described gates that had moved.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: which `STRAND_*` names a doc lists.** Of the names in the tree, only those a shipped binary or a script reads as a variable are worth a table: development.md's "Environment variables". The test and bench knobs stay explained where they are read, and the constants that look like variables (`STRAND_NO_THP`, `STRAND_MIME`, `window.STRAND_WASM` and others) are named there once so nobody sets them. The site gains only `STRAND_ICON_THEME`: it is the one undocumented variable a user has a reason to set, since `STRAND_NO_CACHE` only gives up the last-good fallback, which deleting the directory does for one start.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: the crate graph is a list.** The drawing's columns read as `strand-core` depending on `strand-scene`, drew no `strand-text -> strand-scene`, left out `strand-gpu`, and said nothing depends on `strand-site`, which `strand-web` dev-depends on. Each crate now lists its dependencies, as `cargo metadata` has them. "strand-dev does not link the runtime" was loose: it links `strand-core` and `strand-compiler`, which `strand` shares, and none of `strand`, `strand-services`, `strand-render` or `strand-surface`, so architecture.md says that. **2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: review of the claims migration.** The build now rejects a source that is the claim's own page or `site/claims.toml`, in any form, since both hold the claim's words whatever is true; the migration had removed those citations and nothing kept them out. A bare path still passes, naming a directory or a file with nothing quoted from it: the negatives need bare paths, and a person reading the ledger sees one. Comment-only snippets stay allowed too: of 408 in `.rs` files 178 match only comments, and a comment is often the one place a behaviour is stated, so a rule against them would push people to quote code beside the point; a snippet that cites a comment about something else is fixed when found, as `run/logic.rs` was for an empty directory. A negative claim takes a plain path rather than a quote of something that only sits nearby, so "no alignment for one child alone" cites the schema and leaves the proof to its probe, and Hyprland's only-Lua claim drops the citation of this file, its evidence being the proof's check of the 0.57 package. `install.md` no longer says the `package` job runs on every push, and two snippets now read the same on `laptop/ci-speed`, which moves the apt list out of `ci.yml` and adds `needs:` to the job; they quote the Dockerfile and the job's lines that both branches keep. Snippets tie the site's build to the wording of files `affected` does not test it for, and `affected.sh` belongs to another stream, so CLAUDE.md says to run strand-site's build test after rewording a cited line.

"Return and space press once" held only for the press path. Return on a focused `input` or `list` has no repeat check, and `a_held_return_activates_an_input_and_a_list_again` shows holding it runs `on activate` again with each repeat, so keys.md says that and the test pins it. That is what the code does, not a choice: spec.md's "A repeat does nothing" sits in the sentence about a press and sets those two aside, and whether a held Return should re-run a launcher's `on activate` is left open for the owner. keys.md's `list` row now says the row is selected and `on click` then `on activate` run, and no longer orders the selection against the click, since spec.md orders only those two. The hello bar's line in design.md now matches the README's. A source's path is refused with a `.` or empty part as well as a `..`, so the own-page and ledger check, which compares strings, sees one spelling of each path.

**2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: review round 3.** "Keeps" in surfaces.md now has one meaning: a panel centred on both axes does not span, and it does keep with a `~`, since `keeps` in specs.rs tests no anchor; the old wording read as if such a panel stayed at its content's size. keys.md's first row names `slider` and `segmented`, because a key `slider_key` or `segmented_key` does not take falls through to a press, and `return_and_space_press_a_slider_and_a_segmented` now holds that. **2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: Hyprland's versions are read from its tags, and the help follows.** `strand compositor-rules` said "Hyprland 0.56's Lua config" where running.md said 0.55 and later, and two comments in `wm/hyprland.rs` still said Lua is the only kind from 0.56, which this track had already corrected to 0.57 in decisions.md alone. The tags settle it: v0.54.3 has only `example/hyprland.conf`, v0.55.0 and v0.56.0 have `src/config/lua` beside `src/config/legacy` (and `hl.layer_rule` with `blur`, `blur_popups` and `ignore_alpha`), and v0.57.0 has no `src/config/legacy`. **2026-11-01 · docs-sweep: `affected` runs the site's build test for a file the ledger cites.** Quoting a line ties the site's build to its words, and `affected` looked only at `docs/` and `site/`, so a reworded comment failed at the final `site` step. It reads the paths from the `source` lines (a list here would rot as the ledger does) and adds the pseudo-target `strand-site:build`, as `eval` is one, with `--list` naming the files that brought it in. Only that test runs, not strand-site's suite, and not when strand-site is picked anyway. A changed file is enough: asking whether a quoted line changed would need the build's own check, and that check is what runs. It replaces CLAUDE.md's note to run the test by hand, which the review of the claims migration added.

## robustness

**2026-11-01 · robustness: one press of Return is one `on activate`, on an `input` and a `list` as on a `button`.** The owner's decision. Holding Return in a launcher ran its row's `on activate` at the repeat rate, so a press that launched an app launched several, while a `button` beside it already ignored repeats; the difference held no use. `a_held_return_activates_an_input_and_a_list_once` failed against the old router with `left: 4.0, right: 1.0` (three repeats fired) and passes now, for an `input`, a `list` and an `input` with a `nav:` list, on Return and KP_Enter. The repeat is spent rather than passed on, so nothing further down hears it as a key to type. Arrow keys, Page keys, typing and a held space on a `scroll` or `list` keep repeating (`only_return_stops_at_the_press`, `space_pages_a_focused_scroll`, `space_pages_a_focused_list`), a claim on the key still hears repeats and `on key(k)` still sees them with `k.repeat`. A shell wanting repeated activation uses a timer. `node.activate()` from code is unchanged.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: strand's live-pipeline tests say whether a helper is installed.** `strand_auth::default_helper` looks beside the test binary, where `strand-auth` is only if something else built it into this target, and the laptop rule deletes target/ after each task. With none, `helper_notice` keeps a notice that every new watcher hears first, so `lock_edits_wait_for_the_unlock_and_then_land`, `an_unlock_replay_keeps_the_newer_errors` and `a_replayed_hard_reload_reports_the_newer_errors` read it where they expected the save's event. The logic thread now asks `lock::helper_installed`, which a test's thread can answer (`HELPER_ON_THIS_THREAD`, in test builds only, beside `QUIET_ON_THIS_THREAD`), and `spawn_live` answers yes. Rejected: skipping notice events in those tests' `watch`, which would also hide a notice they should fail on, and building the helper first in `affected`, which leaves the tests depending on the build. The wiring the three no longer exercise is `a_watcher_hears_of_a_missing_helper_only_without_one`, both ways. Measured on a target directory that did not exist: every test of strand passed, `strand-auth` not built.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: `popup-still-pose` survived because a later fix masked it, not because the code moved; `insert-above-view` is regenerated as the same bug.** The patch's target hasn't moved: `Animator::deferred` still reads `exits_due`, and with it gone the product still has the bug. Since 59c95241 (hit-through), `Renderer::update` keeps a surface dirty while its hit boxes differ, and the leaving card's hit box was enough to paint the frame that ends the exit, so the scenario and `an_exit_that_moves_nothing_still_ends_under_the_host_loop` passed with the fix reverted. That made the eval matrix red from then on (41299115146, 41375492987). The scenario's `#card` is now `hit: none`: nothing else keeps its surface dirty, so `deferred` alone decides. With the patch applied it fails with `twin:#card` and `expect` as `mutants.txt` already asked, the patch and that line's expectation unchanged, and the unit test has `hit: none` cases that fail under the patch at `a frame ends the exit (close: false, inert: true)`. The scenario text changed, so its recording was approved again: the only recording line that differs is the popup's `i=0,0,120,40` becoming `i=none`, what `hit: none` asks. Rejected: changing the patch to also revert the hit boxes, which would test a different bug. `insert-above-view.patch` stopped applying when 510e50c0 wrapped the anchor's line for columns; regenerated from today's `list.rs`, it zeroes the same `measured_above` term on the one-column path the scenario takes.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: `the_launcher_filters_selects_and_closes` timed out because a read in the middle of a damage line counted a surface that wasn't there.** Run 41339225373 waited 10 s for `surface_count() > surfaces` while its log showed the launcher's surface drawn. Reading the code gives the race: `eprintln!` writes each piece of its format on its own, and the test takes its snapshot while the bars are still painting (0.187 s and 0.188 s in a local timeline). A scratch writer with that format and a reader of the file saw 690 of 2,371 reads end exactly at `strand: damage surface=`. That partial line's first token `surface=` is a third surface, so the snapshot was 3, the launcher made the real count 3, and `3 > 3` never held. `demo.rs::damage_lines` had already met this and read whole lines only. Fixed at both ends: strand writes a damage line in one write, for all eight test files that read them, and `Desk` counts whole lines (`a_line_still_being_written_is_no_surface`, seen failing with `left: 3, right: 2` on the old reading). It has not been reproduced end to end, since the window is a few microseconds on a run that fails rarely, so should it come back the test now says more: the panic gives the counts before and now and the surfaces, a timeline of the test's steps and strand's lines with times, and a failed test keeps `sway.log`, `timed.log` and `strand.log` in `target/acceptance/logs/<tag>/`, which CI uploads.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: the glitch report's 2 px drift at 236,38 was the replay comparing a tick before the live frame.** Eval step 7 said DRIFTED in five runs, in the writes session's Top bar, with no frames kept. The bar's graph has 3 s columns, and a report landing just after a boundary reproduced it: with a scratch wait that sends `strand report` at a chosen phase of the boot clock, the deltas -22, -16, -10 and -8 ms of 43 swept (-24 to +60) gave exactly `2 differ past 6 from the live frame, in 1x2 at 236,38`. In all four the live shell drew the new column 6.1 to 6.8 ms before the boundary (a tick is reached half a frame early, 8.3 ms), 26 to 31 ms before the report: for -10, at 263.22 ticks on the replay's clock, with the boundary at 263.63. The replay reached that column at tick 264, and `frame_for` looked no further than tick 263, the nearest, which held it to the bar's paint before that, tick 84. A live frame more than two periods before the report had the at-rest rule's two ticks and was never short, so the window was about two frames in every 3 s column, which fits how rarely it failed. `frame_for` now takes the first tick at or after a live frame drawn that close to the report: what the frame shows is of its time or later, so a tick before it can only be short. Rejected: tolerating a column in the verdict, as graph-flake did, since a moved column should still be named. `STEP_FRAMES` and the tolerances stay, with the sum spelled again: under a frame for that tick, which the live frame's lead mostly cancels. Measured: `a_live_frame_near_the_report_is_held_to_the_tick_after_it` failed on the old pick with `left: 1738, right: 1739`; after the fix 40 of 40 sweep runs between -30 and -2 ms were VERIFIED, and 44 of 45 with a spinning process per core. The 45th, delta -20 under load, is another bug and is left open here (the third review's entry has its cause): a press replayed before a service's answer (`service write audio.sink.muted = true live, the replay wrote false`, 4 divergences from -4.22 s on), its verdict drifted by a whole mute chip rather than by pixels of the graph. One edge stays: `frame_for` still caps its tick at the one before the report's, so a live frame within about a tick of the report can be held short the same way. It wasn't seen in the sweep, which covered -30 to -2 ms, and the counts above are local runs. A session that fails now leaves its frames in `target/eval/ci/report-view-failed/`, in the `eval-report` artifact, seen with a forced failure: 680 KiB for one session.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: the debug workspace tests run through cargo-nextest 0.9.148.** `cargo test --workspace` ran 264 binaries one after another. 0.9.148 is the newest release at least two weeks old (published 2026-10-08; 0.9.149 of 2026-10-20 was 12 days old), a prebuilt checked by its sha256 in the image. The workspace step is `scripts/container/workspace-tests.sh`, used by ci.yml and ci.sh alike, with `not (test(random_edits_through_five_save_styles) or test(a_hundred_reloads_reconnect_and_restart_nothing))`: libtest's `--skip` and nextest's `test()` both match a substring. Doc-tests stay `cargo test --doc --workspace`. Everything else keeps its runner, on purpose. `strand-services --no-default-features --lib`, `strand-auth --features faults` and `presented_quiet` are one crate's build with other features, so nextest's scheduling has nothing to gain; `reloads` and the fuzzer's short run want `--nocapture`, and the fuzzer `--test-threads=1` under `tests-ran.sh`. The `budgets`, `acceptance`, `timing`, `eval` and `nightly` jobs measure memory and time in a process laid out as they rest on, and speed is no reason to move a gate. `tests-ran.sh` and `gate-misses.sh` stay with those `cargo test` steps, the only ones they ever read; nextest's own `--no-tests` default fails a run with nothing to run, and `nextest-summary.sh` fails on a missing or empty junit file. No target sets `harness = false` but four `[[bench]]`s (`graph`, `keyed`, `persist`, `clock_tick`), which `cargo test` doesn't run either.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: what each test's lock became under a process per test.** A static `Mutex` keeps nothing apart once no two tests share a process, so every one was read for what it guards. Nearly all guard the process's own state, which a process per test now keeps apart by construction; each directory they use is `tempfile`'s or carries the pid, so two processes can't meet there.

| Test file | What it protects | What replaces it |
|---|---|---|
| strand-services `tests/apps.rs` `SERIAL` | `apps`' config static, `XDG_ACTIVATION_TOKEN`, `STRAND_SOCKET`, `GREETD_SOCK` set with `set_var` | Process per test: both are the process's. Directories carry the pid |
| strand-services `tests/audio_levels.rs` `SERIAL` | the process's device asks (`ASKED`) | Process per test. Each test's PipeWire is its own |
| strand-services `tests/clipboard.rs` `SERIAL` | the process's display and state directory | Process per test; `tempfile` state, its own sway |
| strand-services `tests/contract.rs` `SERIAL`, `CMDS`, `SEEN`, `NOTIFIED`, `GATED`, `DEAF` | one global script for the probe service | Process per test |
| strand-services `tests/greetd.rs`, `tests/polkit.rs` `LOCK` | `greetd::configure`, `polkit::configure`, process-wide | Process per test; `tempfile` sockets, private buses |
| strand-services `tests/history.rs` `SERIAL`, `CPU_SERIAL` | the `TICKS` counter, `cpu::samples`, `cpu::rebases` | Process per test: counters of the process |
| strand-services `tests/idle_after.rs`, `tests/outputs.rs` `SERIAL` | the process-wide display | Process per test; each starts its own sway |
| strand-services `tests/keyboard.rs` `SERIAL` | config, focused report, read counter | Process per test |
| strand-services `tests/notifications.rs` `serial()` | the history config, the stopped server's last save (`WRITTEN`) | Process per test; `tempfile` history |
| strand-services `tests/wm_services.rs` `SERIAL` | the compositor config | Process per test; fake Hyprland per test |
| strand-services `src/audio/service.rs` `ASKS` | the level asks' table, lapsed by a given `now` | Process per test |
| strand `src/services/mod.rs` `APPS_SERIAL`, `WIFI_SERIAL` | apps' config, the wifi body's log | Process per test |
| strand-icons `src/lib.rs` `SERIAL` | base directories and desktop theme, process-wide | Process per test; root carries the pid |
| strand-render `tests/fonts.rs` `SERIAL` | the same font installed and removed; `FONTCONFIG_FILE` once per process | Process per test: `strand-fonts-<pid>` is each test's own |
| strand-theme `tests/decode.rs` `SERIAL` | the counting allocator's peak | Process per test: nothing else allocates in it |
| strand-web `tests/live.rs` `SERIAL` | the process's icon lookup | Process per test |
| strand-render `tests/theme_swap_bench.rs` `TURNS` | timed benches alone, a release-only lock (`turn()` returns `None` in debug, where the gates check shape at sixteen times the budget) | Nothing in debug, as before; the `timing` job stays on `cargo test` and keeps it |
| strand `tests/budgets.rs` `SERIAL` | the shells' idle windows from each other's directories | Test group `budgets`, `max-threads = 1`, for the binary; the `budgets` job stays on `cargo test --test-threads=1` and keeps it |
| strand `tests/budgets.rs` `Bare` (no lock: found failing, 2 of 2 runs) | `an_open_window_costs_what_a_panel_does` kept its config in `/tmp`, whose deletions by every other binary woke the watcher through the ancestors it watches (`never settled`, `an open window woke strand`) | The config in `strand_test_support::dir::own_dir`, the sockets in a `ShortDir`. Passing since |
| `set_var`: strand-core `tests/state_dir.rs`, strand-render `tests/images.rs` and `tests/fonts.rs`, strand-surface `tests/compose.rs` | the process's environment, set before use | Process per test: never seen by another test |
| Shared fixed paths: `target/acceptance`, `target/newcomer` (written on a failure only, one binary each); `CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR/anim_bench`, `/site` (one binary each, as parallel as before); `strand-services-<name>` (`own_dir`, pid below) | a directory two binaries could meet in | None do. `/dev/shm`: `tempfile_in` in strand-watch; bench.rs and the fuzzer's are skipped or `#[ignore]`d in this step |
| Ports and bus names | `TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")` everywhere; bus names on private buses | Nothing shared |
| `$HOME` (`/tmp/home`) | what a shell or a tool writes by default | Read after a whole run: Mesa's shader cache alone, safe across processes |
| Other watchers: `gpu_idle`, `presented_quiet`, `demo`'s budget, `budgets`' `Setup`, `services` | their configs sit below their own `HOME`, and the watcher stops there, so `/tmp` and the target's `tmp` aren't watched | Nothing needed |

The opposite, tests that lean on another test's work in one process: `static` fixtures (`FILES` in animated.rs, `DIRS` in config_icons.rs, `DIR` in images.rs and fonts.rs, `CAPTURE` in introspect's connection.rs, `SESSION` in auth.rs, `SCHEMA`s in the libraries) are `OnceLock`s made on first use, so each test makes its own, slower by little and right. `BUILT` in `m5/plugin.rs` builds the plugin examples only when they're stale; a package or workspace run has built them, and cargo's lock on the target serialises the rare nested build. No test reads what another test wrote, and none reads a `Barrier` with another test. Each test running in its own process leaves more of its `OnceLock` directories in `/tmp` (113 after a whole run), which go with the container. The retries, the parallelism and the timeout are below.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: `strand-test-support`, on std alone.** Twenty-one test files carried a headless sway spawn, with the same nine environment lines and the same hand-written `prctl`; fifteen carried the same scan for its sockets, and eleven services tests the same pumped `until`. **2026-11-01 · robustness: every wall-clock assertion in the tests is a budget, a count, a named deadline or a later event.** Each comparison of `elapsed()`, `Instant` or `Duration` in an assert was read and put in one of four classes. (b) A proxy for "did no extra work" becomes a count of that work, shown failing by a temporary mutation that does the extra work. (c) A deadline saying something didn't hang stays generous and names what it waited for. (d) "This doesn't happen within a time" waits for a later event where the code gives one. No budget moved, every class (a) limit stayed; the bounds of classes (c) and (d) that tell two outcomes apart or say something didn't hang did move, and each such row says from what to what (`present`'s 50 ms to 500 ms, `network.rs`'s 2,500 ms to 30 s, `outputs.rs`'s 3 s to 30 s, `connection.rs`'s question). **2026-11-01 · robustness: a nightly `stress` job in ci.yml, on nextest's stress mode.** The pinned 0.9.148 has `--stress-count`, which carries on past a failing iteration under `fail-fast = false` and writes every iteration's results to one junit file as `binary@stress-N` (seen with a scratch test failing half its runs and one aborting: 5 of 12 iterations failed, all counted), so rates come straight from the file and no loop is needed. It has no shuffle: tests always start in the same order. So each block picks from the seed the `-j` (1, 1.5 or 2 per core), the spinning processes beside the tests (0.5, 1 or 2 per core) and one to three hash partitions in a shuffled order, which changes what runs beside what; a process per test leaves little else an order could change. The job lives in ci.yml, not a workflow of its own, because GitHub dispatches only a workflow already on the default branch, so a new file couldn't have been run from this branch before merging; it also gets `image-publish` for free. Selection by the record: three blocks in four are the binaries talking to a compositor or a bus, every `strand` binary, the compiler's reloads, and the tests named in laptop-flakes, m6-flakes and graph-flake (1,394 tests, a name matching nothing failing the run), the fourth the whole workspace (3,873). Left out: `strand::budgets`, memory measured one shell at a time, and the reload fuzzer, whose saves are timed and which the `nightly` job runs alone. A wall-clock gate under load says nothing, so a miss, judged as `gate-misses.sh` judges one, is listed apart and doesn't fail the run. Three hours of blocks: no block starts that the last of its tier says would overrun, the job's bound is 270 minutes, and a hang costs 15 minutes rather than 40 (`[profile.stress]`, no retries, which `nextest-filters.sh` now holds for every profile but `ci`). Seen locally at 16 spinners beside `-j 16` then `-j 32`: 10,534 test runs in 16 minutes, 12 tests failing, two gates listed apart. It holds up no push: deploy and release name their jobs and a push doesn't run this one.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: a red night files one issue.** What runs only at night has no push to go red on, and GitHub's mail for a scheduled run goes only to whoever last edited the cron line, if their settings ask. So `nightly-red` (`scripts/container/nightly-red.sh`) keeps one open issue labelled `nightly-red`, a comment per red night with the jobs and the stress summary, closed by hand once triaged. It watches `image`, `image-publish`, `compositors`, `lock-vm`, `nightly`, `stress`, `validation` and `prune-caches`, and files on `failure` or `cancelled`, on schedule, and on a dispatch with `report_red=true`; `eval-matrix.yml` has the same job for its matrix and mutants. They are the only jobs writing issues.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: Vulkan validation nightly, on Ubuntu's layer 1.3.275, off the loader's path.** wgpu asks for `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation` in any debug build, by name, where the loader can find it, so installing the package plainly would have put every debug GPU test under the layer, gates included. The manifest moves to `/opt/vulkan-validation`, which only `VK_ADD_LAYER_PATH` reaches; `the_layer_stays_off_unless_asked_for`, in the normal workspace run, fails if it comes back. A newer layer from LunarG's SDK was not tried: running a downloaded binary was refused here, so what the entries below say of the layer holds for 1.3.275.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: a validation error fails through the layer's own trap, set in a settings file.** Proved before anything else, and it took three tries. wgpu's messenger only reaches `log`, which fails nothing: a raw `vkCreateBuffer` of size 0 through wgpu's device was reported (`VUID-VkBufferCreateInfo-size-00912`) and the test passed. `VK_LAYER_DEBUG_ACTION` and `VK_KHRONOS_VALIDATION_DEBUG_ACTION` in the environment did nothing on 1.3.275; the same test still passed. `khronos_validation.debug_action = VK_DBG_LAYER_ACTION_LOG_MSG,VK_DBG_LAYER_ACTION_BREAK` in a file named by `VK_LAYER_SETTINGS_PATH` exits 133, SIGTRAP, with wgpu's messenger still on, and needs no product code. `tests/validation.rs` keeps that bad call, ignored, and each night's first steps require it to trap, and require strand's GPU thread to have the layer mapped, or the job fails saying it can't fail.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: one hazard allowed by its exact accesses, not its ID.** On 117 GPU tests the layer reports one thing: `SYNC-HAZARD-READ-AFTER-WRITE`, 14 times, every one a vertex read against an image layout transition. vello_gpu makes a mapped vertex buffer per clear (`create_buffer_init`, "Clear Rects"), lavapipe has one memory type, so the allocator can reuse memory a freed `Layer Intermediate Texture` had, and the layer holds that texture's last transition against the buffer. wgpu and vello_gpu make those calls; strand makes no Vulkan call. A buffer and an image can only meet in the layer's tracking by sharing memory, which is this reading's basis; it wasn't shown by another allocator. That ID is shared by every read-after-write hazard, so `message_id_filter` on it would be a category. So there are two passes: `core`, `validate_sync = false`, trapping on everything, and `sync`, logging only, where `validation-summary.py` fails any message other than that (ID, submitted access, prior access). wgpu turns synchronization validation on whenever the layer offers it, whatever its flags say, so `WGPU_VALIDATION=0` wouldn't have separated them, and the file's setting does.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: a crash at exit under the layer is counted, not failed.** 9 to 13 of 117 tests under `core` and about 3 under `sync` end in SIGSEGV after libtest printed `test result: ok. 1 passed`, and only with the layer. Two backtraces show why: the crash is inside the layer, under `strand_gpu::thread::run` dropping its `Device`, in `vkQueueWaitIdle` and in `destroy_bind_group_layout`: the process is exiting and the layer's statics go while the detached GPU thread is still destroying its device. `Gpu`'s Drop detaches on purpose, so a slow driver never blocks the main thread, and without the layer nothing crashes (213 of 213 by nextest on the same selection). The summary counts these and fails a SIGSEGV before that line.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: what runs under the layer.** `strand-gpu` but `start_cost`, `strand-render`'s `gpu`, `gpu_effects` and `inspect`, the one report test that draws on the GPU in a child `strand run`, and `presented_quiet` alone (`--workspace` turns on `eval-hooks`, which draws every frame). Not `strand::budgets`, `demo`, `services`, `gpu_idle` or the timing benches, which hold memory or wall-clock numbers. Excluding pixel comparisons by test would have left few draws to check, so `pixel_gates_held` turns them off in a process that has the layer mapped, reading `/proc/self/maps` rather than a variable so that nothing else can turn a gate off; `differ` keeps the checks that a frame changed at all. Eval's GPU leg isn't here: it draws through the same `strand_gpu` and its checks are pixels, and it would add a second workspace's build.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: pushes test a pinned Arch, nights test today's.** This supersedes in part wave4-exit-ci's "the job tracks upstream on purpose": a compositor's package update could fail any push, whatever it changed, so tracking moves to the nights, where a new release turns one red and files the issue. `Dockerfile.matrix` is a base by digest and the archive's snapshot of 2026-11-01. The date comes from the nightly compositors job of run 41433159724 (2026-11-02, green), the digest from that job's own pull, and the archive's 11-02 wasn't there yet (404). The snapshot installs what that run reported: sway 1:1.12-4, niri 26.04-1, hyprland 0.57.0-1, labwc 0.20.2-1, grim 1.5.0-2, seatd 0.9.3-1, mesa 1:26.2.6-1. `-Syyuu` so a base newer than the snapshot moves down to it. The image is published to ghcr once per hash, as the CI image is, through the same two scripts (`STRAND_IMAGE_FILE`): built on every push it would have been an archive.archlinux.org outage failing the pushes the pin is there to protect, and the image is 2 GB from that one server. `compositor-matrix-ci.sh` leaves a pinned image's packages alone (`MATRIX_PINNED`), and its summary and errors say which packages they ran on. `scripts/release/smoke.sh`'s `archlinux:latest` stays: it tests the installer against what users of Arch have today, and changes no compositor, though an Arch update can fail it on a push.

**2026-11-01 · robustness: the pin can't go stale unseen.** The nightly job's `matrix-pin.sh check` says the pin's age in the summary and fails past 30 days, which files the issue; a push never waits on it. Thirty days, since a green night on today's packages says a refresh would pass, and the issue then asks for one a month at most. `matrix-pin.sh refresh` rewrites the date and the digest, and refuses a date the archive lacks; `matrix.sh` and a push then prove it. It isn't automatic: a refresh is a change to what every push tests, which a person or an agent should watch once.

**2026-11-02 · robustness: what the stress runs found and fixed.** Five tests failed under load for reasons the load only exposed. (1) `sways_mode_window_rects_and_moves` (2/20 beside 16 spinners; 1/2 on GitHub): the first half was the test reading the mirror once, but with the test waiting it still failed 2/60 at its deadline, since nothing tells the adapter when sway has laid a window out: the window event precedes the transaction, whose wait for a client runs up to 200 ms, and the read it prompted kept `y 0, height 720` against the tree's `y 25, height 695` until the next event. `wm::sway` reads the tree again 300 ms after a read an event prompted, until a read changes nothing: a product bug, a window's `rect` wrong for as long as nothing else happened; 0/200 after. It costs one `get_tree` per burst. **2026-11-02 · robustness: a file rewritten without pause outside the config directories is never read torn.** `a_watched_file_rewritten_in_place_every_5_ms_is_reported` failed 4 of 28 on the stress night of 1947934e with "a torn read". Outside the config directories a directory is watched for completed writes only (decisions.md, "`MODIFY` only in config directories"), so the only guard against reading an in-place save between its truncation and its bytes is the file's modification time, and that guard is waived once the file has been due for `max_delay`, so a file rewritten faster than the quiet period is read at all. A writer kept off the CPU between its `O_TRUNC` and its `write` at that moment was read empty, as architecture.md allowed for a writer pausing over 15 ms. Now a watched file put off twice running gives its directory `MODIFY` (`Core::churning`), its read is not forced until `max_delay` after that, so any truncation from then on holds it as in a config directory, and the directory goes back to completed writes 2 s after the file was last touched, at a flush the deadline wakes for. One save put off once is no churn, so `~/Downloads` and the like keep one wakeup per closed file. `a_directory_whose_file_is_rewritten_without_pause_hears_its_writes` drives it with a stubbed backend and fails with the upgrade off or the force left at the first put-off. The race didn't show locally: 200 runs, 8 at a time beside 8 spinners on two cores, failed 0 with and without the fix, so the GitHub rate is the evidence and the next nights confirm it.

## compositor-motion

**2026-11-03 · compositor-motion: Hyprland's layer animations are turned off by a rule `strand compositor-rules` prints, not avoided by keeping surfaces mapped.** Hyprland fades a layer surface in as it maps and out as it unmaps, so a launcher that morphs out of a bar showed both surfaces at once, the launcher half transparent (the owner's session, 2026-11-03; on nested Hyprland 0.57.0, a `no_anim` rule made it one box widening). No protocol lets a client opt out: `hyprland-surface-v1` sets only opacity and a visible region, `no_anim` comes only from rules, and an unmap by a null buffer fades too (Hyprland v0.57.1 `src/protocols/HyprlandSurface.cpp`, `src/desktop/view/LayerSurface.cpp`). Shells meet it two ways. end-4's, Noctalia and DankMaterialShell map a surface per open and ship the rule (Noctalia's docs: so they "do not interfere with Noctalia's own animations"). caelestia, and the owner's old Quickshell config, keep one full-screen surface per output mapped and animate inside it. Quickshell's `visible: false` and gtk-layer-shell's hide destroy the surface. Strand takes the rule. Keeping every panel mapped while closed would put a surface per panel on every output, hand the keyboard over by hand (Hyprland gives a mapped surface focus only on a switch to `exclusive`), and a surface kept on `overlay` stops Hyprland's direct scanout and tearing for a fullscreen client (`src/output/Monitor.cpp`). `strand compositor-rules` prints the rule first, always, matching `^strand-.*$`: Hyprland matches a rule's pattern against the whole namespace (`RE2::FullMatch`, `src/desktop/rule/matchEngine/RegexMatchEngine.cpp`), so `^strand-` matched nothing, which is how the owner's first rule failed. It covers scrims and click-away catchers too. niri needs none: its layer surfaces have no open or close animation (niri a8562a1, `src/layer/mapped.rs`), and sway and labwc animate none. The site's concepts page "Strand and your compositor" says this for users. Rejected for now: keeping surfaces mapped (above; the way to go if Strand must look the same with no rule anywhere); pushing the rule over Hyprland's IPC at run time (Hyprland only, and it changes the session's config behind the user's back).
