## wifi-forget

**2026-11-04 · wifi-forget: an access point says whether it is saved (`known`) and can be forgotten (`forget()`), and `network.join(ssid, password)` joins a network by name, hidden ones included.** The owner's shell asks for a password only for a network that is not saved (a saved one joins with `connect()`), lets the user forget a network, and joins a hidden network, which no scan lists, from a name field. Both daemons expose each directly, so nothing is invented: NetworkManager's saved connections carry their SSID (`802-11-wireless.ssid`) and are deleted with `Settings.Connection.Delete`; iwd's networks name their `KnownNetwork`, which `Forget` drops; a hidden network is NetworkManager's `AddAndActivateConnection` of a connection marked `hidden` with no access point, and iwd's `Station.ConnectHiddenNetwork`. `known` over NetworkManager reads the saved connections while the access points are listed (as `connections` does while it is read) and follows their `NewConnection`/`ConnectionRemoved`, so nothing is polled and a closed menu wakes nothing; `connections` itself stays empty unless read. `forget()` deletes every connection saved for the SSID (NetworkManager keeps one per profile, and leaving one would leave the network known); one with nothing saved fails rather than doing nothing silently, as `down()` of a connection that is not up does. `join` reuses the network's saved connection when there is one (its password updated when one is given) rather than adding a second profile each time, which is what `connect()` already does; a new one is WPA personal with a password and open without, the common hidden cases (an enterprise network still needs its profile). Over iwd the hidden network's object exists only once iwd finds it, so its password is held by name and the agent reads the asked network's `Name`. `network.join`'s `password`, and only it, joins the arguments `check::secret_flow` lets a password reach: the allow-list now names a parameter, so a password passed as the `ssid` still warns. Tests: `saved_networks_are_known_and_forgotten`, `a_hidden_network_joins_by_name` (NetworkManager mock), `iwd_knows_saved_networks_and_forgets_them`, `iwd_joins_a_hidden_network_by_name` (iwd fake), `a_known_network_is_known_and_forgotten_through_it`, and the `secrets.rs` cases.

## bt-agent

**2026-11-04 · bt-agent: Strand is BlueZ's pairing agent while a config reads `bluetooth.request`.** A device that wants a PIN, a passkey or a confirmation could not pair through Strand: `d.pair()` relied on the system's agent, and a shell with none (most, on a bare compositor) failed every such device. The agent lives on the existing `bluetooth` service, not a new one: one BlueZ owner to follow, one object cache to name the asking device from, and the count of 28 services stays. It follows a `#[store(stream)]` field, `request`: Strand exports `org.bluez.Agent1` at `/dev/strand/bluetooth/agent` (network/iwd.rs's `/dev/strand/network/iwd` convention) on the shared system connection, the one `d.pair()` calls `Device1.Pair` on (BlueZ sends a pairing to the agent of `Pair`'s caller, else to the default agent), registers it as `KeyboardDisplay` and asks `RequestDefaultAgent`, only while a shown scope reads `request`, and unregisters and removes it when the last reader goes. A shell that never shows requests then never takes them (each would hang until BlueZ's timeout) and the system's agent keeps working for it, as polkit registers only while read. A top-level panel's `open:` is lowered in the file's scope, so a closed `panel Pair { open: bluetooth.request != null … }` keeps it registered (`a_closed_panels_open_holds_a_stream_field`); a config reading `request` only inside the dialog never registers, which the schema's doc says. Default agent: incoming pairings (a phone or keyboard starting it) and `AuthorizeService` reach only the default agent, writing a pairing dialog is opting in, and BlueZ keeps a stack of default agents, so blueman's or a desktop's gets it back when Strand unregisters. `KeyboardDisplay` because a shell both shows and types codes: BlueZ may then compare numbers with a phone, show a passkey for a keyboard, take one a display-only device shows, and ask a legacy PIN (bluetoothctl's default too). `AlreadyExists` counts as registered; any other refusal is one `cx.warn` diagnostic, tried again only when BlueZ restarts or a reader comes back, never on each signal, and a refused `RequestDefaultAgent` leaves the agent registered for the pairings Strand starts. A stopped store tears down on a task of its own (`TEARDOWN`), which the next run awaits before exporting; `Release` from BlueZ withdraws the request and sends no `UnregisterAgent`. Only BlueZ's current unique name is answered; any other caller is `org.bluez.Error.Rejected`. This supersedes m6-service-gaps 2026-10-15 ("Strand registers no pairing agent … an agent can be added later, additively"; it is additive) and the owner-testing settlement's "registers no pairing agent of its own"; `bluetooth` stays on BlueZ.

**2026-11-04 · bt-agent: one request, five kinds, answered by its own actions.** BlueZ's eight agent calls become `BluetoothRequest { device, kind, code, entered, service }` with `kind` one of `pin` (`RequestPinCode`), `passkey` (`RequestPasskey`), `display` (`DisplayPinCode` and `DisplayPasskey`: a code to type on the device, with `entered` its digits typed so far), `confirm` (`RequestConfirmation`, and `RequestAuthorization` with `code` "": nothing to compare) and `service` (`AuthorizeService`). A passkey shows as six digits, zero-padded, so a dialog shows what the device shows. `device` is a whole `BluetoothDevice` from BlueZ's objects, rebuilt at each publish so a name arriving later shows, and for a path not yet listed the address from `dev_AA_BB_…` with no name and `bluetooth-symbolic`. `service` is named from a small fixed English table of the SIG's 16-bit service classes on the base UUID (Audio Sink, Hands-Free, Human Interface Device and the rest in agent.rs), else the UUID as given: a UUID alone tells a user nothing. The actions are the record's, `r.respond(answer)`, `r.accept()` and `r.reject()` like `d.pair()`, not the service's like polkit's: the item a call carries says which request it answers, and it applies only when its address, kind, code and service are the shown request's (`entered` aside), so an answer typed for a request that went is dropped and wiped, never given to the next, and a `confirm` never accepts a code the user did not see, with no `seen` flag. `reject`, not polkit's `cancel`: it pairs with `accept`, it is BlueZ's `Rejected`, and a bare `bluetooth.cancel()` would read as cancelling anything. No queue and no `waiting`: BlueZ holds one request per agent (agent.c refuses a second with EBUSY), so a newer request means BlueZ moved on; it replaces the shown one, which is answered `Canceled`, except a `DisplayPasskey` for the device and code shown, which only updates `entered`. No new `busy`, `error` or `available` fields: an answer that does not fit (a PIN that is empty, over 16 bytes or holds a NUL, as BlueZ counts it, so the doc says bytes; a passkey that is not 1 to 6 ASCII digits) is the existing `bluetooth.failed(address, error)` and the request stays, a refused registration is a warning, and `bluetooth.available` keeps its meaning. No unkeyed record had actions before; the `Call` derive, the VM's item target and the checker took `BluetoothRequest`'s without a key, so the fallback of an `id` key was not needed. Two things the checker showed for examples: a state named `pin` is ambiguous with the variant `pin` where a `BluetoothRequestKind` is expected, so the docs bind `typed`; and `?.` does not carry along a chain, so a dialog reads `bluetooth.request?.device?.name`.

**2026-11-04 · bt-agent: when a request goes, and what refusing a shown code cancels.** A request goes when it is answered, when BlueZ cancels it, releases the agent or restarts, when the config stops reading `request`, and when the store stops; each of those but the answer replies `org.bluez.Error.Canceled`, the user's `reject()` `Rejected`. Every request is also withdrawn after 60 s (`REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, BlueZ's own agent timeout), so a lost `Cancel` cannot leave a dialog up. A `display` has no reply to wait for, so it also ends when its device becomes paired having been unpaired when asked (a bonded device pairing again from its side signals as paired all along), when its device goes once BlueZ had listed it (a display for a device not listed yet waits for it to appear, the minute the backstop), and when the shell's own pair or connect of its address ends. `reject()` of a `display` calls `Device1.CancelPairing` only while the shell's own `pair()` of that device runs, and otherwise only withdraws the request: BlueZ's `CancelPairing` cancels its caller's bonding request, and with none it removes the device's keys (device.c `cancel_pairing`, `btd_adapter_remove_bonding`), so refusing a paired keyboard's code would have forgotten it. A `connect()` creates no bonding request, so it is left out for the same reason; a pairing the device started goes on until the device ends it.

**2026-11-04 · bt-agent: a typed PIN is a password; `bluetooth` is not a secret service.** The answer is a `strand_auth::Password` from the call on (its Debug shows only a length, `an_answer_never_shows_in_debug`), wiped when dropped, and BlueZ's reply is built from a `Zeroizing` buffer; the copy zbus serialises is not Strand's to wipe. `check::secret_flow`'s `INTENDED` gains `("BluetoothRequest", "respond")`, matched on the owner and the name both, so a `from dbus` service's own `respond(pw)` still warns (`kept_or_sent`), and its help and design.md, spec.md 5.1 and the `input` doc name it. `bluetooth` stays out of `strand_services_schema::SECRET`: its device lists stay in glitch reports and replay, a typed answer never reaches the recorder because a call's arguments are never kept (record.rs), and a `display` or `confirm` code is recorded like any service text, being on screen anyway and single-use. `strand call` may answer a request, which makes a pairing scriptable; a single-use code in the process list for an instant is accepted. If the owner wants the codes out of reports, the way is a per-field redaction, which adds a concept.

**2026-11-04 · bt-agent: tested against dbusmock's `bluez5`, with BlueZ's calls to the agent made by the test.** crates/strand-services/tests/bluetooth_agent.rs starts python-dbusmock's `bluez5` template on a private bus (hci0, a paired Headphones, an unpaired Stranger), reads the registrations from its `AgentManager1` call log, and adds `Ask`/`Outcome` on `/` (polkit.rs's BEGIN/OUTCOME pattern): `Ask` calls a method of Strand's `org.bluez.Agent1` from BlueZ's own bus name and records how it ended; the probe that finds Strand's unique name by `Introspect` moved from polkit.rs to tests/support as `serving`. Not shown there: BlueZ routing a `Device1.Pair` to the agent its caller registered (the template never calls an agent itself), which needs a check by hand on real hardware with a phone and a keyboard, since neither the container nor the lock VM has Bluetooth (btvirt in a VM is a later step); BlueZ's own timeouts and `Cancel` timing; and the store loop's minute timer, proven only through `Pairing::expire` under paused tokio time (`a_request_unanswered_for_a_minute_is_withdrawn`). Left as they are: a request arriving under the lock cannot be seen and BlueZ cancels it after its minute; an older BlueZ without the stack of default agents gives the default back to the previous agent only when that agent asks again.

## audio-routing

**2026-11-04 · audio-routing: a program's stream moves with `st.move_to(dev)`, which writes what pipewire-pulse writes for `pactl move-sink-input`, and a move onto the device that is the default now lets it follow the default again.** The owner's mixer sends one app to the headphones and leaves the rest on the speakers. WirePlumber has no usable binding (design.md's crate table), and every tool that moves a stream (pactl, pavucontrol, Plasma through pipewire-pulse) does it the same way, so Strand does it that way too: on the `default` metadata, subject the stream's node id, `target.node` cleared (the legacy key) and `target.object` set to the device's `object.serial` typed `Spa:Id` (pipewire-pulse's `do_move_stream`). Nothing else is written: no node property, no link made or broken by hand, so WirePlumber 0.4 (the container's 0.4.17) and 0.5 (the owner's Arch) both relink the stream and remember it per app. A move onto the device that is the default of its direction now clears `target.object` too, PulseAudio's rule, which pipewire-pulse keeps: the stream follows the default again. That is how a pinned stream is let go, so `move_to` takes a plain `AudioDevice`, with no nullable argument and no `pinned` or `follows_default` field (one concept fewer); the cost, that a stream cannot be pinned to the current default, is PulseAudio's too. A program that named its own target (`pw-play --target`, a `target.object` node property) or set `node.dont-reconnect` may stay where it is when the default changes after a move back: that is WirePlumber's policy, said in the schema doc. A target without a readable `object.serial` (PipeWire 1.x and WirePlumber always give one) is `AudioError::Failed`, unless it is the default, rather than a write by name. The writes go through `Metadata::set_property_cstr` with fallible `CString`s (a NUL is `Failed`): `set_property` `expect`s. Tests: `a_stream_moves_and_follows_the_default_again` (private PipeWire, null sinks, WirePlumber: moved to sink b, kept there when a third sink becomes the default, following the default once moved onto it), `a_move_writes_what_pactl_move_sink_input_writes`.

**2026-11-04 · audio-routing: `st.device` is read from the stream's links, not from the metadata target.** The target is only intent: WirePlumber may not honour it, and a stream that follows the default has none. The links are what pavucontrol shows (pipewire-pulse derives a sink-input's sink from them). The loop now keeps the Link globals in `Follow::Audio` as it did for video (output and input node of each, no binding); they mark the state for publishing only while `audio.streams` is watched, as the streams bind only then. A player's device is the input side of its links, a recorder's the output side; a sink's monitor ports belong to the sink's node, so a `monitor` recording names the sink it reads. Only listed devices count (this shell's meters, another program's stream, a filter's inner node do not); the one with the most links (one per channel) wins, the lowest id on a tie, and none is null (starting, or linked only to another program). It is a device id as `AudioMeter.device` is, compared with `audio.sinks` ids of the same state. Tests: `a_stream_plays_to_the_device_it_is_linked_to`, `streams_are_listed_while_read_and_written`.

**2026-11-04 · audio-routing: a stream moves only to a device of its direction, and refusals are logged as `make_default()`'s are.** A player moves to a sink, a recorder of a source to a source, a `monitor` recording to a sink; any other pair is `AudioError::WrongDirection`. No sink monitors are added to `audio.sources` for moving a recorder onto a sink's sound: a `monitor` recording moves between sinks already. A stream as the target, a device as the stream or a stream that ended is `UnknownDevice`, no `default` metadata (no session manager) `NoDefaultMetadata`. The store refuses an item held past its stream (another app under its key) or a device item whose id now names another node, as writes and `make_default()` are; no error field is added, a refusal is logged and changes nothing, and the outcome shows in `st.device`. Tests: `a_move_is_refused_with_its_reason`.

**2026-11-04 · audio-routing: a card's profiles are listed on its devices (`dev.profiles`) and switched with `p.select()`, not through an `audio.cards` list.** The owner's shell switches a Bluetooth headset between its call and high-fidelity modes from the device it shows; putting the profiles on `AudioDevice` reaches them from there with one concept fewer. Each device node's card is its `device.id` (a Bluetooth node may lack `card.profile.device`). The cards were already bound for their `Route`; each now subscribes `EnumProfile` and `Profile` too, and a new set, announced by those params' flags, is shown only once the core sync issued after it is back, as routes are, so a half-sent set never shows. `AudioProfile` is keyed by `name` (unique on its card, readable), ordered best first by the card's priority then index, as pavucontrol and Plasma order them; `available` is false only for SPA's `no` (unknown counts as available, as pavucontrol does); `active` is per item, not a separate `dev.profile`, as `Player` has `active` and `select()`, the one in use being `profiles.find(p => p.active)`. A card's `off` is not listed: choosing it removes the device it was chosen from, with no way back in Strand. So a card turned off elsewhere is out of reach; `audio.cards` is the alternative if owners need it. `p.select()` writes the card's `Profile { index, save: true }`, what `wpctl set-profile` and `pactl set-card-profile` write and parallel to the route write's `save`, so the session manager keeps it; an unavailable or the active profile is still written, as wpctl does, and a kept item whose card left or whose name is gone is `UnknownCard` or `UnknownProfile`. The card's nodes come back under new ids, which the device and default handling already follow. Profiles are followed whenever `audio` runs: the cards are bound anyway, and a sub-field cannot be watched. Tests: `profile_pods`, `a_card_shows_a_whole_set_of_profiles`, `profiles_are_listed_best_first_without_off`, `a_device_lists_its_cards_profiles_and_select_finds_the_card`, `profile_params_are_told_apart`, `select_sets_the_items_profile_on_its_card`, `devices_of_no_card_list_no_profiles`.

## drives

**2026-11-04 · drives: removable drives are a new builtin service, `drives`, over UDisks2, not more of `disk`.** Three reasons. A service is the unit of the lifecycle (design.md: it starts on its first reader and stops 5 s after its last), and `disk` samples `statvfs` every 10 s whenever a reader is visible and sits in `POLLED`, so a bar that read only removable drives through `disk` would wake every 10 s to measure filesystems it never shows; keeping that out of `disk` would need watched-tracking of non-stream fields in the service core, a cross-cutting change for one field. The sources differ: `disk` reads procfs and `statvfs`, drives come from a D-Bus daemon, and `available` means something only for the second (one daemon per service, as battery is UPower's and bluetooth BlueZ's). And `disk`'s `Filesystem` is keyed by its mount `path`, which an unmounted filesystem lacks. On "does it remove a concept": the new records reuse `disk`'s words (`device`, `path`, sizes as float bytes), so `disk.all.find(f => f.path == v.path)` gives a mounted volume's usage and nothing about usage is duplicated. The names: `drives.all` (like `disk.all` and `outputs.all`), records `Drive` and `Volume` (GVfs's word for a mountable filesystem on a drive; `Filesystem` is taken, under another key), and `failed(device, error)`, bluetooth's (key, error) shape, since every action is a record's. A drive is keyed by its whole-disk block device (`/dev/sdb`), not UDisks2's `Id`, so `device` names the target of every action, `/dev/sdb1` for a volume. `available` is false without UDisks2 or a system bus, and false while a failed run waits to try again (spec.md 12).

**2026-11-04 · drives: what is listed.** A drive UDisks2 calls `Removable` with its medium in (`MediaAvailable`, or a medium that does not come out), so an empty card reader or disc drive is not listed and a bar's "drive plugged in" icon does not stay lit. Internal disks, loop devices (a block whose `Drive` is `/`), blocks with `HintIgnore` and locked encrypted partitions are left out. An encrypted filesystem another tool unlocked is listed under its drive through its cleartext block's `CryptoBackingDevice`; unlocking is out of scope. Drives are in UDisks2's `SortKey` order (those there at its start, then as plugged in), volumes by partition number, then device. `Volume` has both `mounted` (asked for, and `if v.mounted` reads plainer) and `path: text?`, null while unmounted and named like `Filesystem.path` so the two join; with several mount points the first is the `path`. `label` is null when empty, so `v.label ?? bytes(v.size)` is the display idiom. Left out, to add under spec.md 14 if asked: the filesystem type, read-only, usage (`disk.all`'s, by `path`), busy or `mounting` fields (a repeat in flight is dropped instead, as in bluetooth), unlocking and formatting, automounting, and an `added` event (a config can watch `drives.all`).

**2026-11-04 · drives: `d.eject()` is safe removal, one field says whether it can be, and it ends with one step, never both.** The task asked for "can eject/power off"; two fields would make every config write `d.can_eject || d.can_power_off` and choose between two buttons that both mean "make it safe to pull" (design.md, "Defaults remove ceremony"). So there is one action and one field, `can_eject` (`Ejectable || CanPowerOff`): power off is folded in, not dropped. `eject()` unmounts every mounted filesystem of the drive, locks each encrypted one that was unlocked (`Encrypted.Lock`, a step the plan lacked: UDisks2 typically refuses to power off a drive with an encrypted device of it unlocked, and GVfs locks after unmounting), then takes one last step: `Eject` where the medium comes out of a drive that ejects (a disc, a card), else `PowerOff` where the drive can be (a stick, a disk), else `Eject`. The first build ejected and then powered off where a drive allowed both, as the plan read GVfs; the review found that GVfs maps `g_drive_eject` to `Drive.Eject` and `g_drive_stop` to `Drive.PowerOff` and a file manager calls one of them, and that a USB card reader or disc drive reports both flags, so powering it off after its medium went took every slot with it, deaf to the next card or disc until it was plugged in again. The first step refused (a filesystem in use) stops the rest and is `failed(drive, error)`; with neither flag it fails at once, "the drive cannot be ejected", and unmounts nothing. Powered off, the drive's objects leave UDisks2; ejected, its medium is no longer available; either way it leaves `drives.all`.

**2026-11-04 · drives: calls run unbounded, outlive the body once started, and a repeat in flight is dropped.** Mount and Unmount pass empty options: UDisks2 chooses the mount point and its options, `auth.no_user_interaction` is not set so polkit may ask (the session's agent, Strand's own while a config reads `polkit`; on default polkit rules the active local user mounts and ejects removable media with no prompt), and `force` is never used. No call has a timeout: a polkit dialog may stay open as long as the user leaves it and UDisks2 acts once it is answered, as with session's power actions (m6-w2-services, "A builtin `session` service over logind"; review minor 13 in `session.rs`). Each runs as a task. The plan had them cancelled with the body; the review found that an eject is several calls the client makes in turn, and a menu closing on its click lets the service stop 5 s later, which drops the body's future mid-eject and left a drive unmounted, still powered, with no `failed`. So the tasks are held in `Calls`, whose `Drop` detaches them (a `detach_all()` on the return paths would never run when the future is dropped): a started call finishes on the services runtime with its own connection, and what it brings back is dropped. A call repeating one in flight on the same device (a double click's second `mount()`, a second `eject()`) is dropped and shows no busy state; a stalled one holds its guard until the service stops, as for `session`. Refused before it runs (no bus, a backing-off run, the target gone), an action is `failed(device, error)` through `refused`, with "UDisks2 is not running" when no one owns the name. UDisks2 is D-Bus-activated (`Daemon::new`, not `Daemon::watch`), as GVfs and udiskie start it: unlike iwd it contends with nothing.

**2026-11-04 · drives: nothing polls, and the bus drops what the state does not read.** The service subscribes one rule for the ObjectManager root's `InterfacesAdded`/`InterfacesRemoved` and three `PropertiesChanged` rules with `arg0` set to the `Drive`, `Block` and `Filesystem` interfaces, built by a new `dbus::properties_rule`. So `Drive.Ata` SMART refreshes (every 10 min on an internal ATA disk) and `Loop`, `Swapspace` and NVMe property changes never reach the process. Block and filesystem changes of any device do, internal disks and loop devices included, and change nothing in the state (the first module docs said loop devices never woke the process; the review corrected them). Only the drive, block, filesystem and partition interfaces are kept in memory. `dbus_idle.rs::the_dbus_services_sleep_when_nothing_changes` proves it: a SMART refresh leaves the services thread's context switches unchanged and a stick plugged in wakes it once; with a namespace rule in place of the `arg0` ones it fails, and `drives_follow_udisks` fails with the block rule dropped.

**2026-11-04 · drives: how it is wired and tested.** The provisional stubs follow `greetd`'s in builtin.schema, so no earlier record id moves (m6-service-gaps, naming), and `DRIVES` and `Builtin.drives` come last, keeping `schemas()` in registration order. Adding two schema types moved one drag identity in `instantiate__every_snippet.snap`, which `drag_identity`'s docs say a new type may do (precedent 75f5115d). python-dbusmock 0.31.1 in the CI image has no UDisks2 template, so `crates/strand-services/tests/udisks/mod.rs` is a small zbus UDisks2 (in network_iwd.rs's style, `zbus::fdo::ObjectManager` giving the signals), a module directory that `tests/drives.rs` and `tests/dbus_idle.rs` share without it becoming a test target, as `tests/pipewire/` is. It encodes our reading of UDisks2, not udisksd's behaviour. The new `strand-services::drives` binary is not in `.config/nextest.toml`'s ci retry list (a new binary starts with none), and its wake-count assertions stay in `dbus_idle.rs`, which the retry filter forbids. Not yet checked: real drives against a real UDisks2 (some USB enclosures may not set `Removable`, and some bridges refuse `Eject` where `PowerOff` would work; if that bites, an `Eject` failure where `CanPowerOff` could fall through to it, recorded here), and the budgets job's `.text` gate (`TEXT_GATE_GPU`), which the whole CI run measures; if it trips, the gate is raised by its stated rule.

## power-media-kbd

**2026-11-04 · power-media-kbd: the power profile is a builtin `power`, an enum, read from power-profiles-daemon under either name and never started.** The owner's machine runs power-profiles-daemon, and a profile menu is a usual control-centre tile that only the design's `from dbus` example covered. The service is `power`, not `ppd`, `profiles` or `power_profiles`: builtin names are single domain nouns (`battery`, `brightness`, `network`, `keyboard`), design.md's crate table already says "power profiles", `power.profile` reads as one says it, the same noun can take other power facts later (AC online, charge thresholds) without a new service, and `ppd` stays free for the design's and the guide's `from dbus` example, which keeps loading with no shadow warning. `profile` is `PowerProfile { power_saver, balanced, performance }`, not text: the daemon's API fixes the three names, and an enum gives `match` exhaustiveness, a did-you-mean and a typed `strand set power.profile performance`, as `network.security` maps NetworkManager's strings to `WifiSecurity`; a name a future daemon adds is left out of `profiles`, and an unknown active one reads `balanced`. It follows `org.freedesktop.UPower.PowerProfiles` whenever that is owned, else `net.hadess.PowerProfiles` (0.20 and later own both, older ones only the second, tuned-ppd both), chooses again on any owner change of either and reads afresh without restarting, and counts signals only from the chosen name's object. It is followed with `Daemon::watch` and never activated, as iwd is (decisions.md m6-w2-services, gaps 15): TLP, auto-cpufreq and tuned conflict with it, and a shell starting it would fight them; desktops enable its unit at boot, so the cost is only that an activation-only install reads `available` false. `power` is registered after every service before it (`schemas()`, `Builtin`, `register()`, `all()`), so no index into the registration order shifts (recorded dumps, the reference's order); `drives`, merged after it, comes after it the same way. Tests: `crates/strand-services/tests/power.rs` (all four), `src/power.rs::tests`.

**2026-11-04 · power-media-kbd: a profile the daemon does not offer is not asked, and holds stay a declared `from dbus` action.** A write of a profile not in `profiles`, of a value that is no profile, or made while no daemon answers is not sent, and the profile stays as it was. Real power-profiles-daemon refuses such a write anyway; the check saves the round trip and its log line, and python-dbusmock's `Set` takes anything, so only our check makes the test mean something. A write the daemon refuses is logged and the profile reported as last read: there is no `power.failed` event, as `brightness` and `bluetooth.powered` refuse writes the same way. A written profile is also put in the cached properties at once, so another property's signal landing before the daemon's own does not show the old profile for a moment (the builder's addition to the plan). `HoldProfile`, `ReleaseProfile`, `ActiveProfileHolds` and `Actions` are not exposed: nobody asked, a hold needs a cookie the language has no concept for, and the how-to and the guide already show a hold as `action hold(…) = HoldProfile` in a `from dbus` block. So that example stays, with a sentence saying Strand ships the profile itself as `power` and `ppd` is declared to show how any daemon is read (guide level 5, site how-to "Calling a D-Bus method or a declared action").

**2026-11-04 · power-media-kbd: a config file named `power.strand` that exports a name no longer loads.** Adding the builtin made the how-to's own example, `power.strand` exporting `open`, a load error: a file named like a service cannot export, since `power.open` means the service (spec.md 4.2, "File names"), and the error, `check::redeclared`, names the file and asks for it to be renamed ("`power.open` cannot be read: `power` is a builtin service", help "rename `power.strand`; its exports are read as `file.name`"). A file of that name that exports nothing still loads. The plan had foreseen only `state power`, `let power` and `service power`, which warn and keep loading. The example is now `powermenu.strand` (site/how-to/keys.md). A user's config with such a file stops loading after this release until the file is renamed, and `drives.strand`, merged in the same round, meets the same error. That is allowed before 1.0 (spec.md 14 binds 1.x), and the message says exactly what to do, so it is kept rather than given a warning path of its own; a file named like any later builtin will meet the same error, so site/help/troubleshooting.md says it once for every builtin name and the release notes should name the rename.

**2026-11-04 · power-media-kbd: the player's shuffle, loop and own volume, each with a `can_` field.** `media.shuffle: bool rw`, `media.loop: Loop rw` and `media.volume: float rw` are the active player's MPRIS `Shuffle`, `LoopStatus` and `Volume`, and every `Player` has the same for itself, as `position` is on both. The loop is `loop` over `Loop { none, track, playlist }`: MPRIS's own word without its suffix, and `repeat` already means key repeat in the `Key` record (Rust spells the field `r#loop`; the derive strips `r#`). There are three flags, `can_shuffle`, `can_loop` and `can_volume`, not one `can_control`, following `can_next`, `can_previous` and `can_seek`, so each control dims on its own. Unlike `CanGoNext`, where a property the player does not report counts as able, these are false when the property is absent, since MPRIS makes `Shuffle` and `LoopStatus` optional and a `Volume` that cannot be read cannot be set; all are false while `CanControl` is false or no player runs. `media.volume` shows `Volume` as reported, never below 0 and above 1 when the player amplifies, as `audio.sink.volume` does; a write is held to 0 to 1, so a `+5%` key never amplifies by accident; no player, or none reporting it, reads 0. The examples in the schema write `on click { media.shuffle = !media.shuffle }`, not the plan's `toggle { on: <-> media.shuffle }`: Strand has no `toggle` element, and the doc may not invent one. Tests: `tests/media.rs::media_sets_shuffle_loop_and_volume_on_the_player`, `src/media.rs::tests::a_player_without_shuffle_or_loop_says_so`.

**2026-11-04 · power-media-kbd: a player write shows at once, with one call per player and property in flight.** The written value is fixed at once through `Players::changed`, as a seek's position is, so a whole read already in flight cannot undo it and a slider or a toggle never snaps back; the `Set` runs in a task bounded by CALL_TIMEOUT (2 s), so a hung player holds nothing up. One `Set` per (player, property) is in flight, a newer write replacing the waiting value, which is sent when the call lands, so a slider drag lands in order and ends at the last value. A refused `Set` with nothing waiting reads the player whole again, and the refused property is dropped from what reads already in flight are answered over (`Players::reread` takes the property; the review found a refused write made during a read stayed laid over every answer until the player signalled), so the player's real value comes back with a read in flight or not. The cost: a player that neither signals nor takes the write (Spotify does not signal `Volume` or `Shuffle`, Chromium ignores `Volume` writes) shows the written value until its next read or signal. Nothing is polled: the players' own changes come by `PropertiesChanged`, and an invalidated property is read again. Tests: `src/media.rs::tests::{a_write_fixes_the_value_and_waits_its_turn, a_refused_write_comes_back_with_a_read_in_flight}`.

**2026-11-04 · power-media-kbd: the keyboard's backlight is `brightness.keyboard`, not `keyboard.backlight`.** `brightness.keyboard: float rw` (0 to 1) and `brightness.keyboard_present` come from the first `/sys/class/leds/*::kbd_backlight` by name with a `max_brightness` above 0; a write goes to the nearest of the light's steps (the owner's `dell::kbd_backlight` has off and two levels, `max_brightness` 2). It belongs to `brightness` for three reasons. It has the screen backlight's source and writer, a sysfs light read and inotify-watched and set by logind's `SetBrightness` on the caller's session, only the subsystem differing (`leds`, not `backlight`), so `Backlight` became one `Light` with no new backend concept. `keyboard`'s fields are streams read only while a visible reader shows them (the focused `wl_keyboard`, compositor IPC), so an `on change` in a hidden OSD would never fire, while `brightness`'s are plain and followed while the service runs. And an OSD's `enum Kind { volume, brightness }` and a key bound to `strand set brightness.keyboard +50%` extend the design's OSD pattern directly. `keyboard_present` follows `network.wifi_present` and `battery.present` (hardware that exists), since `available` already means the screen's light here; the two lights are independent, a desktop with a lit keyboard having `keyboard_present` and no `available`, and a write to an absent one asks nothing and keeps the value. The light is watched, never polled: `MODIFY` and `CLOSE_WRITE` on `brightness` (any write from user space, logind's included) and on `brightness_hw_changed` where the driver has it (`LED_BRIGHT_HW_CHANGED`, the kernel's report of a firmware change: dell-laptop, thinkpad_acpi). On a driver without it, a change the firmware makes alone (an Fn key, a timeout) shows at the next write or start, a limitation recorded against the no-polling rule; a keyboard plugged in later is found at the next start, as the screen's light is. A watch that cannot be set up is logged and the service runs on without it, as before this change, while a watch failing as it is read still ends the run with a ServiceError retried on the backoff (the plan had a failed setup end the run). logind's `SetBrightness`, unbounded until now, is bounded by READ_TIMEOUT for both lights. `STRAND_LEDS_DIR` and `set_leds_root` point the service at other lights, as `STRAND_BACKLIGHT_DIR` does; strand's budgets, dbus_shells and reloads tests point it at an empty directory, so no test reads the machine's own lights. Tests: `tests/brightness.rs::{the_keyboard_backlight_follows_its_light_and_writes_through_logind, without_a_keyboard_backlight_the_keyboard_is_not_present}` (the firmware step renames a new `brightness` over the watched one, so only `brightness_hw_changed` can tell; it fails with that file not watched), `src/brightness.rs::tests::the_keyboard_light_is_the_first_kbd_backlight`, `tests/dbus_idle.rs::the_dbus_services_sleep_when_nothing_changes`.

**2026-11-03 · services-merge: the `.text` gates re-based on the merged pairing agent, audio routing, power, media and keyboard-light, and drives work.** `laptop/services-round` merges bt-agent, audio-routing, power-media-kbd and drives on `main` at a968880f. Its CPU-only release build measured 25,014,231 B in the container suite, 110,551 B over its gate, and the default build 29,053,463 B, 44,521 B under its own: about 730 KB each over wave-cost's tree (+730,048 B and +727,360 B), the four features' service code (BlueZ's agent object, the PipeWire links, metadata and card profiles, a third MPRIS write path and the keyboard light, a new UDisks2 service) and what reached `main` after wave-cost. `strand-services` and zbus are already built at opt-level "z", so nothing is left to build for size; this is the features' cost, and the gate is a tripwire, never a cap. Both gates follow by the usual rule, measurement plus a 512 KiB reserve rounded up to 256 KiB (CI's budgets job runs in the same image since 2026-11-01, so the container's figure is CI's): GPU 29,622,272 B (113 × 256 KiB) and CPU-only 25,690,112 B (98 × 256 KiB). The default build is re-based too, since 44 KB was all its room. Proof: `the_release_binary_code_stays_within_its_gate`.

## card-params

**2026-11-04 · card-params: a card's profiles and routes are asked for again when their param info changes, and a node stays on its card through an info event that carries no properties.** On the owner's laptop `audio.sink.profiles` was empty for AirPods whose card (PipeWire device 44) listed five profiles, so the shell's headset modes and its "asleep in music mode" microphone row never showed. Two faults, both found against the owner's real PipeWire (1.x, WirePlumber 0.5) with a read-only probe running `strand-services`' own audio thread while the webcam card's profile was switched and back; the container's PipeWire has no card, so audio-routing's only live test never met one. First, the daemon sends a subscriber a param's items only when it subscribes: a later change (a headset switched to its headset profile) comes as the info alone, the serial bit toggled, so `Profiles` started an empty set at each change and showed it at the sync, and `Routes` stayed stale, writing volume past the card's route. The driver now asks for each changed param again (`enum_params`) before it issues the sync, as `pw-mon` and `pw-dump` do, and only while the param is readable (`ask_again`); the items asked for come before the sync is answered, so a half-sent set is still never shown. Second, every node info event replaced the node's card and route link from its properties, but an event without `PROPS` in its mask (a state change, suspended to running) carries none, so the node fell off its card within milliseconds of appearing; `node_place` reads them only from an event whose properties changed, the rule streams' properties already followed. Tests: `a_card_shows_a_whole_set_of_profiles` (each change names the params to ask for), `a_device_uses_only_its_current_set_of_routes`, `a_changed_param_is_asked_for_while_readable`, `a_node_stays_on_its_card_through_an_info_without_properties`; on the laptop, the webcam card kept its three profiles through `pro-audio` and back with the active one marked, where `d6623f12` showed none after the first state change.

## glide-curve

**2026-11-04 · glide-curve: siblings glide on the `$motion.spatial` in effect where they are, so a `set` names their curve; no new syntax.** The owner's island bar placed its workspace highlight by sums of the chips' widths on its own spring, while the chips around an empty workspace's chip that came or went glided on Strand's global `$motion.spatial`, which nothing in the config could change for one row, so the two slid on different curves and the switch wobbled (the shell's issue "Siblings glide on a curve of their own"). Every FLIP glide read the global token table (`flip_curve`), as did a drag's spring back (`Renderer::lift`) and a wheel step or snap of a `scroll` or `list` (`Renderer::scroll_curve`), although a size spring (anim/sizes.rs) and a surface's growth (`step_curve`) already read the tokens in scope at their node. All three now do the same: `glide_curve` evaluates the default spatial transition with `flatten::scope_tables` at the node that glides or is let go, and `scroll_curve` at the node it scrolls (spec.md 6.6 says movement uses `$motion.spatial` and 9.4 that a `set` holds for its node's subtree, with no exception for a scroll), so `set { $motion.spatial: spring(520, 0.78) }` in a row (spec.md 9.4, which already takes any token, a spring included) gives its children's glides that spring, and a node outside the set keeps the global one. The issue offered a `~` on the container instead; that adds a concept (a transition on a container that animates nothing of its own) where the scoped token removes one, the glide following the rule every other spatial spring follows, and the value set is any spring, a `let` included, so the island's `let glide = spring(520, 0.78)` can be both its highlight's `~ glide` and its row's `set { $motion.spatial: glide }`, which is what lets a highlight and its chips share one spring. The other half the issue offered, a node following another's laid-out box without scaling, is not taken: a shared token is enough to keep the two in step. One exception is kept from growth: while a content-sized surface's box springs over a step, everything a pass glides on that surface takes the step's curve, as before, so what the step moves rides the box rather than lagging it on a slower curve of its own. That holds for the change that starts the step too: a row mounted in a panel that will grow is laid out before its step begins (the pass awaiting the configure), where its siblings took their own scoped curve, so under a slow set the rows it pushed went up with the box, then crawled back down over the set's second; the pass that starts the step now gives the step's curve to the glides the passes before it gave since the frame, none of which has begun (`glide_moved`). At rest the siblings take their own scoped curve, the curve the set asked for. spec.md 6.6 names the curve; architecture.md's animation paragraph says where it is read; the site's motion concept page says a `set` in the row picks it, with the island's case. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/motion.rs::a_glide_follows_the_spatial_token_in_effect_where_it_is` (two columns reordered alike, the one under a 100 ms linear set gliding 8 px a frame and never past its slot, the one beside it on the default spring; it glided the set's column on the spring before), `crates/strand-render/tests/drag.rs::a_row_let_go_springs_back_on_the_spatial_token_in_effect` (it sprang back on the global spring before), `crates/strand-render/tests/motion.rs::a_wheel_step_follows_the_spatial_token_in_effect_at_the_list` (two lists side by side, the one under a 100 ms linear set stepping 7.5 px a frame and never past its step; it overshot on the global spring before), `crates/strand-render/tests/growth.rs::a_mount_that_starts_the_growth_glides_on_the_steps_curve_under_a_set` (a row mounted above the red one at rest: its path on screen is the same under a 1 s linear set as without; it went 13 px up and crawled back before), `::a_glide_mid_growth_takes_the_steps_curve_under_a_set` (a row mounted above the red one mid-growth: the red row's path on screen is the same with the column under a 1 s linear set as without; it fails when every glide takes its scoped curve), `crates/strand-compiler/tests/theme.rs::a_set_overrides_the_spatial_motion_with_a_spring` (a `spring(…)` and a `let` naming one reach render as the subtree's `$motion.spatial`; the `motion` tokens are typed `Spring`, so a duration in the set is a type error).

## path-tilde

**2026-11-04 · path-tilde: a declared action's `path` parameter takes the home folder for its `~`.** The owner's shell declared `action rec(file: path) ["wf-recorder", "-f", file]` and called it with `"~/Videos/a.mp4"`; wf-recorder got the `~` as written and failed (`avio_open failed`, exit 255), so the shell ran it through `sh -c` for the shell to expand `$HOME`, the script-from-a-value shape `check::shell_script` exists to steer away from. Spec.md 5.7 passed every parameter "as `text` shows it", so `path` and `text` behaved alike, while everywhere else Strand takes a path (a settings file, `from file`/`dir`, an image, a shader, a Lottie file) `~/…` is the home folder: the `path` type read as if it expanded and did not, a concept with two meanings. Now a `path` parameter whose value starts with `~/` reaches the program with `$HOME` in place of the `~` (`vm::Vm::request` through `with_home`, the lowered action keeping which parameters are `path`s as `ExecAction::paths`), in an action with a result too; a bare `~` and `~user/…` (no other place expands either), a `~` further in and every `text` parameter stay as written, so a value meant literally is still passed by declaring it `text`. A `$HOME` that is unset, relative or not UTF-8 leaves the value as written rather than inventing a folder. The alternative the issue offered, a builtin naming the home folder for the config to join itself, was not taken: it adds a concept where this removes one. A `from dbus` service's `= Method` action is unchanged: its `path` arguments go to a method that reads them its own way, and no shell hit it. spec.md 5.7 and design.md ("Declared actions") say so, and the guide's level 5 and the site's D-Bus and actions how-to tell a shell author (`crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::a_path_argument_reaches_the_program_with_the_home_folder`, `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/mod.rs::tests::a_path_argument_takes_the_home_folder_for_its_tilde`).

**2026-11-04 · path-tilde: the review of 1e0c431c: only `~/…` is expanded, and a written `~/…` still keeps a result action's answer in the flight recorder.** Two findings. First, 1e0c431c expanded a bare `~` too, while saying it did as every other path Strand takes does; those places (a settings file through `instantiate::resolve` and `check::paths::resolve`, a `from file` or `from dir` service's path through `services::custom::resolve`, an image, a Lottie file, a shader) expand only `~/…`, so a bare `~` would have meant the home folder in an action and a file named `~` in a settings path, the two meanings this track removes. The bare `~` now stays as written in an action too: one rule, and `"~/"` names the home folder for a program that wants it. Second, the recorder decides whether to hold a result action's answer (`Recorder::exec_answered`) by asking whether every argument after the program is a text of the config (`Program::is_text_literal`), and it now sees the expanded argument: `ls("~/Pictures")` reached it as `$HOME/Pictures`, which is no literal, so the answer a replay needs was written as `{"~text": n}`. `argument_literal` now also takes an argument under an absolute `$HOME` whose `~/…` form is a literal. It is decided from the argument, not from a flag the VM would add to `ExecRequest`: a typed path naming the same file as a written `~/…` counts as written, which keeps nothing a written call would not, and no cross-crate field is added. The expanded path is never recorded itself (an action's record keeps its argument count). (`crates/strand/src/run/record.rs::tests::a_written_home_path_keeps_its_actions_answer`, `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/mod.rs::tests::a_path_argument_takes_the_home_folder_for_its_tilde`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::a_path_argument_reaches_the_program_with_the_home_folder`.)

## removed-state-notice

**2026-11-04 · removed-state-notice: a `state` cell is renamed only to a cell its own owner gained, and the reload overlay lists the reload's notices, nothing more.** The owner's shell (Strand `fb75dc93`) saved `notify.strand` without `shown`, `grown` and `filled` while `launcher.strand` renamed `wide` to `out`, and the overlay opened as "strand: reloaded with notices" with a row `notify.grown: reset (renamed)` for each removed cell, while `strand watch --json` listed them under `reset` and its `notices` were empty. Two faults. First, a reload took a cell nobody claimed for a rename when its scope (its place in the instance tree) gained any cell, and every file's cells live in the root scope, so `launcher.out` made each removed `notify` cell a "rename". The pairing is now by owner, the cell's reload key without its name (`<scope>#<owner>`, `cell_owner`): the same file or component in the same place. A cell whose owner gained none was removed and goes without a word, as removed cells always did when nothing was added anywhere; the design's table has no row for a removed cell, and nothing the user set is lost by a name the config no longer reads. When an owner lost more cells than it gained, some were removed and Strand cannot tell which ("Strand never guesses"), so each says `renamed or removed`, never only `renamed`; a 1:1 loss and gain stays `renamed`, the table's row, though a removal beside an unrelated addition reads the same. Not taken: dropping the warning for a renamed cell still at its default, which would also have quieted `launcher.wide`, since the table's row resets a renamed cell with a warning and the fuzzer holds every rename to a reported reset. A file renamed in one load is one owner under both names (the modules gone and the modules new in that load pair as one owner per scope), so its cells still reset as `renamed`, set or at their default, the 2026-10-05 rule the live-pipeline fuzzer holds a one-load module rename to (`renamed or removed` when the new file has fewer cells); a cell of a module that is gone with no new module gaining a cell meets the `removed with its module` rule (wave2-exit, only when set) instead of being called renamed because another file gained one, and that rule is the one case where a removed cell still warns. Second, the overlay built its reset rows and its cancelled-`await` row from the report's other fields, so its box held rows the event's `notices` never had (the `Report::notices` doc already said it held a restart's line). `Report::reset_cell` now records a reset cell and its notice (`t.b: reset (renamed)`) together, for every reset a reload makes (a rename, a retype, `@reset`, a value that no longer fits its type, a surface's kind changed, a module gone), and `Report::finish` notices a restart's cancelled `await`s, so `report_lines` is the notices alone (a reset row keyed by its cell, so `[reset]` and IPC `reset` still take it away) and every row the box shows for a reload is in the `reload` event's `notices`; the cell stays under `reset` for readers that want cells, as a kept cell is both in `kept_over_default` and the notices. `strand watch`'s text form lists a reset cell once, as the overlay words it (`  t.b: reset (renamed)`, where it said `  reset: t.b (renamed)`), and an older strand's event, its reset only under `reset`, still prints it. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/reload.rs::{a_cell_removed_from_one_file_is_not_renamed_by_another, more_cells_lost_than_gained_are_renamed_or_removed, a_module_renamed_in_one_load_resets_as_renamed, a_value_that_no_longer_fits_is_reset_with_a_notice, handler_restart_cancels_its_await}`, `crates/strand/src/run/tests.rs::a_removed_cell_opens_no_overlay_and_the_overlay_lists_what_watch_says` (the owner's save opens no overlay, through its quiet period and past it; a rename's overlay rows equal the event's `notices`), `crates/strand/src/overlay.rs::tests::reload_notices_and_their_reset`, `crates/strand/src/ipc/describe.rs::tests::events_read_as_text`; each fails with the old pairing or the old rows.
