## save-blank

**2026-11-04 · save-blank: a flush that finds a watched file or module gone takes the inotify queue before it reports a removal, so a delete-then-create save made as an earlier batch is cut waits its removal grace instead of blanking the shell.** `five_save_styles_land_on_a_cold_boot` failed with "round 23 (style 3, missing 16 ms): a blank frame" about one run in ten when 32 ran at once (28 of 320 on `035ac995`, and 29 of 320 with a temporary trace added; all but one on round 23, the other on round 3), and once on GitHub; the shell repo's strand-issues.md guessed that a reload already running read the folder while the file was missing. Close: it was the watcher's own flush. Round 22 renames `theme.strand` away and back, a change the scene does not show (round 18's bar reads neither the label nor `Pill`; round 2 before round 3 likewise), so the test goes on to round 23 at once while round 22's batch is still due. That batch lists the module set again (a module's `MOVED_FROM` sets `pending.config`), and when its 15 ms are up as round 23 has just deleted `bar.strand`, `rescan_config` lists the folder in the gap, before the watcher thread has read the `DELETE`: the removal grace only starts from a removal it has heard, so the listing's miss went out as `bar.strand` `Removed`, the loader dropped the bar, and the next batch brought it back. Proved with a temporary trace in the two places a flush decides a file is gone: in every failing run (29 of 320) the listing dropped `bar.strand` while it was missing from disk, and in no passing run did either fire. Since inotify queues `DELETE` inside the `unlink`, a flush that misses a file has its event in the queue: `rescan_config` now drains the queue when the listing leaves a module out, and when that queue shows such a module removed, created or being written the module set stays as it was that flush, pending again, so the next flush lists it a grace after that event; the same rule covers the other place, a read that fails with the file's event queued behind it (`Err` counted as torn when the drain names it), which this test did not hit but is the same gap. A removal that stays is reported at that grace, as before. Rejected: a longer grace or a pause before listing (the gap can fall anywhere), and making the test wait for each round's batch (the shell blanks for a real user saving twice in quick succession just as well). Tests: `a_module_missed_by_a_listing_before_its_removal_is_heard_waits_for_the_grace` and `a_file_read_in_a_save_gap_before_its_removal_is_heard_waits_for_the_grace` (`crates/strand-watch/src/core.rs::tests`, each failing with its half of the fix taken out); `five_save_styles_land_on_a_cold_boot` passed 640 of 640 run 32 at a time afterwards.

**2026-11-04 · save-blank: the listing's miss is judged by the queue alone, and the module set waits whole.** Review of the first fix found three gaps, each checked and fixed. First, `rescan_config` drained the queue only when a module the listing left out was still gone at a second look at the disk after the listing (and its re-lists); a file re-created between the last re-list's look and that one went out as `Removed`, the same blank in a narrower window. The drain now follows the listing alone: whenever it leaves a module out, the queue is taken (a non-blocking read, nothing when empty), and a module that really left the set (a directory now too deep) still has no event there and is removed as before. Second, the first fix kept only the missed module back, so a rename in the same gap (`mv bar.strand panel.strand`, the listing already showing the new name) added `panel.strand` at once and removed `bar.strand` a grace later: for those 50 ms the loader saw every declaration twice (`check::redeclared`) and held the new file back, where `035ac995` and the events-heard-first path both made it one batch. Now while any module is kept for a queued event, no module leaves or joins the set that flush; the next flush, a grace after the event, lists it whole, so the rename is one batch, `Removed` and `Created` together. Third, the guarantee needs a queue: a polled directory (NFS, a failed watch) has none, its `drain` returns nothing and its listing decides, which design.md, spec.md and architecture.md now say. Tests: `a_module_back_on_disk_after_a_listing_missed_it_waits_for_the_grace` (each listing in a save gap, the file back before the flush looks; fails with the second look restored) and `a_rename_made_as_a_listing_batch_is_cut_is_one_batch` (fails keeping only the missed module), in `crates/strand-watch/src/core.rs::tests`.

**2026-11-04 · save-blank: a module whose removal was heard before the flush waits with the set.** Review of the second round found the set's wait held only inside `rescan_config`: a module in the batch whose removal had been heard before it was cut (the old name of a rename heard normally, `mv bar.strand panel.strand`) was still read by the flush, found missing, and reported `Removed` by that read, its event not in the flush's drain, while `panel.strand` joined only at the next flush a grace later; so when another module's delete-then-create save was in its gap at that flush, the rename was split again, the loader without the bar's declarations for 50 ms (the bar gone, or the batch held back when something referenced it), where the first round's commit had reported both names together. When the set waits, every module the listing left out now counts as unsettled for that flush, so its read is put off like the waiting module's, and the next flush's listing reports the rename (or a removal) in one batch with the other save. Test: `a_rename_heard_while_another_module_waits_is_one_batch` (`crates/strand-watch/src/core.rs::tests`; fails without the change, the first flush reporting `bar.strand` `Removed`).

**2026-11-04 · save-blank: a module waiting with the set keeps the grace, not its batch's bound.** Review of the third round found that putting the old name's read off (`defer`) gave it a `Deferred` entry dated by its batch's first event, and a deferred read keeps the bound of the batch it was first due in, `max_delay` after that event. For a batch cut at `max_delay` because events kept coming, that bound is the 15 ms retry, shorter than the 50 ms grace of the removal the set was waiting for; the next flush then listed the set inside that save's gap, its `DELETE` already drained by the flush before, nothing in the queue to wait for, and reported `colors.strand` `Removed`: the same blank. The modules that wait with the set are now not read at all that flush: they go back to the open batch unread, with its event times (so the next batch still reports the rename's first event) and without a `Deferred` entry (one an earlier flush left is dropped), so the next flush comes the removal grace after the drained event. Test: `a_rename_waiting_with_the_set_at_max_delay_keeps_the_grace` (`crates/strand-watch/src/core.rs::tests`; fails without the change, the next flush 15 ms after the cut).

**2026-11-04 · save-blank: the invariant, not another path: a module or watched file whose removal was heard and whose removal grace has not run out is never reported `Removed`, whatever flush, deadline or deferral brought that flush about.** A read-only check of the fourth round found a fifth path to the same blank: the flush that waits with the set still reads every other touched file, and one that reads as torn there (a `MODIFY` drained with the `DELETE` it waits for) is put off with its batch's bound, 15 ms on for a batch cut at `max_delay`; the next flush listed the set inside `colors.strand`'s gap, its `DELETE` drained the flush before, the queue empty, and reported it `Removed`, since `rescan_config` looked only at what its own flush drained, never at the removal already heard. Each round had closed one way a flush could come inside the grace; the fix now holds the property itself. The core keeps `removals`, each path (as events name it) whose latest event was a removal with when it was heard, dropped by a later write to it and once its grace is over. `rescan_config` keeps the set as it was when a module the listing left out has such a removal in its grace (`removal_in_grace`, the module's path, the file it resolves to or a link or directory on the way), as it already did for one the queue it drains shows removed, created or being written; and a flush's read that finds a watched file gone does the same for that file, which covers files no listing looks at (a settings file in a batch cut at `max_delay`, its `DELETE` drained, read again 15 ms later: the same blank for that file). Either way the file goes back to the open batch unread, with the batch's event times, no `Deferred` entry and its removal among the batch's removals (`wait_for_grace`), so the next flush comes the grace after it, and if it is still missing then it is `Removed`. What the earlier rounds added stays where it still does work: draining the queue when the listing leaves a module out (a removal not yet heard has no entry, round 1 and 2), the read's `Err` counted as torn when the drain names the file (now only a re-creation queued behind the read, the removal before it superseded), and the whole set waiting with every module the listing left out (a rename's old name whose own grace is over, round 2 and 3); round 3's putting those modules back unread without a `Deferred` entry is now `wait_for_grace`, shared with the read, and done inside `rescan_config`, so it no longer returns the modules for `flush` to put back. design.md's coalesce step, spec.md 10.5 and architecture.md's `FileBatch` state the property. Tests: `a_torn_read_while_the_set_waits_keeps_the_grace` (the reviewer's path; fails without `rescan_config`'s check, `colors.strand` `Removed` 15 ms after the cut) and `a_file_read_in_a_save_gap_at_max_delay_keeps_the_grace` (fails without the read's check), in `crates/strand-watch/src/core.rs::tests`, each also run `again` and not (the file back within the grace is one `Modified`; still gone, it is `Removed` once the grace is over); the earlier rounds' tests pass unchanged. `five_save_styles_land_on_a_cold_boot` run 32 at a time passed 1280 of 1280 afterwards; the same loop on `main`'s watcher failed 31 of 320, every one "round 23 (style 3): a blank frame".

## power-reask

**2026-11-04 · power-reask: a profile the daemon settles away from right after a write is asked once more, within two seconds, then followed.** On the owner's laptop `power.profile = power_saver` while on `performance` ended on `balanced`: the firmware offers only balanced and performance (`/sys/firmware/acpi/platform_profile_choices`), so power-profiles-daemon writes `balanced` to it for power saver, then reads its own write back as a switch to `balanced`; from `balanced` the same write takes, since the firmware's value does not change. Strand reported the write as done and then followed the daemon, so a menu that cycles skipped power saver, and the owner's shell had to remember the profile it asked for and ask again itself. The service now does that: after a `Set` the daemon took, a `PropertiesChanged` within `SETTLE` (2 s) that names another active profile asks for the written one again, once, before the change is shown, so the shell never sees the passing `balanced`; whatever the daemon says after that second ask is followed, so a daemon that will not take the profile is not argued with, and a switch it makes on its own (a key, `powerprofilesctl`) after the window is followed as before. Two seconds, not less, because it is what the owner's shell used on the machine, and the daemon's file monitor need not report its own write at once; a real switch from elsewhere inside two seconds of the shell's own write (a firmware key, `powerprofilesctl set`) comes through the same path in the daemon as its own write read back, so it cannot be told apart: it is asked back to the shell's profile once, which undoes it, and a second press is followed. That is accepted because it needs the switch within two seconds of the shell's own write. The alternative the issue allowed, documenting that a write may settle elsewhere and leaving the retry to each config, was not taken: it adds a concept every profile menu has to know, while the service already knows the write it made. The re-ask is skipped when the profile is no longer offered, and a refused re-ask is logged and the daemon's profile shown, as a refused write is (power-media-kbd). The test stands in for the daemon with a client of its own on the private bus, as `target/try/notes/looks/ppd_quirk.py` did on top of python-dbusmock's template: it watches `ActiveProfile` and switches the mock to `balanced` 80 ms after `power-saver` lands from `performance` (or always), through the mock's `UpdateProperties`, so the mock's log holds only the service's `Set`s. Tests: `crates/strand-services/tests/power.rs::{a_profile_the_daemon_settles_away_from_is_asked_once_more, a_daemon_that_settles_elsewhere_again_is_followed}`; both fail with the second ask removed (one `Set`, `balanced` shown), and the second fails with the window removed (the daemon's own later switch asked away).

**2026-11-04 · power-reask: a hold is never asked away, and the daemon's signals are read before the next write.** Review of the first cut found two holes. A hold another program takes (gamemode, `powerprofilesctl launch -p performance`, a config's own `from dbus` `HoldProfile` action) right after the shell's write switched the profile inside the window, so the service asked the written profile back, and power-profiles-daemon treats a `Set` of `ActiveProfile` as a manual switch that releases every hold: the hold was cancelled, where before it was followed. The daemon's `HoldProfile` reports the profile and `ActiveProfileHolds` in one `PropertiesChanged` (`send_dbus_event` with both bits of its mask), and the shell's own `Set` empties the holds, so a non-empty `ActiveProfileHolds` once the change is applied means a hold made the switch: it is followed and the second ask is spent (`held`). Second, the loop picked between a ready signal and a ready write at random (`tokio::select!`), so after two writes in a row (a cycle key pressed twice) the echo of the first could be read after the second write as the daemon settling away from it, spending the second ask on it and leaving the daemon's real bounce followed, the bug this track fixes. The daemon emits a write's echo before it answers the `Set` and zbus queues signals in order, so the echo is always waiting when the next write is read; the loop is now `biased` toward the daemon's signals, which reads it first. Rejected: skipping a stale echo by comparing it with the profile written before (a bounce to `balanced` after `balanced` then `power_saver` were written would look stale too). The first test's check that the shell never showed `balanced` is what the shell showed at its pumps, a few milliseconds apart, so it cannot see a blip shorter than that; the service's single update after the second ask is what guarantees it. Tests: `crates/strand-services/tests/power.rs::{a_hold_taken_right_after_a_write_is_followed, a_profile_withdrawn_or_refused_is_not_asked_again, two_writes_in_a_row_still_ask_once_more}`, `crates/strand-services/src/power.rs::tests::an_active_hold_is_one_listed`; the first fails without the hold check (a second `Set` of `balanced`), the second fails with the offered check removed and with a refused second ask shown as taken, and the third fails without `biased` in three runs of four at four rounds (it runs eight).

## screen-position

**2026-11-04 · screen-position: a `Screen` has its place in the layout, `x` and `y`, and `screens.all` is in layout order, left to right by `x` first, then top to bottom by `y`.** The owner's shell sets a wallpaper per monitor left to right and had to ask `hyprctl -j monitors` and sort by `x` with jq, so it worked only on Hyprland: `Screen` had its size and scale but not where the monitor sits, and `screens.all` was in plug order, which nothing documented. Both halves of the issue's "done when" are taken, since each alone leaves a config guessing: the place lets a config order or lay out monitors its own way, and the order makes the common case (`for s in screens.all`, `screens.all.first`) right with no sort. The place is xdg-output's logical position, which the surface layer already kept as `Monitor::position` for the tray's click point, in logical pixels like `width` and `height` (and `float` as they are); a compositor that never says gives 0, as an unknown size does, since every compositor Strand targets sends xdg-output and a nullable field would make every reader write `?? 0`. The order sorts by `x` first, not by rows (`y` first): a monitor to the right that sits a little higher (a common offset between two panels of different heights) stays after its left neighbour, where reading order would put it first; monitors at one `x` (stacked) go top to bottom, and monitors at one place, or with none known, keep their plug order (a stable sort), so a compositor without xdg-output keeps today's order. The sort is on the logic thread where main's list arrives (`Focus::screens`), so `screens.focused`'s fallback while no compositor names a focus, "the first monitor", is now the leftmost rather than the first plugged in; bars and per-monitor panels are keyed by `Screen.id`, so a monitor moved reorders them without mounting anything again. A monitor moved is already a `monitor_changed` (its position is part of `Geometry`), so the order follows the layout live (the lock's surfaces too: this track's last paragraph). The eval sandbox gives each screen its scenario `x` and `y` (a replay's: each live output's recorded position), so a config reading `screen.x` replays as it ran; its screens stay in the scenario's order, which for a replay is the live `screens.all`'s (`bundle.json`'s `order`). Tests: `screens_are_in_layout_order`, `screens_all_has_each_place_in_layout_order` (fails without the sort), `screens_all_follows_the_layout_as_the_monitors_move` on headless sway (HEADLESS-2 moved left of HEADLESS-1, back to its right but raised, then stacked above it; fails without the sort and without the position), `eval/tests/smoke.rs::each_screen_has_its_place_in_the_layout` (fails without the harness's `x` and `y`).

**2026-11-04 · screen-position: the lock's first monitor is the leftmost on both threads.** Review found that sorting `screens.all` split the lock: with no monitor focused (always on labwc, wayfire and river, which have no focus adapter, and on the others until the follower first reports), logic gives a `screens: focused` lock's single instance `screens.focused`, now the leftmost monitor, while the surface layer put that instance on the lowest `wl_output` global, the first advertised; before, both were plug order and agreed. On a laptop whose built-in panel is advertised first but sits right of an external monitor, the lock showed on the panel laid out for the other monitor's size, its `thumbnail screen` showing the other monitor. The surface layer's fallback (`lock_output`, through `first_in_layout`) now takes the output whose monitor is least by `x`, then `y`, an unknown position as 0, 0, as logic's sort does; at one place the lowest global stands in for plug order (the two differ only for monitors at one place replugged in another order, where either is a guess), and an output whose monitor is not known yet comes last, since logic does not list it. Logic does not send main its pick instead: the order is one rule the two threads apply to the same positions, and `follows_focus` panels stay the compositor's to place while no focus is named. The sandbox keeps a scenario's screens in the order given; docs/eval.md now says to list them in layout order, the only order live has (a replay's already are), rather than the harness sorting them, which would part `screens.focused` from the screen its surfaces map on. `screens_are_in_layout_order` also checks the sort is stable over 48 screens at two places, since a short slice is insertion-sorted and stays in order under an unstable sort too. Tests: `the_first_monitor_is_the_leftmost` (fails with the lowest global), `an_unfocused_lock_shows_on_the_leftmost_monitor` in the lock VM (HEADLESS-1, advertised first, placed right of the second output; fails without the fix).

**2026-11-04 · screen-position: a monitor moved while locked moves the lock's content to the new leftmost.** Review found the fix above held only for the layout at lock time: `lock_output` reads each monitor's place, but only an output added or removed, a focus set and the lock's own spec changes placed the lock's surfaces again, while a monitor that only moved arrives as `update_output` (its `Geometry` changed), which refitted the layer surfaces and told logic (`monitor_changed`, so `screens.focused`, and with it the lock instance's `screen`, became the new leftmost) but left the content where it was. With no monitor focused (labwc, wayfire and river always; main is told a pick only for a named screen) nothing else moved it, so docked while locked and then rearranged by kanshi, the lock showed on the old leftmost with the new one's `screen`, the split the paragraph above closed. `update_output`'s geometry branch now calls `sync_lock_surfaces` after `monitor_changed`, every geometry change rather than only a moved one, since it returns at once with no lock and changes nothing when the outputs it wants are the ones it has. Test: `an_unfocused_lock_shows_on_the_leftmost_monitor` in the lock VM now also moves the second output right and HEADLESS-1 to 0, 0 while locked and waits for the content on HEADLESS-1 and the solid on the other (fails without the call: no content on HEADLESS-1 within the wait).

## player-raise-seek

**2026-11-04 · player-raise-seek: a player raises with `raise()`, seeks by an offset with `seek(by: duration)` and names its app with `icon` and `app`.** The owner's Media page could not take you to the browser tab that plays, its 15 s skips wrote `position` as a fraction of `length` (nothing on a stream of unknown length), and a row could not show the app's icon beside the art. `media.raise()` and `p.raise()` call MPRIS `Raise` on the root interface; `can_raise` is its `CanRaise`, a player that does not say counting as able as `can_next` does (decisions.md m6-service-gaps: "an unreported property counts as able"; and MPRIS makes `CanRaise` a required property, as it does `CanGoNext`, so a player that leaves it out is not saying it cannot), and unlike `can_next` it does not read `CanControl`, which MPRIS scopes to the `Player` interface; `raise()` is not sent while it is false. `seek(by)` calls `Seek` with the offset in microseconds, so it needs only `CanSeek` (and `CanControl` not false), not the track's length, and `can_seek_by` says so (the paragraph below). The time shows the target at once, as a `position` write's does, held to 0 and to a known length (MPRIS: a seek past the end acts as `Next`, whose `Metadata` follows), and the player's `Seeked` corrects it; a failed `Seek` asks the position again. `icon` and `app` follow `Window` (decisions.md m6-w2-services): the app name is `DesktopEntry` (without a `.desktop` its writer may add), else the bus name without the MPRIS prefix and an `.instance…` part, which is how players name multiple instances (`chromium.instance12345`, `firefox.instance_1_42`); it is found with `AppIndex::find` and drawn with `window_icon`, so an entry's icon wins, then the name when the theme has it, else the name as it is, as a window's `icon` is its app id then: `media.icon` is null only with no player, so a fallback for an unknown app is `media.app?.icon ?? "audio-x-generic"`, which gives up the theme's icon for a name no entry matches (the track's last paragraph). `Player.icon` is `text` as `Window.icon` is, `media.icon` `text?` as `media.player` is (null with no player). The issue offered `icon` or `app`; both are given, as a window has both, so `p.app?.name` and `p.app?.launch()` need no second lookup. Tests: `tests/media.rs::players_raise_seek_by_an_offset_and_name_their_app`, `src/media.rs::tests::{seeking_by_an_offset_moves_from_where_it_is, the_root_names_the_player_and_whether_it_raises, a_players_icon_and_app_come_from_its_desktop_entry}`, strand's `the_players_raise_seek_and_app_check`.

**2026-11-04 · player-raise-seek: `can_seek_by` says `seek(by)` works, and `can_seek` keeps saying a `position` write does.** As first landed, `seek(by)` had no flag of its own: `can_seek` (`CanSeek` and a known length, decisions.md m6-service-gaps) is false on exactly the stream the issue is about, so a shell gating its skips on it lost them there, and one showing them always had dead buttons on a player that reports `CanSeek` false (a browser's live stream), while `raise()` had `can_raise`. Two readings were weighed. Letting `can_seek` mean "the player seeks" (`CanSeek` and `CanControl`) and a scrubber gate on `can_seek && length != null` removes a flag, but it changes what an existing field says: every shell that shows its scrubber on `can_seek` (the owner's Media page does, `if p.can_seek` around its slider) would show a slider on a stream that a write cannot move, a regression in a config that did nothing wrong. So `can_seek` keeps its meaning, the very test a `position` write makes, and `media.can_seek_by` and each `Player`'s `can_seek_by` are MPRIS `CanSeek` as `can_next` reads `CanGoNext` (a player that does not say counts as able, `CanControl` false makes it false), whatever the length, read by the same `Player::can_seek_by` that `seek_by` asks, so the flag and the action agree as `can_raise` and `raise()` do. A shell's skip buttons gate on `can_seek_by`, its scrubber on `can_seek`. Tests: `src/media.rs::tests::seeking_by_an_offset_moves_from_where_it_is` (true on a stream where `can_seek` is false, false with `CanSeek` or `CanControl` false and with no player), `tests/media.rs::players_raise_seek_by_an_offset_and_name_their_app` (the stream's `can_seek_by`, and an item's raise reaching that player while another is active), strand's `the_players_raise_seek_and_app_check` (read only, and a skip gated on it checks).

**2026-11-04 · player-raise-seek: a negative duration crosses to a service with its sign.** `seek(by: -15s)` is how a skip back is written, and `-15s` already checks (unary `-` takes any number, durations included) and is −15,000 ms in the VM; but `Data::Duration` holds a `std::time::Duration`, so `to_data` turned it into 0 and the skip back did nothing. The other readings were worse: a `back: bool` argument or a second action adds a concept the language already has (a signed duration), and an argument in seconds as `float` drops the unit the issue named. So `Data` gains `NegDuration(Duration)`, a duration below zero by its size, written by `to_data` (and read back by `to_value` and a custom service's typed conversion, so the round trip is lossless) and as negative milliseconds in a report's JSON. `strand_services::Offset` (seconds, `schema_type` `duration`) reads it with its sign; `Duration`'s `FromData` reads it as zero, which is what every service taking a duration (`idle.after`, `battery.history`) received before, and `idle.after`'s own match goes through that `FromData` so its answer is unchanged. A duration no `Duration` holds (NaN, infinite) is still zero. architecture.md's `Data` paragraph says so. Tests: `src/data.rs::tests::a_negative_duration_keeps_its_sign_as_an_offset`, strand's `services::convert::tests::values_and_data_convert_both_ways`.

**2026-11-04 · player-raise-seek: the root interface is followed, and the desktop entries are read only for the players' app names.** `Identity` was read once on arrival; now the root interface is read whole (`GetAll`: `Identity`, `CanRaise`, `DesktopEntry`) in the same read, and each root `PropertiesChanged` is applied at once and asks the root again under a newer number, an older answer landing later being dropped (`Player::root_asked`): root signals are rare, so a reread per signal costs nothing and no change can be undone by a read asked before it. A player whose root does not answer has no name from it and counts as raisable, as before it had no `Identity`. The app lookup copies the windows service's shape without its standing index: the names not looked up yet (or, after `apps::changes()`, every name) are looked up in one blocking task that reads the entries, answers each name with `AppIndex::window` and drops the index, so the media service holds a few strings per player rather than every entry; one lookup runs at a time, answers stand until newer ones land, and a player shows its app name as its icon until then, as a window shows its app id. An answer that shows nothing new (the name itself, no app) updates nothing, so a shell that reads only `media.title` is not woken by the lookup (`media_follows_the_active_player_without_polling` caught that). A failed lookup answers its names as unmatched until the entries change, so a panic is not retried in a loop. Tests: as above, and `src/media.rs::tests::the_root_names_the_player_and_whether_it_raises` for the stale root answer.

**2026-11-04 · player-raise-seek: `icon`'s two fallbacks are named, and no flag says the theme has it.** The docs gave `image media.app?.icon ?? "audio-x-generic"` as the fallback "when the theme lacks the name", but `app` is null whenever no desktop entry matches, so a player with no entry whose name the theme has (a `spotify` icon, no `spotify.desktop`) drew the generic icon where `image media.icon` drew the right one. `image` draws nothing for an icon name it cannot find, and `icon` is never null while a player runs, so no `??` keeps a themed bare name and still falls back. A `media.icon_found`-style flag (or `icon` null when neither the entry nor the theme has it) would make one expression do both, but it adds a field `Window.icon` lacks for the same case, and a shell that wants the theme's icon already has it in `image media.icon`. So `icon` keeps `Window.icon`'s meaning and the docs (`media.icon`, `Player.icon`, design.md) name the choice: `image media.icon` keeps the theme's icon for an app with no entry and shows nothing for one neither knows; `image media.app?.icon ?? "audio-x-generic"` always shows an icon, the generic one whenever no entry matches. Test: `src/media.rs::tests::a_players_icon_and_app_come_from_its_desktop_entry` (an unmatched name's icon is the name itself and its app null).

## list-selection

**2026-11-04 · list-selection: a `list` says where its selection starts with `selected_index: n`, the row it starts on in place of the first, waited for until the rows reach it.** The owner's launcher opens its Themes page on the theme in use, and took three handlers and a hold on the preview to do it: the list mounts once the box has dropped (110 ms after it opens), its first row selected, and the themes, read only while the page shows, come in about then, so `results.select(theme_at)` either ran before the list was there or after the first theme's colours had flashed (strand-issues, "A `list` has no way to start on a row"). The issue suggested `selected: theme_at`; the prop is `selected_index:` instead, since `selected` is already a row's own `bool` (`when self.selected`, `r.selected`) and a list is often a row of another, while `results.selected_index` is already the list's `int?` place among its rows: one name for one thing, as `open:` written on a popup and `p.open` read back are, and no new concept, since it only says which row the existing first-row rule picks. It is one-way: `results.selected_index` already reads the user's moves back, so `<->` would add a second way to say the same. It is selected wherever a `nav:` list would select its first row (it mounts or comes back, its rows arrive, a new query, its surface opening again, its rows changing under the same text) and, on any list, when it mounts and whenever its value changes, while the user has not moved the selection since; that is the rule rows changing under the same query already follow (`moved`: an arrow, a click or a list action), so a start that follows the data (`names.index_of(n => n == current)`) never takes the selection from someone using the arrows, and a new query lets it follow again. A row past the rows is waited for rather than clamped to the last, which is what "kept until the rows it names are there" asks and what keeps a page whose rows arrive in pieces from landing short: nothing is selected meanwhile, `selected_index` reads `n` (as for a row on its way past the window), and the start lands, scrolled into view, when its row arrives; an arrow moves from there as from any row on its way, and Return goes where `select(n)` would (the last row) rather than waiting for a row that may never come. Null starts as the list would without it, and turning null leaves the selection alone, so `selected_index: view == theme_list ? theme_at : null` changes nothing on the other pages. The router reads it as `Prop::SelectedIndex`, follows a change after `prune` and before rows on their way land, so rows and their start arriving in one change go straight to the start, the first row never selected (and never told) on the way. Tests (`crates/strand-compiler/tests/selection.rs`): `a_list_starts_on_its_selected_index`, `a_start_past_the_rows_waits_for_its_row`, `rows_and_their_start_arriving_together_land_on_it` (the Themes page), `a_changed_start_moves_the_selection_until_the_user_moves_it`, `return_while_the_start_waits_activates_where_select_would`, `a_start_beyond_the_window_is_scrolled_to`.

**2026-11-04 · list-selection: when the selected row leaves and other rows stay, the selection stays at its place, on the row that takes it.** Clearing the selected notification on the launcher's Notifications page moved the selection to the list's first row, Do not disturb: the router dropped a selected row logic removed and left the list with none, and a `nav:` list's first-row rule then picked row 0; `results.select(i)` in the clearing handler ran before the row went, so the launcher kept the place in a `keep_at` state and selected it again on `found_notes.len` (strand-issues, "A list's selection goes to its first row when the selected row leaves"). A list now keeps a selection whose row logic removed (a `Remove` without `window`; a window scrolling past it already kept it by its index) at its global index, landed as a row on its way: the row after it moves up into its place, or the new last row takes it when it was the last, and `selected_index` does not change, so a preview read from it shows the row that came up. This is what a file manager or a mail client does when the selected entry is deleted, and the arrow the user would press next is where they were. It applies only while some row that was in the list before the change is still in it: when every row is replaced (another page of a shared list, a tray menu entered) or none is left, the selection starts again as before, on the list's start or a `nav:` list's first row, since the place belonged to rows that are gone. A new query in a `nav:` input still starts its results at the top, as it did. Tests: `a_selected_row_that_leaves_leaves_the_selection_at_its_place` (a `nav:` list and a focused one, the row in the middle and the last), `a_selected_row_leaving_a_windowed_list_keeps_its_place`, `rows_replaced_whole_start_the_selection_again`, with `selected_index_is_reactive_and_null_without_a_selection` and `a_remounted_list_stays_correct_with_nav` unchanged.

**2026-11-04 · list-selection: a list that starts again forgets the user's move, Return on a start with no rows does nothing, and the first-row rule still shows its row.** Review found three faults in the two decisions above. First, starting again kept `moved`: the user moving on one page of a shared list (the launcher's `results`, whose pages are `if view == …` blocks under one unchanged query) and then opening another whose rows are all replaced left the list marked as moved, so the start that came with the new page's rows (`theme_at`, the place of the theme in use, arriving with the themes a tick after the page) was never followed, the waiting start for the empty page landed on row 0, and the first theme was selected and previewed, the very flash the start was for. Whatever starts a list on its start (the rows replaced whole, its surface opening again, a new query, the first-row rule finding no selection) now forgets the move, since the place the user moved to belonged to rows that are gone or another query's; spec.md 6.7 already said such a list "starts again" and follows its value "while the user has not moved the selection since", and a list without a start keeps the old behaviour. Second, Return on a list whose start waited with no rows at all queued an activation that fired on the start row whenever rows came, possibly much later, on a row the user never saw; `select(n)` on an empty list does nothing, so Return now does nothing too. Third, a `nav:` list the user had not moved, scrolled away from the top by the wheel or `scroll_to`, no longer scrolled its new first row into view when the first row left, because the kept place landed without a reveal and the first-row rule then found its row already selected; the kept place is revealed on a focused input's `nav:` list the user has not moved, so that rule shows its row as it did, and stays unrevealed elsewhere, where a row leaving moves no view. Tests: `a_start_after_the_rows_are_replaced_is_followed_again`, `return_while_the_start_waits_activates_where_select_would` (its empty case), `the_first_row_rule_still_shows_its_row_after_one_leaves`, each failing before the fix, and two cases the first decision named without a test: `a_surface_opening_again_starts_on_the_start`, `rows_changing_under_the_same_text_go_to_the_start`.

**2026-11-04 · list-selection: a selection away from the mounted rows starts again too, and starting again forgets the move with or without a start.** A second review found the decision above held only while the selection was on a mounted row. The router records a selected row logic removes, but a virtualised list's selection the wheel had scrolled out of its window is not on a row: it waits as an `Away` by its global index, so a page change replacing every row recorded nothing, kept the move, and landed the old index on the new page (the launcher's Apps page scrolled away from its selection, then Themes: the wrong theme selected and previewed, `theme_at` never followed). A `Remove` names only its row, so the router now notes the rows of each list whose selection is away when it finishes routing (nothing while none is), and a diff removing one of them is a row leaving that list: while rows from before stay the selection stays on its way, as a scrolled-away place should, and when none does the list starts again as one with a selected row does. Starting again also forgot the move only through the start itself, so a page whose start was null while it was empty (`names.index_of(…)` over no names) kept the move and never followed the start that came with its rows; the move is now forgotten whether or not there is a start, since the reason given above (the place belonged to rows that are gone) does not depend on it. And a `nav:` list whose surface opens again dropped its selection and its move but not a selection away, which then landed on the old row instead of the start; it is dropped too. Tests: `rows_replaced_whole_start_an_away_selection_again`, `a_start_after_the_rows_are_replaced_is_followed_again` (its null start) and `a_surface_opening_again_starts_on_the_start` (its windowed list), each failing before the fix.

**2026-11-04 · list-selection: the rows of a list whose selection is away are noted only when they can have changed, and a Return waiting on such a selection goes with rows replaced whole.** A check of the decision above found two loose ends. The router noted those rows at the end of every routing, pointer motion included: with a selection scrolled away (the launcher's common case) that cleared and refilled a map of every mounted row of the list, up to the 1,024 rows of a virtualised window, on each motion event, where routing was constant time before. Only logic's diffs change which rows the tree has (a window's rows too are mounted by a diff), so the router now notes them again only after a diff that creates, removes or moves nodes, or when the set of lists whose selection is away changes; `Router::away_rows_noted` counts the notes for the test. Second, a Return pressed on a selection away from the mounted rows (or on a waiting start whose row is not mounted yet) waits for its row to land, and when logic replaces the rows whole before it does, the list starts again and the waiting Return is dropped: it was for a row that is gone, and activating whatever row took the old index on the new page (as before the decision above) would act on a row the user never chose, which is the reason Return on a start with no rows does nothing. spec.md 6.7 says so. Tests: `pointer_motion_does_not_note_the_away_rows_again` (failing when the rows are noted on every routing) and `a_waiting_return_goes_with_rows_replaced_whole` (failing with the old behaviour, which activated row 5 of the new page).

## panel-change-closed

**2026-11-04 · panel-change-closed: a closed surface's handlers wait and run once for what they missed when it opens, and an `on change` there notes each tick's value, so a change made in the tick that opens the surface is seen too.** The owner's launcher (strand-issues.md, "A panel's `on change` handlers seem not to run while it is closed") wrote `on change view { theme_held = view == theme_list }` inside `panel Launcher`, and Alt+T, a handler that sets `view` and `open` together while the panel is closed, never set `theme_held`; the same line at the top level worked. Reproduced offline, on a copy of the owner's four files and on a reduced panel (`a_panels_on_change_sees_the_tick_that_opens_it`), two ways. A surface's content mounted the first time it was shown, so its `on change` was created in the tick that opened it and took the new `view` as its first value (spec.md 8.4: never for the first value). Later, the content was frozen with `rt.suspend`, whose held sinks run once on resume and compare with the value they last saw: the launcher closes from the Themes page, its `on hide` sends `view` home while frozen, and Alt+T puts `themes` back, so the handler saw themes then themes and did not run; only opening on a page other than the one it closed on worked. spec.md never said whether a surface's handlers run while it is closed. The rule now (spec.md 5.1 and 8.4, design.md "Events and time"): while a `bar`, `panel`, `osd` or `window` is closed only its own events run, its `on change`, service and timer handlers and its elements' wait and its timers pause, as before; when it opens, what they missed runs once, as before, an `on change` running if what it watches differs from what it last saw while the surface was open; and an `on change` also runs for a change made in the tick that opens the surface, compared with the value at the end of the tick before, even one that puts back what it last saw (the second failure). In a surface that starts closed the `on change` handlers written in its body exist from the start (each mounted with the surface in its own scope, frozen), so the first opening counts too; before it they have seen nothing open, so a change made earlier does not run them, as when they mounted at the first opening. Its elements and components still mount the first time it opens, and an `on change` in one of them takes the value it mounts with as its first, so it does not see the tick that first opens the surface: the issue is closed for the surface's own handlers, and for its elements' from the second opening on; a handler that must see the first opening is written in the body. A popup mounts its content each time it opens, so its handlers start from the values it opens with, and the lock keeps its own logic (`lock_logic`, plain `suspend`; lock code is tried only in the lock VM). Rejected: running a surface's handlers while it is closed, like top-level ones, which needs its whole body mounted from boot (its `let`s and element ids are its content's), wakes what a closed menu should not, and is a different program from the one the owner wrote; mounting the whole content at boot, frozen, which puts every closed panel's tree on the scene at boot and still needs the note of each tick for later openings; and dropping the old catch-up (an earlier draft of this fix), which left a handler that keeps state in step with something outside (`on change src { mine = src }`, in a component that has no `on show` to catch up with) stale after the surface reopened. Compatibility (spec.md 14): no syntax changes; the behaviour of a handler in a closed surface was unspecified and its catch-up undocumented; what is new is the run for the opening tick's change and, in a surface that starts closed, its body's handlers reading what they watch from boot, so a watched value from an action with a result (`let r = calc(q)`) runs the action while the surface is closed (`a_closed_panels_body_on_change_reads_what_it_watches`; on the old code nothing read it until the first opening). Keeping such a handler out of the early mount would need the checker to trace what each watched value loads, and a handler that sees the first opening only sometimes is a rule more to learn, so the read is documented instead. A top-level `on change` and one in an open surface behave as before, and the handlers of one tick still run in the order written: a surface that starts open mounts all of its body at once, and one that starts closed renumbers each early handler's scope where it is written when the rest mounts (`Runtime::renumber`, what `reparent` already did to a moved subtree), since sinks of one rank run in the order made. In strand-core, `Runtime::suspend_closed(scope)` is `suspend` with one difference: a sink marked `keep_up_while_closed` (the compiler marks its `on change` effects and its debounce-duration effect, so an `on change … after` in a closed body exists before it opens) that only closed scopes hold is not left held but run when the flush has settled (`keep_up_closed`, each once per flush), an `on change` then only noting the value (`keeping_up`), and run once more when released (`kept_up`), when it compares the value with both the one it last saw open and the noted one. The mark is opt-in: a `persist` or settings tracker in a closed surface is held as before, so a value written in the tick that closes the surface is still saved when it opens (with keep-up on every `on change`, the tracker took the new value as its baseline and never armed its save). A scope also suspended for a fault holds everything as before. Tests: `crates/strand-core/tests/disposal.rs::a_closed_scopes_on_change_keeps_up_and_sees_the_flush_that_opens_it`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::{a_panels_on_change_sees_the_tick_that_opens_it, a_panels_handlers_see_the_tick_that_opens_it, a_closed_panels_on_change_runs_once_for_what_it_missed, a_reopened_panels_handlers_catch_up, a_surfaces_handlers_run_in_the_order_written, a_persisted_state_written_as_its_panel_closes_is_saved}`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/flex.rs::a_closed_panels_body_on_change_reads_what_it_watches`; the first two fail on the old code, the catch-up, order and save tests on the earlier draft; the owner's launcher with the line back in the panel sets `theme_held` on every Alt+T with the fix and never without it (a throwaway test, not kept).

The rule now (spec.md 5.1 and 8.4, design.md "Events and time"): while a `bar`, `panel`, `osd` or `window` is closed only its own events run, its `on change`, service and timer handlers and its elements' wait and its timers pause, as before; when it opens, what they missed runs once, as before, an `on change` running if what it watches differs from what it last saw while the surface was open; and an `on change` also runs for a change made in the tick that opens the surface, compared with the value at the end of the tick before, even one that puts back what it last saw (the second failure). In a surface that starts closed the `on change` handlers written in its body exist from the start (each mounted with the surface in its own scope, frozen), so the first opening counts too; before it they have seen nothing open, so a change made earlier does not run them, as when they mounted at the first opening. Its elements and components still mount the first time it opens, and an `on change` in one of them takes the value it mounts with as its first, so it does not see the tick that first opens the surface: the issue is closed for the surface's own handlers, and for its elements' from the second opening on; a handler that must see the first opening is written in the body. A popup mounts its content each time it opens, so its handlers start from the values it opens with, and the lock keeps its own logic (`lock_logic`, plain `suspend`; lock code is tried only in the lock VM). Rejected: running a surface's handlers while it is closed, like top-level ones, which needs its whole body mounted from boot (its `let`s and element ids are its content's), wakes what a closed menu should not, and is a different program from the one the owner wrote; mounting the whole content at boot, frozen, which puts every closed panel's tree on the scene at boot and still needs the note of each tick for later openings; and dropping the old catch-up (an earlier draft of this fix), which left a handler that keeps state in step with something outside (`on change src { mine = src }`, in a component that has no `on show` to catch up with) stale after the surface reopened. Compatibility (spec.md 14): no syntax changes; the behaviour of a handler in a closed surface was unspecified and its catch-up undocumented; what is new is the run for the opening tick's change and, in a surface that starts closed, its body's handlers reading what they watch from boot, so a watched value from an action with a result (`let r = calc(q)`) runs the action while the surface is closed (`a_closed_panels_body_on_change_reads_what_it_watches`; on the old code nothing read it until the first opening). Keeping such a handler out of the early mount would need the checker to trace what each watched value loads, and a handler that sees the first opening only sometimes is a rule more to learn, so the read is documented instead. A top-level `on change` and one in an open surface behave as before, and a surface's handlers that mount together still run in the order written: a surface that starts open mounts all of its body at once, and one that starts closed renumbers each early handler's scope where it is written when the rest mounts (`Runtime::renumber`, what `reparent` already did to a moved subtree), since sinks of one rank run in the order made. That is all the order spec.md 5.1 promises: a handler in an `if` or `match` branch, a `for` row or a popup that mounts later is made then and may run after a handler of its rank written below it, as on the old code (the review of this track found a first wording, "wherever they are", promised more). In strand-core, `Runtime::suspend_closed(scope)` is `suspend` with one difference: a sink marked `keep_up_while_closed` (the compiler marks its `on change` effects and its debounce-duration effect, so an `on change … after` in a closed body exists before it opens) that only closed scopes hold is not left held but run when the flush has settled (`keep_up_closed`, each once per flush), an `on change` then only noting the value (`keeping_up`), and run once more when released (`kept_up`), when it compares the value with both the one it last saw open and the noted one. The mark is opt-in: a `persist` or settings tracker in a closed surface is held as before, so a value written in the tick that closes the surface is still saved when it opens (with keep-up on every `on change`, the tracker took the new value as its baseline and never armed its save). A scope also suspended for a fault holds everything as before. Tests: `crates/strand-core/tests/disposal.rs::a_closed_scopes_on_change_keeps_up_and_sees_the_flush_that_opens_it`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::{a_panels_on_change_sees_the_tick_that_opens_it, a_panels_handlers_see_the_tick_that_opens_it, a_closed_panels_on_change_runs_once_for_what_it_missed, a_reopened_panels_handlers_catch_up, a_surfaces_handlers_run_in_the_order_written, a_persisted_state_written_as_its_panel_closes_is_saved}`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/flex.rs::a_closed_panels_body_on_change_reads_what_it_watches`; the first two fail on the old code, the catch-up, order and save tests on the earlier draft; the owner's launcher with the line back in the panel sets `theme_held` on every Alt+T with the fix and never without it (a throwaway test, not kept).

## dictionary

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: `xs.contains(x)` on a keyed `state` or a service's keyed list follows the collection.** The query read the item by its key through core's `KeyedSignal::get_key`, which is untracked, so a binding that read the collection only through `.contains` never re-ran: a chip showing `pins.contains(p)` stayed `false` after the push. `KeyedQuery::Contains` (`vm/exec.rs`) now takes the key and the item inside one tracked `KeyedSignal::with`, still a lookup by key with no copy of the list, as `.len`, `.first`, `.last` and `[i]` already did. A view `let`'s `.contains` already read through the tracked `KeyedMemo::with`; it keeps a test beside the fix. It is the first step toward dictionaries (`[K: V]`, this track), whose reads go through the same accessors. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::a_binding_over_contains_reruns_when_the_keyed_state_changes` (fails on the old code: `false` through every write), `::a_binding_over_contains_on_a_view_reruns_when_the_keyed_state_changes`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a number key is one key whatever its tag: `int` and `float` are one plain number in `ValueKey`, not two units.** The design asked for key conformance: the key argument of `remove_key`, `move` and `update` conformed to the key field's declared type with `exec.rs::conform`, so a whole number computed as a float finds the `int` key 3. The code says that is not enough. A record is built without conforming its fields (`Op::MakeRecord`), and a whole-number literal where a `float` is expected is held as a float while an `int` state widened there keeps its tag, so the keys stored in a keyed collection already carry either tag: with `type Row { at: float; … }`, `Row(at: 3, …)` is keyed `3.0`, and `rows.remove_key(three)` with `state three = 3` missed it, as did `move`, `update`, `.contains` and `push`'s duplicate check (a second row keyed 3 went in). Conforming the argument alone would move the miss to the other side, and with `remove_key` now quiet on a miss (the next entry) a miss would be silent. So the rule is at the identity: `ValueKey`'s equality and hash take `int` and `float` as one unit (`key_unit`), on both sides of every keyed lookup, core's keyed collections, a service's keyed lists, a view's keys and a `for`'s row identities, whose text (`ident_of`) already showed `3` and `3.0` alike. A fractional number still misses an `int` key (3.5 is not 3), and every real unit stays a key of its own, as m5-docs3 settled (`2px` and `2ch` are two keys). The persisted keyed list, a plain cell, already found its items with `builtins::equal`, which compares numbers by value. A dictionary's sorted entries (a later step) must order `int` and `float` keys as this one unit, so its lookups agree with `ValueKey`. spec.md 6.5 says so. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::remove_key_finds_a_key_whatever_its_number_tag` (on a keyed `state` and a persisted one; the keyed `state` fails on the old code: nothing found, a duplicate pushed), `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/value.rs::tests::keys_hash_by_value` (`1.0` is the key `1`, `1.5` and `1px` are others).

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: `remove_key` of a key the collection does not hold does nothing; `move` and `update` of one stay errors.** The owner's answer to the design's third question: forgetting an item is idempotent, as a dictionary's `m.remove(k)` will be, so a handler can forget a key without first asking whether it is there. On a keyed `state` (core's collection) and on a persisted one (a plain list cell), the miss returns before any write, so an `on change` of the list does not fire. `move` and `update` name an item to act on, and a missing one is still the handler's error value ("`move`: no item with this key"). `handler_errors_are_values`, which raised its error through `pins.remove_key("x")`, now raises it through `pins.update("x", p => p)`. spec.md 6.5, guide level 5 and the reference's `remove_key` (`schema/members.rs`) say so. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::remove_key_of_a_missing_key_does_nothing` (both cells; each fails with its half of the change reverted), `::handler_errors_are_values`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a dictionary is written in brackets, `[K: V]` and `[k: v, …]`, and braces where one was meant are their own error.** The owner chose brackets (design question 1): braces hold a block or a record's fields, and grammar.md promises an expression never takes a `{` but after `match` or `=>`. `[ … ]` is a dictionary when a `:` follows its first item (newlines inside are already insignificant), every item then needs a value, and a list's item with one, an entry without one, or `[:]` is `syntax::dict_item` with both items labelled ("a `key: value` item, so this is a dictionary"). The empty form is `[]` alone, read by the type expected in the checker; the AST keeps it an array. A ternary key has taken its own `:` first, so `[c ? a : b: v]` keys by the ternary. The design asked `fmt` to print that key parenthesised; the formatter is a layout normaliser that holds the tree equal and never adds a token (`fmt.rs`, `shape`), and the key already reads one way, so it prints `[c ? a : b: v]` as written. The owner's first targeted diagnostic is `syntax::dict_braces`: a value starting `{` that holds `"text":`, `number:`, `name:` or nothing (`{}`) is skipped whole and reported "dictionaries use brackets: `[k: v]`", with the fix rewriting the braces as brackets when it is on one line; a type in braces with a `:` at its top level is the same code, "`[K: V]`". In a prop value a name then `:` in braces can be a sub-block's prop, so only a quoted or number key is taken as a dictionary there. In a type a dictionary's `:` is spaced, `[int: text]`, as a prop's is. The tree-sitter grammar has `dictionary` (of `dictionary_entry`, `key:` and `value:` fields) and `dictionary_type`, with no new conflict, and its indents treat a dictionary as a list. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/grammar_rules.rs::a_bracket_whose_first_item_has_a_value_is_a_dictionary`, `tests/diagnostics.rs::dictionary_mistakes_are_one_error_and_recover`, `tests/fmt.rs::dictionaries_format`, `tests/negative/dict_braces.strand`, `dict_item.strand`, `crates/strand-dev/tests/tree_sitter.rs::dictionaries_parse_as_the_parser_reads_them` and its named syntax errors.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: the checker types `[K: V]`, reading an entry as `V?` and writing one as `V`.** A key is an `int`, a `text` or an alias of one, a `path`, a `bool` or an enum; any other key type is `check::dict_key`, its help by kind (a `float`'s fraction, a unit's two keys for `2px` and `2ch`, a keyed record's `id`, an optional key's `?`). A value type `V?` is `check::dict_value`, so `m[k] == null` means only "absent". Both are checked where a type is resolved, and for an untyped literal on the type it infers. `m[k]` is one hir `Index` whose type depends on where it stands: the checker's context carries `place` while it checks an assignment target down through fields, indexes and parentheses, so a target `m[k]` is a `V` (`m[k] = null` is a type mismatch whose help names `m.remove(k)`, and `m[k].f = x` needs no `?.`) and a read is a `V?`; the key is expected as `K`, so a `K?` key is `check::nullable` as a list index is. A literal takes K and V from the type expected; untyped, its keys and its values each join as a list's items do, a whole number giving an `int`. Dictionaries do not join the whole-number widening of 5.3: an untyped `state m = ["a": 1]` is a `[text: int]`, and writing `0.5` to an entry is a type mismatch, since a widening would need every entry's write traced as a list's are; declaring `[text: float]` is the fix. The same constant key twice in a literal is `check::dict_duplicate`, keys compared as `ValueKey` will (a number by value). `Entry<K, V>` is made per pair from the schema's `record Entry key key`, as `Match<T>` is, so `m.entries` is a keyed list and a `for` over it needs no `key` clause; a config's own `type Entry` takes the name. The members (`len`, `keys`, `values`, `entries`, `filter`, `remove`, `clear`) are `schema::dict_members`, which the checker, completion and the reference share; an unknown `get`, `has`, `set`, `put` or `push` says how `m[k]` does it. The owner's second targeted diagnostic is `check::dict_untyped`: an untyped `[]` indexed by a `text` says "to key by text, declare it: `state m: [text: V] = []`", and an untyped `[]`'s `check::needs_type` help offers the dictionary form beside the list one. A compound `m[k] += x` is `check::dict_compound` (the entry may be missing; the fix starts from `?? 0`, or `?? 1` for `*=` and `/=`), `for x in m` is `check::dict_for` with an `.entries` fix, a `key` clause on a dictionary `state` is `check::dict_keyed`, `<->` to an entry is `check::dict_two_way`, and a service field, an action's parameter or a command's output holding one is `check::dict_service` ("not yet": D-Bus and JSON maps are phase 2). Each is its own code, so the troubleshooting page can name each fix. `persist` and settings fields take dictionaries of plain data. `check::secret_flow` follows a password into a dictionary through an entry write's key as well as its value. Lowering a dictionary is the next step: until then its literal lowers to an error value ("dictionaries are checked but cannot run yet"), never a panic, and a templated dictionary is `not_theme`. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::dictionaries_check_by_their_key_and_value_types`, `::dictionary_reads_and_writes_keep_to_their_rules`, `src/ty.rs::tests::dictionaries_assign_join_and_store_by_their_parts`, `tests/secrets.rs::a_persisted_dictionary_keyed_or_filled_by_a_secret`, and the negative fixtures `dict_key_float`, `dict_key_record`, `dict_nullable_key`, `dict_optional_value`, `dict_assign_null`, `dict_compound_assign`, `dict_duplicate_key`, `dict_for_without_entries`, `dict_key_clause`, `dict_two_way`, `dict_untyped_empty_is_a_list`, `dict_in_service_field`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a dictionary runs as one value whose entries are kept sorted by key.** `Value::Dict(Rc<Dict>)` holds a `Vec` of key and value pairs in key order (`value::key_cmp`): numbers by value, `int` and `float` one plain number as `ValueKey` has them, texts and paths by their UTF-8 bytes (the Unicode scalars' order), enums by declaration index, `false` before `true`. A lookup and an insert are a binary search. A key is held as `dict_key` makes it, a whole number as an `int`, so the derived `PartialEq` (the graph's cut-off), `builtins::equal` (the language's `==`, which compares values as `==` does, `2 == 2.0`) and a reload's comparison agree. The design's "normalised to `Int` on lookup" is therefore the order's, not a separate rule. A literal lowers to `Op::Dict(n)`, its keys and values pushed in source order, and the VM inserts them in turn, so a later computed key wins. `m[k]` is `builtins::index`, which reads a dictionary by key. `m[k] = v` and `m[k].f = x` go through `PlaceSeg::Index` in `set_in`: a plain set inserts or replaces, and anything below the entry (a field, or a compound op if one ever reaches the VM) needs it present, else the handler's error is "no entry for this key", as a list's index past its end is an error there; the key conforms to `K` and the value to `V` as list items do. `remove` and `clear` are `Op::Mutate`, as a list's mutations are; `remove` of a missing key and `clear` of an empty dictionary return before the write. `m.entries` and `m.filter` need their `Entry<K, V>` record at run time: the lowering finds the record the checker made (`schema::find_entry`) and passes it, as `Op::Entries(RecordId)` and as `filter`'s last argument the way `fuzzy` gets its `Match<T>`, so a dictionary value carries no type of its own. A dictionary `state` is one `Signal<Value>`: a binding over `m[k]` re-runs on any write and the equality cut-off stops it unless its entry changed, so `on change m[k]` fires only for its key; per-key read slots in core stay a later optimisation needing no language change. "Copy on write" is a copy per write: `Signal::update` clones the current value, which always shares its `Rc` with the cell, so `Rc::make_mut` could never skip the copy; one write is O(n) plus the binary search, and several writes in one handler are one change. `for e in m.entries` needs no new mount path: `Entry`'s key is `key`, so the `for`'s rows are keyed by it and a value change updates its row in place. A reload's `translate` translates each key and value and re-sorts (an enum's variants may have moved); until the persist step, a key or value that no longer translates resets the cell as a list item does, rather than dropping that entry with a note. Persisting a dictionary (its JSON), a settings table and IPC are later steps: until then a persisted dictionary's value encodes as `null` and starts from its default. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/vm.rs::dictionaries_read_by_key_in_key_order`, `::dictionary_writes_insert_replace_remove_and_filter`, `::dictionaries_compare_by_their_entries`, `src/vm/value.rs::tests::dictionaries_keep_key_order_and_one_key_per_number`, `tests/instantiate.rs::a_let_over_one_entry_does_not_rerun_its_dependents_when_another_changes`, `::rows_of_entries_keep_state_across_writes`, `::on_change_an_entry_fires_only_for_that_key`, `::the_last_window_on_each_workspace_is_remembered_by_key`, `tests/reload.rs::a_reload_keeps_a_dictionary_in_the_new_key_order`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a persisted dictionary is stored as `[key, value]` pairs in key order, and reads back from pairs in any order or from an object of key texts.** A JSON object's keys are only texts, so an object would turn an `int` key into `"3"` and need the type to read it back; pairs keep an `int` key a JSON number and an enum key its variant's name, as `persist::encode` writes any value of the type: `[[3,"0x55"],[5,"0x7a"]]`. An `int` key is written as a JSON integer (`3`, not the `3.0` every persisted number is today); values are not, since changing how an `int` value is encoded would change the stored default of every `int` cell already persisted and report each one once as kept over a changed default. Because the entries are always in key order, the same entries are the same bytes, so the default's hash, and so 10.3's adopt rule, is exact however a literal was ordered. Decoding builds the dictionary through `Dict::from_entries`, so a store edited by hand with pairs out of order or a key twice reads in key order with the later entry winning, and an object (`{"3": "0x55"}`, the form `strand get` will print) is read too, each key's text parsed by `K`. Anything else that does not read (a pair without its value, a key or value of the wrong type, a fractional `int` key) fails the whole value: core moves the file aside and the cell starts from its default with `PersistFailed`. A `[Seen]` list turned into an `[int: text]` is that case: there is no migration, as the design says. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/persist.rs::tests::dictionaries_store_as_pairs_in_key_order`, `tests/instantiate.rs::a_persisted_dictionary_survives_a_restart`, `::a_changed_default_follows_the_adopt_rule`, `::a_type_change_resets_with_a_warning`, `::a_corrupt_store_gives_the_default`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: an entry whose enum key is gone is dropped with one line, at a reload and at a start; a value that no longer fits still resets the cell.** The design's reload rule: `translate` drops an entry whose key no longer translates (only an enum key can stop naming anything) and counts it (`value::Dropped`), and `adopt_value` gives the reload report one notice per cell, `island.used: dropped 2 entries (key no longer in Urgency)`, the overlay's and `strand watch`'s line; the cell is kept, not reset, so the report's `reset` stays empty. The line names the enum without an article: "an U" and "a Urgency" are both wrong, and no rule on letters gets both right. A value that no longer translates still resets the whole cell (`value does not fit`), as a list's item does: an entry's key going is the program forgetting a name, a value not fitting is the data changing shape. The stored form has to follow the same rule, or a persisted dictionary could not keep its entries through such a reload: a kept persisted cell whose translation changed is handed over through core, and the new cell reads the store, which still names the removed variant; with a strict decode it fails and the cell starts from its default, every entry lost (the reload test fails that way with the decode made strict). So `persist::decode` drops an entry whose enum key is not declared and counts it too (`decode_bytes_dropping`), and a start that drops one says so with the same line through the mount's notices. Core writes a cell only when it changes, so the store keeps the dropped entries until the cell is next written, and each start says so until then; rewriting the store on read would need a new core call, an interface change not worth one line. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/reload.rs::an_enum_key_variant_removed_drops_its_entries_with_a_note` (plain and persisted, the store holding the kept entries after a restart), `tests/instantiate.rs::a_stored_entry_whose_enum_key_is_gone_is_dropped_with_a_note`, and `tests/reload.rs::a_reload_write_is_the_baseline_for_on_change_of_an_entry` for the design's reload-write rule, which needed no code (a guard).

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a glitch report holds a dictionary as pairs with its text keys held back, and two held keys of one length are a fidelity note naming the cell.** `vm::json::to_json` writes a dictionary as the store does, `[[key, value], …]` in key order, and writes each key as any value, so `keep` holds back a key that is not a text of the config (`{"~text": 2}`): a dictionary keyed by window ids or titles keeps them out of a report as a list of them would. `from_json` reads through `persist::decode`, so the replay's `[seed]` takes pairs or an object. Two keys held back as the same length read back as the same placeholder `x`s, and the later entry is kept (the owner's answer 7, over holding keys by index): `json::keys_read_as_one` counts the entries a seed loses so, the harness logs each such `[seed]` cell (`ReplayLog::keys_read_as_one`) and the fidelity comparison turns each into a note naming the cell and how many it lost. Only seeds are counted: a replay `set` of a whole dictionary would come from a `strand set` request, and a whole dictionary is not settable over IPC (step 8). The design's secret-flow rules landed with the checker; a literal's key and an entry copied from one dictionary into another are now checked too, and already warned. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/vm.rs::dictionaries_round_trip_through_report_json_with_held_keys`, `eval/tests/replay.rs::a_dictionary_cell_replays_with_no_divergence`, `::two_held_keys_of_one_length_are_a_fidelity_note`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/secrets.rs::a_persisted_dictionary_keyed_or_filled_by_a_secret`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a settings dictionary is a TOML table, read by its key type and written back key by key into the table the file has.** `persist::decode_item` reads a dictionary field from a `[section]` (an `Item::Table`, whose entries may be nested sections) or an inline `{ … }`, each key's text read by the key type as a persisted object's keys are (`key_text`: an `int` in decimal, an enum's variant by name, `true`/`false`, a `text` or `path` as written). One bad entry fails the whole field, so core's per-field rule keeps its last good value, and the message names the key: `"DP-1": expected path` for a value, `key "three": expected int` or `key "urgent": expected one of low, normal, critical` for a key. A persisted store drops an entry whose enum key is not declared (the reload paragraph above), but a settings file is the user's: an unknown key there is a mistake to show, not a stale name to forget quietly. Two keys that read as one (`3` and `03`, `3` and `+3`) are a bad entry too (`key "03": the same key as "3"`), where a persisted store lets the later win: TOML itself refuses a key written twice, so two spellings of one key in a hand-edited file are a mistake rather than an edit. `encode_item` writes a dictionary as a `[name]` section of its entries in key order (an empty one as its bare header, so it stays distinct from the field left out), and one inside a list or record as an inline table. The design's write rule needed strand-core: `apply_edits` replaced a whole top-level item, and removed and reinserted a table the user wrote, losing its comments and order. It now merges a table written over a table key by key (`merge_item`, `merge_table`, `merge_inline`): a key the new table lacks is removed with its comment, one both have is written in place keeping its decor, a new one is appended at the table's end, and a section written over an inline table the user wrote stays inline. Two inline tables merge the same way, so a record written as one keeps each field's spacing, as the design said it would. `Edit`'s shape is unchanged; architecture.md says the merge. Tests: `crates/strand-core/src/settings.rs::tests::a_table_is_written_key_by_key`, `::an_inline_table_keeps_its_spacing_field_by_field`, `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/persist.rs::tests::settings_dictionaries_are_tables`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::a_settings_dictionary_reads_a_table_and_keeps_its_last_good_value`, `::a_settings_dictionary_writes_back_key_by_key`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a reload carries a settings file's values into the new program by name (`FieldSpec::with_carry`).** Checking the design's reload rule against the code showed a gap the design did not name: a kept `state` and a persisted one are translated into the new program (`value::translate`), but a settings file kept through a reload is redeclared in core (`Settings::redeclare`), which kept every value it held as the old program made it. A value of a config enum is its variant's index, so a reload that reordered the enum showed the wrong variants: `enum U { low, mid, high }` became `{ high, low }` and a `[U: int]` field read `high=3,low=3,=4`, and a plain `e: U` field showed nothing. The type string core compares cannot catch it (`[U: int]` is still `[U: int]`), and resetting every such field would lose unsaved writes and say "type changed" when it did not. So `FieldSpec` gains `with_carry(f)`, an addition to strand-core's interface: a redeclare that keeps a field's type passes each layer it holds (the file's, the overlay's, the snapshot's, what it last showed) and the field's cell through `f`; the cell's new value is a reload write, so `on change` takes it as its baseline, and a write not saved yet is saved as carried. A field one of them no longer fits is read again from its files, as a type change is but without its notice. The compiler passes `translate` from the old program to the new, and before the redeclare notes the entries the carry drops (`t.prefs.m: dropped 1 entry (key no longer in U)`), once per field, as a kept `state`'s are; the store-less path (settings without a settings store) uses `translate_dropping` with the same line. The file may still name the removed variant: its next read is a bad entry naming the key and keeps the carried value, which is honest about the file the user has to fix. Tests: `crates/strand-core/tests/settings.rs::redeclare_carries_each_layer_through_its_carry`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/reload.rs::a_settings_file_keeps_its_enums_by_name_through_a_reload` (fails on the old code with the stale indices above), `::a_settings_dictionary_without_a_store_drops_entries_with_a_note`.

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: `strand get` and `strand set` reach one entry, the rest of the path after a dictionary being one key.** `Instance::path_to` walks a `get`, `set`, `set_text` or `toggle` path by type: a record's fields, and at a dictionary the rest of the path joined back with its dots as one key, read by the key type with `parse_text` (so `prefs.scale.org.gnome.Nautilus` is the key `org.gnome.Nautilus`, and an entry of a dictionary of records cannot be walked into, which keeps the rule one sentence). `get` answers the entry or `null`; `set` writes it through the ordinary place (`PlaceSeg::Index` with the key), so it inserts or replaces, conforming the key and value as a handler's `m[k] = v` does; `toggle` flips a `bool` entry, an absent one becoming `true`; a settings entry's `layer` is its field's. `get`'s JSON answer is an object keyed by each key's text (`value_json`), as the design said, while its `text` keeps key order; a persisted store and a report keep pairs. Refusals name their fix: a whole dictionary from text ("`strand set` writes one entry, `strand set <path>.<key> <value>`", as lists are not settable from text either), `null` (the owner's answer 6: "`strand set` does not remove an entry …; a handler removes it with `m.remove(k)`", naming the dictionary as a handler writes it), and a key that does not read ("`three` is not a key of `t.names`, a [int: text]: its keys are int"). A `strand set` of an entry is recorded for a replay as the entry's path and value, which a replay sets back the same way. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::strand_get_and_set_reach_one_entry_of_a_dictionary`, `::a_settings_dictionary_writes_back_key_by_key` (a dotted key written to the file), `crates/strand/src/run/tests.rs::strand_get_and_set_reach_one_dictionary_entry` (over the request channel), `crates/strand/src/ipc/query.rs::tests::values_are_json_where_json_has_them_and_set_text_elsewhere`.
