**2026-11-05 · dictionary: a keyed list reads one item by its key, `xs.get(k)`, a `T?`; a key never goes in a list's brackets.** The owner's answer to the design's second question. `get` is a list member (`schema::list_members`) whose `key` parameter the checker types as the collection's key, as it does `remove_key`'s; a list with no key is `check::missing_key`, whose help for `get` adds that `xs[i]` reads by position and `xs.find(x => …)` by a test. `xs[i]` stays positional on every list. The design said what to read through, and the code agreed with one change: the key an item is found by has to be the one the checker typed. A `state`'s `key` clause is that key for the `state` itself, but a view `let` over it (`let shown = pins.filter(…)`) or a chain written in place (`pins.take(3).get(k)`) holds the same items with no clause of its own, and `Pin` has no `key` of its own to fall back on. So the checker follows `let`s and the steps that keep items (`filter`, `take`, `skip`, `sort_by`, `reverse`; `fuzzy`'s `Match<T>` by `item.<key>`) back to the `state` (`Checker::key_path_of`, the new `view_keys` for `let`s), and lowering follows the same steps (`Lowerer::get_key`) and passes the path as a last argument the source doesn't write, as `fuzzy` gets its `Match<T>`; with none, an item is found by its own identity (a keyed record's `key`, as service items are). A mapped view's items are new values, found by their own key, not the source's. The reads: on a keyed `state` and a service's keyed list, one lookup by key inside core's tracked `with` (`KeyedQuery::Get`), never the untracked `get_key`, so a binding over `xs.get(k)` follows the collection as `.contains` now does; on a view, a scan of its items inside `KeyedMemo::with`; on a persisted keyed `state` (a plain cell) and any other list (`n.actions`, a chain), a scan of the list read as usual (`builtins::get_by_key`). Keys compare as `ValueKey` does, so `3` and `3.0` are one key. This is the design's step 9; the shell's `tray.items.find(i => i.id == tray_open)` (launcher.strand) can be `tray.items.get(tray_open)`. **2026-11-05 · dictionary: the docs pass, and what the owner's answers leave out of the language.** The owner's answer 4 is recorded here, as the earlier paragraphs had no place for it. **2026-11-05 · dictionary: a mutation through `?.` skips a null and writes nothing: a null `[K: V]?` stays null, and an absent entry is never created by a list mutation below it.** Review finding. `Op::Mutate` chose the dictionary branch from the runtime value, so `m?.clear()` and `m?.remove(3)` on a null `[int: text]?` (or `s?.m?.clear()` under a null record) fell into the list code: `clear` stored `[]` into the cell, which then held a list (`.entries` read null, the persisted cell encoded as null), and `remove(3)` raised "`remove`: no item at 3". The receiver's type is known when lowering emits the call, so `Op::Mutate` now carries `dict`, set when the receiver is a `Ty::Dict`, and the VM takes the dictionary branch from it: on a null, `remove` and `clear` do nothing, as `remove` of a missing key already did. Likewise `m["b"]?.push(1)` on a `[text: [int]]` read null for the absent entry, treated it as an empty list and inserted `"b": [1]` through `set_in`'s insert-or-replace arm, against the rule that anything below an entry needs it present; `m["d"]?.remove(0)` raised "no item at 0". The place read (`read_place_at`) now says when it passed through an absent entry, and a list mutation there writes nothing, which is what `?.` reads as. Raising "no entry for this key" instead, as `m[k].f = x` does, was the other choice; it was not taken because the checker already demands the `?.` here (`m["a"].push(1)` is `check::nullable`), and a `?.` that raises would be the only one that does. A list mutation on a null optional list outside a dictionary (`xs?.push(1)` on `[int]?`) keeps creating the list, as on main. Test: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/vm.rs::a_mutation_through_a_null_or_an_absent_entry_writes_nothing`, which fails on the old code at its first click (`List([])` where `Null` was meant) and, with only the dictionary half fixed, at the absent entry (`b=1,x=1`).

**2026-11-05 · dictionary: the dictionary diagnostics' help and fixes after review.** `m[k] = null`'s help ("to remove the entry, `m.remove(k)`") replaced the help of any optional value written to an entry, so `last_win[at] = windows.focused?.id` was told to remove the entry instead of to give a fallback; it now replaces it only for a value whose type is `null`. `check::dict_compound` started the missing case from `0` or `1` whatever the value type, wrote `…` for the right side and gave no fix: it now starts from the value type's zero (`""` for text, `[]` for a list, `0s` for a duration, `0px`, `0%` and `0deg` for those units, 1 for `*=` and `/=` on a number), writes the right side as written (in parentheses unless it is one term), and the fix rewrites the statement. ## inplace-gate

**2026-11-05 · inplace-gate: a file rewritten every 5 ms is read first within 2 s, not 800 ms.** `rewritten_every_5_ms` (crates/strand-watch/tests/saves.rs) gates the first read of a file rewritten without pause at 800 ms: `max_delay` (500 ms) with slack. GitHub's `test` job missed it on main twice (1.01 s on `6827541b`, 995 ms on `d6623f12`) and on branches that never touched the watcher (`laptop/glide-curve` 830 ms, `laptop/path-tilde` 1.00 s, 2026-11-05), always as one slow sample on a loaded runner, never as a read that did not come. The gate is there to catch the old fault, a file never read while the writes go on, so it is raised to 2 s, four times `max_delay`, which still fails that fault and no longer fails a slow runner (memory budgets and timing gates are tripwires, not caps). Test: `a_watched_file_rewritten_in_place_every_5_ms_is_reported`, `a_module_rewritten_in_place_every_5_ms_is_reported`, `a_module_renamed_over_every_5_ms_is_reported`.

## list-start

**2026-11-05 · list-start: `results.selected_index` reads a start in the tick that sets it, not a tick after the list takes it.** The owner's launcher mirrors its list's selection into state for a preview (`on change results.selected_index { results_at = results.selected_index ?? 0 }`, the Themes page previewing `found_themes.skip(results_at)`), and opening the Themes page, whose start is the theme in use, flashed the first theme's colours across the shell for a frame (a logged `launcher.peek` went `catppuccin-frappe, nord` on every opening), which the launcher worked around with `on change view { if view == theme_list { results_at = theme_at } }`. The router takes a start as it settles the diff that sets it, and logic heard where the selection was only from its `Intent::SelectedIndex`, a tick later, so the frame between showed the list on its start and everything read from `selected_index` on the row before. A frame hold until logic answered (as a container query's) was rejected: the render thread never waits on logic (design.md, "One tick, one diff"), the preview recolours every surface, not the list's, and an `on change` that acts outside the shell (a file written, a service told) would still run with the old row. Logic knows its start when it sets it, so it reads it there: when, at the end of a tick, the list has just mounted with a start, its start changed while the user has not moved the selection, or it starts again and forgets the move (every row it has came in that tick and it had a selection, its rows replaced whole; or the tick set a new text in the focused input it is the `nav:` list of, a new query, which the router sees only in the diff that carries the text), its `selected_index` becomes the start (below 0 the first row, as render reads it) and the tick flushes again, at most three more times, so its `on change` and what reads it go in the same diff; a move a handler asked of the list in that tick is the router's to place, so logic leaves it. Whether the user moved is the router's to know, so `Intent::SelectedIndex` (and `ToLogic::SelectedIndex`, `Instance::set_selected_index`) carries `moved` with the place, told when either changes. The router tells logic where the selection is after every start it is given and for every list whose selected row logic removed, changed or not, so a start logic read and the router did not take (the user's move still on its way to logic) is put right a tick later rather than kept; in that race the `on change` hears the start and then the user's row, the one case it hears two changes for one. A prop the second flush sets again is sent once, at its first place with its first transition and its last value, so the router, which reads some props op by op (an input's text answering its edits, a list's start), never sees a value no frame was to show. A `nav:` list whose surface opens again starts on its start as the keyboard enters (the router does it with that input), and logic reads it a tick after, as it reads the keys; a list without a start keeps the first-row rule's tick, as before. Tests (`crates/strand-compiler/tests/selection.rs`): `a_start_is_read_in_the_tick_the_list_takes_it` (the launcher's pattern without the workaround, with and without a move on the page before; its first frame is drawn and shows the theme in use), `a_start_that_comes_with_its_rows_is_read_with_them`, `a_list_that_mounts_with_a_start_reads_it_at_once`, `a_changed_start_is_read_in_its_tick_until_the_user_moves`, each failing before the fix, `a_start_the_list_did_not_take_is_put_right` (failing without the router's telling again), `a_text_typed_reads_the_start_with_the_key` (failing without the new-text rule), and `instantiate::starts::tests::a_prop_set_again_for_a_start_is_sent_once`.

**2026-11-05 · list-start: a changed start is read in the flush that changes it, before what reads it runs; the rest at the tick's end.** The owner's launcher, run headless without its workaround (`target/try/notes/cfg-list-start`, `peek.steps` logging every value `peek_theme` took), still logged `catppuccin-frappe nord` on each opening with the first decision: the diff and the frame had only Nord, but the second flush ran after the first had computed the preview with the old row and run its `on change`, so an `on change` of anything read from the selection heard a row no frame showed, and one that acts outside the shell would act on it. A changed start is now read by an effect each list with a `selected_index:` has (`read_start` in `instantiate/mount.rs`), which reads the start's binding and writes `selected_index` while the user has not moved, a declared write, so the runtime ranks everything that reads `selected_index` after it and the preview is computed once, with the start; the run logged `nord` alone on every opening after the first, and on typing a search, where 9f19dfc6 logged `rose-pine-moon nord` and `everforest-light nord`. The end-of-tick read stays for what the effect cannot see as it runs: a list mounting with its start, and one starting again under the user's move (rows replaced whole, a new text). A mount is left there on purpose: an `on change results.selected_index` mounted with the list (the launcher's, whose panel body mounts on the first opening) would otherwise take the start for its first value and never mirror it, where the second flush makes it hear it once; the price is that on the first opening the launcher's `peek_theme` log still hears the first theme before Nord inside the tick, never in a frame. **2026-11-05 · list-start: the review's fixes: a start's read is input to the write-rate guard, and the one start read a tick late is said where the read is.** The effect that reads a changed start (`read_start`) wrote `selected_index` as any graph handler does, so the 30 writes/s guard counted it: a start changing faster than that while the user has not moved (one read from a search a key auto-repeats, or from a value reported every frame such as `scroll_y`) warned of a feedback loop (`list start -> #n`) in the overlay and `strand watch`, and its writes were held, where nothing on this path was a writer before. The start is the list's own place, which the router takes as it takes a key, and its report of the place (`set_selected_index`) was never counted, so the read is input too: strand-core gains `Runtime::as_input(f)`, which runs `f` as an input handler's synchronous part runs (its writes not counted, a task it spawns an input task), and `read_start` writes through it; a loop through the start is still bounded by the runtime's cycle guard and by `MAX_START_PASSES`, and a handler writing the value the start reads is counted as before. spec.md 8.7 lists the start among what is not counted. The docs of `results.selected_index` (builtin.schema, reference/elements.md and types.md, spec.md 6.7's opening, the keys how-to) said it reads every start from the first frame, which the first decision's own exception contradicts: a `nav:` list whose surface gets the keyboard again starts on its start as the keyboard enters, on the render side, and logic reads that a tick later. Closing that gap was not taken: logic hears the keyboard enter only from render, a tick after it, so it cannot read the start earlier without the render thread waiting on it (design.md, "One tick, one diff"); the docs name the exception instead. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/selection.rs::a_start_changing_every_frame_is_not_a_feedback_loop` (a start changed every 16 ms for 90 ticks, list and logic agreeing on each and no `WriteRate`; it failed with `list start -> #231` before the fix), `::a_start_taken_as_the_keyboard_enters_is_read_a_tick_later` (pins the named exception), `crates/strand-core/tests/feedback.rs::writes_run_as_input_are_not_counted`.

## caret

**2026-11-05 · caret: the caret blinks.** The owner, typing into the island's admin-password prompt, asked for a caret that blinks like a normal one (and only that: its height, width, colour and place stay). This replaces p3's "a steady 1.5 px `$accent` caret (no blink wakeups)". A focused `input`'s caret shows for 600 ms and hides for 600 ms, GTK's default 1200 ms cycle (`gtk-cursor-blink-time`), which the other text fields of a Linux desktop blink at, and a little fewer frames than Windows' 530 ms halves. Every key the input takes, caret move, click, change of its text (from logic too) and focus gained shows it at once and starts the blink anew; 10 s after the last (GTK's `gtk-cursor-blink-timeout`), at the end of that cycle (10.8 s), it stays shown and asks for nothing, so a focused field left alone does not wake the shell, which is p3's worry with a bound on it. No prop or syntax: everyone gets it. The blink is a clock of its surface's (`Clocks`, as a capped clock is): the render thread's own timer wakes its loop half a frame before a turn, the frame nearest it paints, and logic is never woken or told. The phase is read off the frame's presentation time from the painted frame that restarted it (`widgets::Blinks`, kept by the `Animator`, keyed by the input's text, caret and anchor), so it is a function of the frame clock, not the wall clock. A restart that a preview finds (a key that left a shown caret where it was) keeps its surface dirty for one painted frame, which starts it and changes no pixel. The caret is a glyph cell of its input's record, so a turn damages its pixels alone, 5 × 17 px at scale 1 and 6 × 25 at 1.5 for a 13 px font, a CPU paint of 0.12 ms at scale 1 and 0.18 ms at 1.5 in a release build in the container (0.28 and 0.34 ms in a debug one; `a_turn_damages_only_the_caret` prints it): 18 frames in all per edit, then none. It does not blink under `reduced_motion` (frozen, as time signals are), in a frame at time zero (every offline PNG, so no pixel reference changed), while blurred or hidden (no caret drawn, no clock) or when a host holds it steady with `Renderer::set_caret_blink(false)`: the evaluation sandbox does, so its recordings, `rest`s and the site's media do not depend on the phase, which `crates/strand-render/tests/caret.rs` holds instead. So does `strand run` under `STRAND_MOCK` (the mock desktop of the shell's tests on headless sway and of headless shots): the acceptance test's `launcher_open` reference and the design launcher's caret check were taken a while after the last key and saw the caret hidden half the time. A glitch report's live frame may show the caret hidden where the replay, steady, shows it (the e2e report sessions DRIFTED by the 2 × 16 px of the Ask field's caret): `drawn.json` gives a node whose caret blinks its box (`DrawnNode::caret`, shown or not at the report), and the verdict leaves those pixels, grown by 1 px, out of its comparison, as it leaves out what moves. A caret drawn at a selection's moving end blinks as well, as it was drawn there before. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/caret.rs` (`the_blink_is_600_ms_on_600_ms_off_and_ends_shown`, `a_focused_caret_shows_then_hides_then_shows`, `the_loop_paints_once_per_turn_then_stops`, `a_key_a_move_or_new_text_shows_the_caret_and_restarts_the_blink`, `a_key_while_shown_restarts_the_blink_in_one_unchanged_frame`, `blurred_or_hidden_the_caret_wakes_nothing`, `reduced_motion_holds_the_caret_steady`, `a_frame_at_time_zero_shows_the_caret_steady`, `a_host_may_hold_the_caret_steady`, `a_turn_damages_only_the_caret`, `a_reports_drawn_input_carries_its_blinking_caret`), `crates/strand/src/demo/host.rs::tests::a_blinking_caret_tells_logic_nothing`.

**2026-11-05 · caret: the review's fixes: a turn flattens nothing, an empty field's turn damages only the caret, and every key and the keyboard's return restart the blink.** A turn was a clock in `Flattened::clocks`, and a scene with clocks is never reused, so each turn flattened its whole surface and cost what the surface holds, not what the caret does: 0.98 ms on an 800 × 600 panel at scale 1.5 with 400 text cells (the review's probe), where the paragraph above measured 0.12 ms on the 240 × 40 field alone; a key also flattened once more than with a steady caret. A scene now keeps its carets apart (`Flattened::carets`). Each is in the display list whether shown or not, its `$accent` fill made transparent while hidden so it keeps its place, and its record carries it apart (`NodeRecord::caret`: its cell, whether it shows, its look), out of the node's signature, glyph cells and box geometry, its pixels inside the node's bounds either way. Every painted frame, a reused scene's included, turns each caret in place to its phase at that frame (`Flattened::turn_carets`) and hands the next turn to `Clocks::turn`, which wakes the loop as a capped tick does but is not a running clock (`Clocks::running`), so a scene whose only change in time is a caret's is reused. On that panel a turn now costs 0.13 ms (the loop's `update` and paint, release build in the container; 0.06 to 0.12 ms on the field alone) and flattens nothing; a key flattens as often blinking as held steady (`set_caret_blink(false)`), the frame reusing its preview, 3.1 to 3.4 ms a key either way there, the difference between the two only the order they ran in. A caret's fill not found in the finished scene (nothing known moves it so) turns as a clock as before, its scene not reused. With the caret out of the glyph cells, an empty field drawing its own background (no text, so no glyph cells; a password prompt just opened) no longer damages its whole box each turn (3400 px for the 200 × 17 field): its turn damages the caret's cell, 72 px at scale 1 and 130 at 1.5. The docs promised a restart on every key, but only a key that edited or moved the caret restarted it, so an arrow through a `nav:` list, Ctrl+C or a key the input does not take could leave it hidden for up to 600 ms. The router now restarts the focused input's blink on every key press its surface takes (`InputScene::restart_caret_blink`, as GTK restarts on any key press), and when the keyboard comes back to a surface that kept its focus (a popup's grab ended with no leave between), which changed no flag and so restarted nothing. Not done: a caret held steady while a popup has the keyboard. The surface is not told the keyboard left, and the blink stops on its own within 10.8 s. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/caret.rs` (`a_turn_flattens_nothing_and_a_key_no_more_than_a_steady_caret`, which prints both costs; `a_turn_damages_only_the_caret`, now with empty fields drawing their own background; `a_key_that_edits_nothing_still_shows_the_caret`; `the_keyboard_back_shows_the_caret_and_restarts_the_blink`), `crates/strand-render/src/clock.rs::tests::a_caret_turn_wakes_the_loop_without_running`.

**2026-11-05 · caret: a caret under a GPU filter turns by flattening.** The review's fix turns a caret in place in a reused scene, which a bundled GPU filter (`bloom`, `crt`, `chromatic`, `tilt`, `wobble`, `aurora`) over its input does not see: the group is drawn from the GPU's pixels of it, hashed with the caret's paint at the flatten, so once they were back the caret stayed as that flatten left it, shown or hidden, until something else flattened the scene. A caret inside a group asking for a filter pass (`filter_pass`) now leaves the scene's carets for its clocks, as a caret whose fill is lost does: each turn flattens the scene and asks for the group again, and the frame after shows the GPU's answer. Test: `crates/strand-render/tests/caret.rs::a_caret_under_a_gpu_filter_is_drawn_again_on_each_turn` (each of six turns asks for the group, 600 ms apart; none did before).

## lock-gpu

**2026-11-05 · lock-gpu (OWNER RULING): a lock surface is presented by the GPU like a panel, with a CPU safety net; it is never read back.** This supersedes m4-audit's correction ("a lock's surfaces never reach the GPU thread"). On the owner's laptop (Hyprland, Arc B390, three monitors) a lock that faded its whole output was promoted like any surface, but since its handles were refused it was attached for readback: its first GPU frames took 217, 141 and 76 ms, one monitor after another, with Hyprland's own background showing meanwhile, then 32 to 40 ms a frame against 15 to 18 ms on the CPU, and CPU and GPU frames alternated, each drawing the lock a little differently, so it flickered (strand-issues.md). Why they alternated, read from `gpu_readback_paint`: readback frames run one behind, a frame sent holds its surface `GPU_WAIT` (8 ms), and a paint with no pixels back by then is drawn by the CPU; with GPU frames of 32 to 40 ms against 16 ms of frame time, CPU paints kept coming between the copied GPU frames. The owner approved: (1) the first frame of every lock surface is the CPU's, committed as fast as before, since Hyprland counts the session locked once every output has a lock frame, so first-frame latency is lock latency; `State::raw_handles` lends a lock surface only once it has committed a buffer; (2) a lock surface that animates a large area is promoted to `GpuPresent` as a panel is, and never to `GpuReadback`: where it cannot be presented it is not attached, or is released at once, and stays on the CPU, since readback buys a lock nothing: for good when the refusal lasts (its output renewed, a `Readback` answer: `Renderer::keep_on_cpu`, `Promotion::pin_cpu`), and until a later frame asks again when it passes (not mapped yet, a configure pending at another size, the device starting, an ending or stalled thread: `Renderer::refuse_promotion`, the review's correction below); (3) once presented every frame of it is the GPU thread's: the manager never paints or commits a handed-off surface, and the host has one frame in flight per surface, so nothing can alternate; the only way back to the CPU is (4), onto another surface, once; (4) the lock's progress never waits on the GPU: the lock surfaces of a thread that answers nothing for `LOCK_GPU_BOUND` while a lock surface's `Attach` or frame waits on it, a lock surface whose frame fails (render's `Demote`), whose thread ends or loses its device, or on which the built-in fallback must show (painted by the main thread only), is renewed; (5) lock semantics stay as they were: configures are acked with buffers, `locked`, the unlock and outputs plugged in while locked are untouched.

**2026-11-05 · lock-gpu: the bound is 500 ms of the GPU thread's silence.** `LOCK_GPU_BOUND` (strand's `run/gpu.rs`) gives up on the GPU thread once it has answered nothing for 500 ms while a lock surface's `Attach` or frame (or paced `Commit`) waits on it. Each such request is timed from its sending or from the thread's last reply of any kind, whichever is later (`lock_deadline`): the one GPU thread works through every output's requests in order, so a request queued behind others starts no earlier than the last answer, and the bound times the thread's silence, never the queue. (The first version timed each request from its sending; the lane's review found that three outputs' first frames, sent in one pump and answered one after another, were each timed for all those ahead of it as well.) Time spent waiting for the compositor's frame callback is not counted, since nothing is sent then (an output turned off while locked is no stall). Measured on the owner's Arc B390 (`gpu.sh`, Mesa 25.2.8 ANV, its own headless sway with three 1920 × 1200 outputs, the owner's lock's content as an overlay panel on each, presented through the WSI; a release build of this change with every request and reply timestamped, four openings, each a fresh surface per output): the three `Attach`es sent in one pump were answered 9.5 to 21.4, 11.4 to 25.6 and 12.2 to 29.5 ms after their sending, one after another; each surface's first frame was presented 0.3 to 8.3 ms after it went and every later one within 5.4 ms; the thread's longest silence with such a request waiting was 21.4 ms (the first `Attach`). strand-issues.md's 217, 141 and 76 ms were readback frames, which a lock no longer has. 500 ms is more than 20 times the longest silence measured, room for a far slower or busier machine, and still short of what reads as a hung lock: 30 frames at 60 Hz, at most once per lock. A lock surface is also attached only to a device that is up (`GpuStatus::Up`; one still starting puts the promotion off), so the bound never times the device's start and pipeline build. FIRST_FRAME (1 s) does not come into it: a lock surface is lent only once its CPU first frame is committed, so every GPU stall starts after that bound was met. What the user sees of a stall is the bound, then the compositor's solid colour on that output until the renewed surface's first CPU frame, which comes as any new lock content's first frame does (18 to 20 ms after the request on the owner's laptop, strand-issues.md; in the lock VM about 510 ms when this lane was measured, the same as the lock's own first frame there, a wait that lock-polish then removed: it was `refresh_size_holds` holding a lock that did not fill its output for a configure that never came; on the merged branch, lock-int's second review, the renewed surface draws 10 to 20 ms after the renewal in a debug build in the VM, four runs of `a_lock_whose_gpu_stalls_goes_on_on_the_cpu`). A false alarm (a slow machine) costs only the GPU for the rest of that lock, never correctness. The loop wakes at the bound (`GpuHost::wait`), since a stalled thread sends nothing. (Corrected 2026-11-06, lock-4k: the bound is 2 s. A false alarm costs more than the GPU: the renewal leaves each output without a lock surface until its new one's first frame, which past the lock's first second is Hyprland's dead-lock screen; see that track.)

**2026-11-05 · lock-gpu: a lock surface given up on is renewed, never taken back.** Taking a live swapchain back for `wl_shm` can freeze a surface on Hyprland (gpu-stay), so a lock surface the GPU thread held is never committed by the manager again: `State::renew_lock_content(surface)` destroys it and makes its output a fresh content surface with a new id, drawn on the CPU until the lock ends (its output is remembered for the lock session, `SessionLock::cpu_outputs`). The old surface goes the way of any surface the GPU thread holds (`gpu_release`, then `take_back` once its swapchain is gone), but its `ext_session_lock_surface_v1` is destroyed at once (`LockSurface::drop_role`), before the new one is asked for: the protocol makes a second lock surface on one output a `duplicate_output` error, and a destroyed one frees its output (the manager already relied on that when a reload moved a content). Meanwhile the compositor shows its own colour on that output for the new surface's first CPU frame; the session stays locked (a destroyed lock surface on an active output falls back to a solid colour, the protocol says). A stalled thread may never let go: its old `wl_surface` then stays until the thread ends, shown nowhere. A new id, not the old one again, so the GPU thread's, render's and the host's state of the old surface (an `Attached` or `Presented` still to come, the swapchain's `Release`) can never be taken for the new one's. Keyboard focus on the old one moves to the new one with a `KeyboardEnter`, as when a content moves to another output; what was typed lives in logic's `state` (or the fallback's one field), not in the surface, so it survives. When the thread ends, the old `wl_surface` goes at once (taken back, then destroyed).

**2026-11-05 · lock-gpu: a lent or presented lock surface's configure.** A configure at the size its frames have is acked at once, since the GPU thread's next present is at that size, whichever order the ack and that commit reach the compositor in. A configure at another size, or a new scale, is never applied under the GPU thread's commits (a present at the old size after the ack, or a new `wl_surface` buffer scale before the new buffer, would be a protocol error ending the connection with the session locked): the manager renews the surface instead (`draw_handed_off`, the configure handler). Output geometry changing while locked is rare, and the renewed surface is drawn on the CPU at once.

**2026-11-05 · lock-gpu: the lock VM gets lavapipe.** The VM's guest had `libvulkan1` and no driver, so no lock VM test could present. `Dockerfile.lockvm` now installs `mesa-vulkan-drivers` (lavapipe, which presents on the pixman sway as on the check image); only a run with `STRAND_GPU_SOFTWARE=1` sees a device, so every other lock VM test stays on the CPU as before. The `faults` build gains `gpu_stall`: after the first frame the GPU thread presents for a lock, the thread stops for good inside its waker after its next reply, which is a GPU thread that hangs. The `damage` log line gains `gpu=1` on a frame the GPU thread presented. Tests: `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::a_lock_that_animates_is_presented_and_never_alternates`, `::a_lock_whose_gpu_stalls_goes_on_on_the_cpu` (lock VM, lavapipe); `crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::a_lock_surface_is_handed_off_after_its_first_frame_and_renewed_on_the_cpu` (replacing `a_lock_surface_is_never_handed_to_the_gpu`), `::a_presented_lock_surface_given_a_new_size_is_renewed` (lock VM, no GPU); `crates/strand/src/run/gpu.rs::host::tests::a_lock_surface_is_given_up_on_at_its_bound`, `::a_lock_surface_in_flight_wakes_the_loop_at_its_bound`; `crates/strand-render/src/promote.rs::tests::a_pinned_surface_is_never_promoted`. Measured in the lock VM (KVM, 4 vCPUs, pixman sway 1.9 at 1280 × 720, lavapipe), release builds of 3714cc62 and of this change, the test's lock (a full-output colour spring, 250 ms) toggled 16 times 500 ms apart, three runs each: the first lock frame came 509, 509 and 512 ms after the lock was asked before and 508, 514 and 512 ms after (the same CPU frame both times, the first paint itself 3 to 5 ms; the rest is a wait the lock VM has before any new lock content's first frame, not `LOCK_STILL_WAIT`, since the test's lock has no thumbnail and takes no stills; on the owner's laptop a lock's first frame comes 18 to 20 ms after the request, strand-issues.md). Before, the lock surface was attached `Readback` and of its 289 frames 19 were drawn by the CPU (raster 1.1 to 5.5 ms, the copied ones 0.0x) among 270 copied from the GPU (4.0 to 4.5 ms median a frame on the GPU thread): one CPU frame at each animation's start, when no pixels were back yet, 31 switches between the two in a run; on the owner's Arc, whose readback frames took 32 to 40 ms, the CPU drew far more of them. After, it was attached `Present`: 2 CPU frames (the first, and the frame whose spring asked for promotion; 2.2 to 3.2 ms median) and 255 presented, median 4.4 to 5.3 ms, p95 5.1 to 6.1, the first presented one 17 to 20 ms (its swapchain new), and not one CPU frame after the first presented one. In the debug test build, `a_lock_that_animates_is_presented_and_never_alternates` saw CPU frames of median 4.13 ms before the hand-off and 112 presented frames of median 5.44, p95 7.67 ms. Not measured: a lock on the owner's Arc under Hyprland, where the flicker was seen (lock code runs only in the lock VM, which has lavapipe only); the Arc was measured presenting the lock's content as a panel (the bound's entry).

**2026-11-05 · lock-gpu: the review's corrections: a stalled thread gets no lock, a refusal that passes is not for good.** (1) A stalled thread: once a lock surface's bound passes, every lock surface the thread holds is renewed at once (one with no frame in flight would otherwise be sent one and wait a bound of its own), and the host marks the thread (`GpuHost::lock_stalled`): no lock content is attached to it until it replies again or a new thread starts, since `cpu_outputs` goes with each lock, and a later lock, or a monitor plugged in during this one, would each have waited a bound frozen and then shown the renewal's gap. `HUNG_AFTER` (10 s) cannot stand in for this: it times only a submission the thread itself waits on, so a thread blocked anywhere else (a WSI acquire or present that never returns, the `gpu_stall` fault) is never given up on, and panels keep going to it as before; only locks are kept from it. (2) A refusal that passes only puts the promotion off (`Renderer::refuse_promotion`, which undoes it as a failure does, so the next large animated frame asks again): a lock surface not mapped yet or with a configure pending at another size (`State::raw_handles` refuses it), the device still starting, the thread stalled, or an ending thread holding it. Only a refusal that lasts pins the surface to the CPU for its life (`keep_on_cpu`): its output already renewed in this lock (`State::lock_kept_on_cpu`) or an `Attached { Readback }` (a device that cannot present it). The first version pinned every refusal, so a lock asking for the GPU from its first frame while a fractional scale was still arriving would never have been presented. (3) A lock surface's handles are asked for only when it will be attached: `raw_handles` lends the surface, and a lent surface skips the manager's paints until it is taken back, so a promotion refused after lending froze the lock (the VM test of the second lock on a stalled thread caught it). Tests: `crates/strand/src/run/gpu.rs::host::tests::the_bound_counts_from_the_threads_last_answer`, `::a_stalled_thread_gives_up_every_lock_surface_until_it_answers`, `::a_lock_promotion_is_refused_for_now_or_for_good`; `crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::a_lock_surface_is_handed_off_after_its_first_frame_and_renewed_on_the_cpu` now holds the first frame back so its not-lent check always runs (lock VM); `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::a_lock_whose_gpu_stalls_goes_on_on_the_cpu` types the password before, during and after the stalled presentation and locks again on the stalled thread, `::a_presented_lock_that_faults_shows_the_fallback_on_the_cpu` (the fallback renews a presented lock whose thread is healthy), `::a_lock_that_animates_from_its_first_frame_is_presented` (lock VM, lavapipe), which shows only that a lock opening animated is presented after a CPU first frame and never alternates: on sway the first promotion comes after the first commit, so it reaches no refusal that passes, and it passes on the code before (2) as well. (2) is pinned by the rule's unit test `a_lock_promotion_is_refused_for_now_or_for_good` alone; the binary's wiring of `refuse_promotion` against `keep_on_cpu` has no test (lock-int's second review). In the VM the stall test's lock was renewed 507 to 517 ms after the fault armed (four runs; the fault arms at the first presented frame, so this is the bound plus the thread's last answers), and the renewed surface drew its first CPU frame 499 to 523 ms after that, the VM's first-frame wait then (above), which lock-polish's fix of content-sized locks removed: 10 to 20 ms on the merged branch (debug build, the log read every 10 ms; lock-int's second review, which also took the figure before the test's later 300 ms wait for `lock.locked`). The lock VM's CI filter gains the files this behaviour now lives in (`manager/layer.rs`, `promote.rs`, `renderer/backend.rs`, strand-gpu's `present.rs`, `thread.rs`, `device.rs`), and `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/build.sh` finds the lock test by `/deps/lock-`, since a checkout under a directory named `lock-…` matched the binary's own path too.

## lock-polish

**2026-11-05 · lock-polish: a lock is its output's size, and a shadow in it is paint.** Any `shadow:` inside `lock { }` drew the whole lock smaller than its output (on the owner's lock in the VM, inset 73 px left and right and 91 px top and bottom of 1280×720, black around it) and held its first frame about 530 ms (600 ms against 70 ms without the shadow). Render treated a lock as any surface with no `width`/`height`: sized by its content (`content_sized`), and asking for its shadows' room around its box (`reserve_reach`, which holds and releases for every kind but a panel or OSD). A lock surface has neither: the compositor gives it its output's size and strand-surface sends it no margins or overhang (`lock_config`). So the box was laid out inset by the room inside a buffer of the output's size, and since the size the spec asked for (content plus room) never came, `refresh_size_holds` held the first frame for the first-frame wait (500 ms in the binary) for a configure that never comes. A lock is now never content-sized (`refresh_specs`: its axes are the compositor's) and asks for no room (`reserve_reach` returns none for `NodeKind::Lock`), so it fills its output and a shadow inside it is cut at its edge, as one past an output's edge is. The same hold cost every lock whose content did not fill its output, shadow or not: the VM's `a_healthy_lock_draws_its_first_frame_in_time` (a field and a text) drew its three first frames 529, 509 and 513 ms after the request, and 41, 7 and 6 ms with the fix; the owner's lock filled its output, which is why it took 70 ms without its shadow. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/shadow_overhang.rs::a_shadow_inside_a_lock_is_cut_at_its_edge` (PNG `lock_shadow_cut`: the lock fills 640×360, the card's shadow cut at the bottom; no overhang, no spec size, no frame deadline), `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::a_shadow_inside_the_lock_is_cut_at_its_edge` (lock VM: the last row and column are the lock's colour; first frame 31 ms, 521 ms with the fix reverted).

**2026-11-05 · lock-polish: a lock's first frame shows its stills.** A `thumbnail screen` inside a lock showed nothing in the lock's first frames and then cut to its still: the still, taken before the lock (`Feeds::take_lock_stills`), was handed to the thumbnail only by the demand a painted frame makes (`Feeds::demand`, through the channel, so a frame or more later). A panel's first frame waits for its stills (`Feeds::before_map`, `HOLD`) because they are taken as it maps; a lock's are taken before the lock is asked for, bounded by `LOCK_STILL_WAIT`, so they are always in by the time a lock surface exists and its first frame need not wait at all. Read as the design asks ("a lock can open on the desktop as it was"): once a lock surface is configured and its first frame's scene is laid out, the thumbnails that frame will draw (`Renderer::first_feed_demand`, read from the flattened scene `update` keeps, with the sizes the painted frame's demand will ask) are fed their stills on the spot (`Feeds::feed_first_lock_frame`, called from `surface_configured`), scaled as the demand would, and their taps stand until a demand names them, so the still is not sent again. A monitor with no still (plugged in while locked, oi-lock) is fed nothing at once and reads `blank`; a lock with no thumbnail feeds nothing; neither holds a frame. Not chosen: holding the first frame as a panel does (there is nothing to wait for, and on Hyprland lock latency is first-frame latency), or feeding the whole still (a thumbnail draws its frame bilinearly with no filter, so a large still in a small thumbnail aliases). Left: a thumbnail mounted in the lock after its surface was configured (a later diff) still shows its still from the frame after the one that mounts it. Tests: `crates/strand/src/demo/host.rs::tests::a_locks_first_frame_shows_its_still` (the first painted frame holds the still's pixels, nothing sent again, a monitor without one blank and unheld), `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::the_locks_first_frame_shows_its_still` (lock VM: shots grabbed back to back from the request; the first that shows the lock shows the still, as do the eight after it, and the log says it was fed before the first frame; with the feed removed the first shot of the lock showed no still); `the_locks_thumbnail_is_a_still_from_before_the_lock` now waits for the lock's colour, since its first frames show the desktop's bar in the still. Also: `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/build.sh` matched its test executables by `/<name>-` anywhere in the path, which picked the strand binary in a checkout under a directory named `lock-…`; it matches `/deps/<name>-` now.

**2026-11-05 · lock-polish: the lock plays its way out before the session unlocks.** The lock went the moment its password was accepted, so it had no closing animation (strand-issues.md, "A lock can't play its way out"); the owner approved (2026-11-05) that the exit plays on the lock's surfaces before `unlock_and_destroy`, as hyprlock and Quickshell shells do, capped at about a second by the code that sends the unlock, with keys typed meanwhile ignored, and with nothing but what unlocks today starting it. *Language:* nothing new. A lock closes as a popup does: logic now unmounts a closed lock's content (`mount_surface_body`: `keep` for a lock as for a popup; its `state`s are the lock scope's and its handlers its logic's, so nothing of them goes), and render plays what that removal plays anywhere. The lock's own `exit { }` carries all of it as drawn (owner-2026-10-21: the removed root's exit carries all); without one, each node at the top of its content is a removed root and plays its own `exit` (or its mirrored `enter`), so an island can shrink back up into the bar and a blurred still fade off. The one rule added is render's: what leaves a closing lock with no pose stays drawn as it was until the rest has played (`Renderer::lock_closing`, through the `closing_content` a popup's closing pose already uses), since a lock that went blank at its exit's first frame could not end on the desktop's still; a popup still drops it at once. Read against "does it remove a concept?": a lock's content now behaves as a popup's (one rule fewer), each lock mounts it anew so its `enter` plays every time (the owner's lock remounts its face by hand for that, `lock_n`), and its first frame stays well inside `FIRST_FRAME` (26, 7 and 7 ms for three locks in `a_healthy_lock_draws_its_first_frame_in_time`, the first the run's first lock). *The handshake:* `auth`'s token goes to `State::unlock_after_exit`, which keeps it and reports `LockState::Unlocking`; logic (`SessionLock::Unlocking`) lets go of the hold and writes the two-way `open` false then (it wrote it at `Unlocked` before, and still does when no `Unlocking` came); render holds each lock open while its exit plays and says so (`SurfaceSpec::closing`, set on a lock only, so no other surface's spec changes); strand-surface spends the token once every lock node it waits for (those shown with a two-way `open` when the token came) has closed or gone. A lock with nothing to play closes in the diff that closes it and unlocks one logic round trip after the token. The built-in field's token, a lock whose `open` is one-way or unset (nothing closes it), and a lock still pending unlock at once, as before. *The cap* is `LOCK_EXIT_CAP`, 1 s from the token, a calloop timer of strand-surface's own, so neither a stalled frame, a pose that never settles, render's own stall rule (`EXIT_STALL`, 1 s of no frames, else `MAX_MOTION` + 1 s) nor logic can hold the session past it; with no timer the unlock goes at once. A second is two to four times what a closing pose on Strand's springs takes (`$motion.spatial` settles in about 0.2 s, the owner's `spring(380, 0.86)` in about 0.5 s), the bound the lock already gives a first frame (`FIRST_FRAME`) and render a stalled exit, and a small wait for someone who has typed their password; an exit longer than that is cut. *Input:* while it plays, strand-surface's `send_input` drops every event but focus and pointer enter and leave, so nothing typed reaches the host, logic, `auth` or the screen, and the binary tells `auth` no lock is shown (PAM's conversation ends) and counts no fault, heartbeat or first-frame deadline. *Security:* the exit only delays the unlock: the token is the one `unlock` took, held in the exit and spent only by it, and every other way out of the exit keeps the session locked or is the protocol's own end. *Edge cases, decided:* a lock asked for again during its exit (a node seen leaving opens again) stays locked: the session never unlocked, so the token is dropped, the host hears `Locked` again and the password is asked for again, with no desktop shown between (a request that comes before render shows the node leaving looks like logic not having closed it yet; if the cap ends that exit, the unlock is sent and the lock still open is spent, as on any unlock: see the review's paragraph below). A monitor unplugged during the exit takes its content with it (the exit waits for that node no more, followed when the outputs are reconciled as when a spec changes); one plugged in shows the solid in the lock's colour, as no instance is mounted there to play anything, and each content stays on its output meanwhile. A reload during the exit waits for the unlock as it does while locked (`lock_shown` is true while `Unlocking`). The compositor sending `finished` during the exit ends it: the unlock goes at once (`unlock_and_destroy` is also the protocol's answer to `finished`), the host hears `Unlocked`, and no new lock is asked for, since the password was accepted and asking would only make the user type it again. Measured in the lock VM: a card leaving on a 600 ms linear fade ended its exit 613 ms after the token, grim catching 8 of 9 shots with the card part way out and none with the desktop until then (0 shots with the old immediate unlock); an 8 s exit was unlocked by the cap 1.17 s after Return; the lock's `on key` took 11 keys for the password, 12 with its Return, and still 12 after five more keys typed as it played out (16 with the drop disabled). Tests: `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs` (lock VM: `the_lock_plays_its_way_out_before_it_unlocks`, `the_exit_cap_unlocks_an_exit_that_does_not_settle`, `keys_typed_while_the_lock_plays_out_go_nowhere`, `a_lock_asked_for_again_as_it_plays_out_stays_locked`, `an_output_plugged_in_as_the_lock_plays_out_shows_its_colour`), `crates/strand-render/tests/lock_exit.rs` (`a_lock_stays_open_while_its_content_plays_out` with PNG `lock_exit_mid`, `a_lock_with_nothing_to_play_closes_at_once`, `a_lock_opened_again_as_it_leaves_is_not_closing`), `crates/strand-compiler/tests/lock.rs` (`the_lock_closes_and_its_content_leaves_before_the_unlock`, `an_unlock_with_no_exit_writes_open_false`), `crates/strand-surface/src/manager/session_lock.rs::tests::an_exit_ends_when_its_nodes_close_and_not_before`; and the review's below. Not tested end to end: `finished` during the exit (the proxy of `finished_after_locked_locks_again_with_the_fallback` sends it on a timer, not on an exit).

**2026-11-05 · lock-polish review: a lock still open at the exit's cap is spent, not locked again.** The exit's unlock took a two-way lock spec still open and not leaving as asked for again and locked at once, on the reasoning that logic closes every one at `Unlocking`; but a logic slow to close it (busy, or stopped, inside the watchdog) leaves it just as open when the cap fires, and the two cannot be told apart in strand-surface. Locking again then asked for the password just accepted, and the guard kept the old lock's start (`Guard::since`, only dropped on a turn that saw no lock), so the new lock's first-frame deadline had already passed and the built-in field took over. Now an unlock after an exit spends an open lock as every unlock does (`spent = lock_spec_open()`; "an open spec is not a new request until it closes"), and nothing locks in the dispatch that unlocked; a lock asked for again is still seen and kept when render has shown the node leaving and it opens again (`ExitStep::AskedAgain`), and one asked for before that is lost as it is to an unlock with no exit. The `finished` branch therefore asks for no new lock, as the paragraph above says. The guard also starts a lock anew when the lock screen was reset since it took `since` (`LockScreen::ended`), so a lock asked for in the dispatch that unlocked the last gets its own deadline and heartbeat. And the exit is followed when the outputs are reconciled (`reconcile_all`), so a node whose output goes while its spec stays (a `screens: focused` lock) no longer holds the unlock until the cap. The lock's `open` going false at `Unlocking`, up to the cap before the unlock, is the accepted semantics: design.md says so. Tests: `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs` (lock VM: `a_slow_logic_at_the_cap_does_not_lock_again` under the new `STRAND_FAULT=logic_slow_unlocking`, which holds logic 1.5 s at `Unlocking`; `the_locks_still_stays_drawn_as_it_plays_out`, a `thumbnail screen` kept drawn while a card fades; `an_exit_whose_output_goes_ends_then`, a `screens: focused` lock's monitor unplugged mid-exit), `crates/strand/src/run/lock.rs::tests::a_lock_asked_for_as_the_last_ended_is_a_new_lock_to_the_guard`, `crates/strand-render/tests/lock_exit.rs::the_locks_own_exit_carries_all_of_it` (PNG `lock_exit_root_mid`: the lock's own `exit { opacity: 0 }` fades it whole, painted in its buffer).

## lock-blur

**2026-11-05 · lock-blur: a large `filter: blur` is drawn once at reduced scale, in the frame that first shows it.** The owner's lock (a full-screen still under `filter: blur(36)`, `backdrop: blur()` over it and a `filter: blur(22)` card whose size springs in) froze on the Arc: the still's group was blurred at full size on the CPU, 1,682 ms in the one frame that drew it (gpu.sh, 1920 × 1200, 3714cc62), and the blurred image did not appear in the 1.4 s of grabs after locking. A group whose blurs are 8 device pixels or more is now drawn at half size, from 32 at a quarter and from 64 at an eighth (`offscreen::filter_reduction`), blurred there and scaled back up bilinearly, then cached as before by its contents. On a desk photograph, a quarter-scale blur 8 of its pixels wide is within 2 levels of a full-size Gaussian (the photograph through scipy's, point-sampled as vello draws an image small), while 4 wide at a quarter was 9 off, hence the thresholds. A group with a colour matrix after its blur (a glow's doubled coverage, a stroke's edge) stays at full size, as the matrix would sharpen what the scaling up smoothed. The task asked what a frame shows if the first blurred frame cannot be ready in time. It shows nothing new: the blurred group is drawn in the frame that first shows it, synchronously, as before, and that frame is late rather than unblurred, because a sharp lock over a sharp desktop for a frame is the glitch the owner reported and an empty or tinted one is a flash. That frame now costs about 45 ms once (cpu 42.99–47.76 ms in v1–v3 on the Arc, 70 ms for v5's image drawn at an eighth and scaled 8×), every later one about 1 ms, and the blurred still is on screen 144–158 ms after `lock.locked` (base: never within the grabs). Both backends show the same: a GPU frame draws the CPU group's pixels, uploaded once. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::a_large_filter_blur_is_drawn_once_and_kept` (within 3 levels of a full-size Gaussian, one build kept across a repaint; ref `effects_filter_blur_large.png`).

**2026-11-05 · lock-blur: a plain rounded box under `filter: blur` is drawn as a blurred rounded rect.** A box that draws only its rounded background, one solid colour, no border, squircle, fillet or children, under a `filter:` that is only `blur(r)`, under a similarity transform, is the shape a `shadow:` draws: the flattener replaces its layer with `Item::Shadow` (`Flattener::blurred_box`), which vello draws analytically and the GPU lowers to `Op::BlurredRect`. Its size can spring with no offscreen group built per frame, so the lock's `filter: blur(22)` card that grows in costs about 1 ms of CPU and 1.5–2.6 ms of GPU a frame on the Arc where it cost 70–100 ms (a 1920 × 1200 group per frame), inside a 120 Hz frame. vello's blurred rect is `erf(d / std_dev)`, so its `std_dev` is √2 σ for a Gaussian of σ; at that it is within 3 levels of the group's Gaussian (2.3 measured). Anything else under the filter keeps the group, which is correct for any content. Test: `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::a_blurred_plain_box_is_drawn_as_a_shadow` (no group at two sizes, a bordered box makes one; ref `effects_blurred_box.png`).

**2026-11-05 · lock-blur: a `backdrop: blur` looks the same on both backends from its first frame.** On the Arc the lock's first frame, the CPU's, was lighter and softer than the GPU frames after it (patch luminance 77.7 and sharpness 0.21, then 76.6 and 0.30): the CPU blurred what is behind as transparent past the surface's edge, so the sharp desktop showed through there, and above 0.2 Mpx the GPU blurred at full resolution, a different blur. Now the CPU's blur repeats what is behind past the edge (`offscreen::blur_edge`, `Edge::Repeat`), as the GPU shader clamps, every backdrop blur is drawn at the CPU's reduction on both (a quarter, half or full under 8 or 2 device pixels, and an eighth from 64, where it is still 8 of its pixels wide), and the large blur is no GPU pass of its own: a GPU frame draws it in its frame as any other (`Op::Backdrop` with `reduce`) and a surface the CPU draws draws it itself, so nothing is read back. design.md's bundled GPU effects are seven, the eighth (a large full-resolution backdrop blur) gone. On the Arc the frames now hold at 76.7 / 0.14 from the first blurred one through the switch to the GPU, and the first CPU frame's raster fell from 162 ms to 42 ms. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_backdrop_blur_looks_the_same_on_either_backend` (CPU against lavapipe at scale 1 and 1.5, sigma 2, 8, 16 and a full-surface 36: no pixel past 6, worst 1), `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu_effects.rs::a_large_backdrop_blur_is_the_cpus_on_a_cpu_surface`; refs `effects_backdrop*.png` re-blessed for the edge.

**2026-11-05 · lock-blur: a filter blur's radius is in the node's own space; a backdrop blur's is the surface's.** A `filter:` is drawn before the node's transform, as in CSS, so `blur(r)` is `r` of the node's own logical pixels and scales with its `scale` and its ancestors': an image at an eighth under `blur(4)` and `scale: 8` is as blurred as the whole image under `blur(32)` (`effects::under_transform`, the radius times √|det| of the transform). It had been in surface pixels whatever the transform, so v5 of the probe (an eighth-size image under `blur(4)` scaled 8×) came out barely blurred (sharpness 0.61, against 0.15 for `blur(36)` at full size; now 0.16). A `backdrop:` blurs what is behind the node, which its transform does not scale, so its radius stays in the surface's logical pixels. Test: `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::a_filter_blur_scales_with_its_node`.

**2026-11-05 · lock-blur: the review's fixes: a colour function after a large `filter: blur` keeps its reduction.** A group with any colour matrix after its blur was drawn at full size, so the lock's dimmed wallpaper written `filter: blur(36), brightness(0.7)` took the old path while `brightness(0.7), blur(36)` did not: on the Arc (gpu.sh, 1920 × 1200, v10 of the probe: v2 with `brightness(0.7)` after the blur) its first frame cost 437–459 ms of CPU in two runs, and the blurred still first showed at 609 ms. The full-size exception was for the matrices that change alpha after the blur, a `glow:`'s doubled coverage and a `text_stroke:`'s growth, which sharpen what the scaling up smoothed. A matrix whose alpha row is the identity (`brightness`, `contrast`, `saturate`, `grayscale`, `hue`, `invert`, `tint`) is linear in premultiplied pixels, its offsets times alpha, but for its clamping, so it gives the same before or after the scaling up, and now keeps the reduction (`offscreen::group_reduction`); the same probe's first frame costs 45.6–47.0 ms, as the plain blur's 42.9–43.9, the still showing at 158 ms, blurred and dimmed from its first frame, and settled the same as before (patch luminance 55.7 against 55.6, sharpness 0.10 both). The exceptions left are stated in design.md: a mosaic, and an alpha-changing matrix after the blur, which draw at full size, their first frame as long as the blur takes there, as does a blur under 8 device pixels over a large image. The backdrop blur's eighth (sigma 64 device pixels and up, the owner's lock at scale 2) is now in the CPU-against-lavapipe parity test (worst 2 of the GPU tolerance's 6). Tests: `crates/strand-render/src/offscreen.rs::tests::a_colour_matrix_after_a_blur_keeps_its_reduction`, `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::a_dimmed_large_blur_is_drawn_at_its_reduction_in_either_order` (the two orders within 1 level; 3 apart with the old rule), `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_backdrop_blur_looks_the_same_on_either_backend` (a scale-2 case).

## lock-int

**2026-11-05 · lock-int review (lock lifecycle and GPU): a lost request never disarms the next, `finished` in an exit fails closed, only `auth` closes a lock, and a hand-off to the GPU holds the lock's clock.** The second review of the merged lock lanes found four faults, all checked before fixing. (1) A lock request in the tick that wrote `open` false at `Unlocking` (`on session.lock_requested { locked = true }`, or any request while logic was busy) netted no change, so render never showed the lock leaving and strand-surface unlocked at the cap with the spec still open, spending it as the lock-polish review decided; but logic's `Unlocked` after `Unlocking` wrote nothing, so `locked` stayed true, every later request wrote the same value, and nothing locked again until strand restarted. `Unlocked` now always writes the two-way `open` false (`LockTrack::report`): the cap's unlock drops that request, as decided, and re-arms the next. The one cost is a narrow race (a `true` written after render showed the lock leaving that reaches strand-surface only after the exit ended, which it takes as a new lock): that lock is held and shown as any, with its state false until its password unlocks it, never open. (2) `finished` during the exit sent `unlock_and_destroy` on the finished object, reported `Unlocked` and asked for nothing, against the module's own fail-closed rule (the compositor may keep the session locked, and the restart marker went with the lock); it is now `finished` after `locked` like any other: the exit's token goes unspent, a new lock is asked for once and the binary shows the built-in field on it (`LockScreen::changed` arms it after `Unlocking` too), at the cost of one more password where the compositor really unlocked. (3) A renewal (a stalled or failed GPU, a new size, the fallback) wrote `locked = false` while the session stayed locked, and the owner's config cleared the password typed before it (the review's VM run: `lock.locked` false 900 ms after the renewal, the field empty): the compositor's `wl_keyboard.leave` of the old `wl_surface`, kept alive for the GPU thread, was taken for the focused surface's, which by then was the new one, and the router's focus-loss rule closed its two-way `open`. A leave of a `wl_surface` no longer ours is now ignored (only a solid lock surface's counts as the focused content's), and the router never closes a lock (Escape, click-away, focus loss), since only `auth` does and the hold kept the lock open but not the state it is bound to; the keyboard moving between two monitors' locks did the same before. (4) The lock's first presented frame showed the pose of when it was asked, 50 to 200 ms before it came back (attach, new swapchain, the blur group built again), and the next frame jumped over that time: 64% of the owner's island's travel in one frame. Render now holds a lock surface's clock across its hand-off (`HandOff` in `renderer/backend.rs`): the first presented frame is drawn one period after the last CPU frame, the one after it one period after that, and every later one behind the time asked by what was lost (`Renderer::presented_lag`, logged once per hand-off as "clock was held"), so the animation freezes for the hand-off's length, which nothing can show sooner, and does not jump. (Re-check, same day.) The lag is at most 500 ms (`HAND_OFF_MOST`, the GPU silence strand allows a lock's request) and is dropped once a presented frame draws nothing moving: it was set once, from the gap before the second presented frame, so a first presented frame that ended the animation took the wait before the next (a caret's blink, a key) in as lag, seconds of it. On one surface a constant lag is not seen, since whatever starts in a frame leads from that frame's time; it is seen against other clocks: the same lock on another output samples the same node's motion at the real time (a shake started 5 s in the past ended there in one frame, the test below), and, read from the code but not tested, a theme swap starts at the latest surface's time and a `graph` places its columns on the boot clock. Only locks: a panel promoted mid-animation pays the same jump and is left as it was, a candidate for the same hold if the owner sees it. The review's fifth point, keys lost while a renewed surface waits for its first CPU frame (the compositor has no lock surface on that output to give them to), is documented in design.md rather than fixed: carrying the old surface's offscreen groups over would shorten the gap but not close it. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/lock.rs::a_request_lost_to_an_exit_does_not_disarm_the_next` (and `the_lock_closes_and_its_content_leaves_before_the_unlock` now expects the `false`), `crates/strand/src/run/lock.rs::tests::finished_after_locked_is_a_fault_and_a_refusal_is_not`, `crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::nothing_but_auth_closes_a_lock`, `crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::a_lock_surface_is_handed_off_after_its_first_frame_and_renewed_on_the_cpu` (lock VM; re-check: the renewed content is never sent a `KeyboardLeave`, which on the code before (3) it was, between its two enters), `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_locks_hand_off_to_the_gpu_holds_its_clock`, `::a_locks_hand_off_hold_never_takes_in_the_wait_after_it` (the other output's card at 0 of 150 before the re-check), `::a_locks_hand_off_hold_is_bounded`; lock VM: `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::finished_as_the_lock_plays_out_locks_again_with_the_fallback` (the `finished` proxy fired once the exit started), `::a_lock_whose_gpu_stalls_goes_on_on_the_cpu` (its config now clears the field when `locked` turns false, and `lock.locked` must stay true across the renewal), `::a_lock_that_animates_from_its_first_frame_is_presented` (the hold is logged). On the code before these fixes the two changed VM tests fail (`lock.locked` read `false` after the renewal; the `finished` in the exit left the desktop showing, no field), and with them all pass; in the lock VM's lavapipe the fade's hand-off held its clock 16 ms (the review measured 64 ms on the owner's draft, whose blur group the first presented frame builds again). Also: `offscreen::rasterise` is compiled only with the `gpu` feature, its one caller's, so strand-render builds without it again (the lock-blur review left it dead there, failing `-D warnings` for crates that use strand-render without the GPU, strand-compiler among them).

**2026-11-05 · lock-int review (rendering and blur): an `exit` under a node with none plays in a closing lock, a filter blur repeats its edge where the surface cuts it, and a large blur is kept at its reduction.** The second review's blur findings, each checked before fixing. (1) In the owner's draft the island never played its exit: it is a `stack` with `enter` and `exit` poses inside a full-screen `col` that has none, and render ghosted only a removed node with an exit of its own, so the `col` stayed drawn at rest, island and all, until the unlock took it in one frame, while its `enter` had played (each created node enters). In a closing lock, a removed node with no pose now has the first nodes down its subtree that have one play their exits (`Renderer::posed_under`, the outermost only, as a removed ghost plays its own and not its children's), the rest staying drawn as it was, and the lock is held for them like any exit; design.md's "each node at the top of its content" was amended rather than the draft changed, since a centring column is how a lock places its content and its enter already played. Popups and panels are unchanged (their content leaves with the surface's own pose). In the lock VM on the owner's draft the island now shrinks up into the bar and fades as the blurred still fades, the exit ending after 561 ms (frames grabbed back to back, CPU). (2) A `filter: blur` blurred its group as transparent past its pixels' edge, and the group is cut to the surface, so a full-screen still under `blur(36), brightness(0.6)` faded out over 3σ at every screen edge and the sharp still under it showed there (the review: lum 50 against 38 inside on a row, the bar's sharp orange in the corner). A side where a group's region meets the surface's edge now repeats the edge pixels there (`offscreen::cut_sides`, `blur_edge` per side), as the backdrop blur does: what the surface cut is unseen, not absent, and a group whose content ends short of the edge has only its blur's faded tail there, which repeats as the near-transparent tail it is. A group cut by an ancestor's clip inside the surface still fades, as before. The one ref this changed is `album_art_blur.png`, blurred art filling a panel, which now stays blurred art to the panel's edges instead of fading to its background (re-blessed); `effects.rs::a_filter_blur_scales_with_its_node` was moved 30 px clear of the surface's edges, since a scaled group's antialiased edge row, repeated, weighed up to 17 levels differently from the unscaled one's, which is not what it measures (a group whose content ends a pixel or two short of the surface's edge is the same gray zone: its partly covered edge row goes on past it). In the VM the owner's settled lock now has 38 at the edge as inside, the corner the blurred dimmed bar (133, 70, 7) and no step under the bar's edge. The alternative, the draft using `backdrop: blur` over the still, was not taken: a filter blur of something that fills the screen fading to what is under it is never what a shell wants. (3) A large blur's group was kept scaled up to full size, 9.2 MB for a 1920 × 1200 still, so the owner's three monitors took 25.8 MB of the 32 MB budget and larger ones thrashed it (the review: three outputs at 43 MB rebuilt the blur on every frame, 35 to 48 ms each, the caret's blink included); its build spent most of its time scaling up and the GPU frame uploading 9 MB. A group is now kept at its reduction (`offscreen::Drawn::k`, its `transform`; the backdrop blur's too, tinted there, a colour drawn over being linear in the pixels) and scaled up bilinearly, edge pixels repeated, where it is drawn: by vello_cpu's image paint on a CPU surface and by the GPU's smooth image (`Op::Image`, its scaling in `image_transform`) on a presented one, uploaded at its reduction; only a GPU pass's input is scaled up whole (`Drawn::full`). The two backends match within 1 level (lavapipe and the Arc, scale 1 and 1.5, the full-surface case included), the refs passed unchanged within their tolerance but one, and a full-surface composite on the CPU costs about twice what a 1:1 one did (18 against 9 ms for 1920 × 1200 on one thread, measured), paid only where a frame repaints the group. The finding that the first frame showing the blurred still froze the lock (frame 2, the first GPU frame, building it: 47 to 61 ms on the Arc, three monitors 105 to 110 ms) is answered by making the build cheaper, its option (c): in a release build on the laptop the owner's group (a 1280 × 720 still drawn over 1920 × 1200 under `blur(36), brightness(0.6)`) builds in 7.0–7.3 ms where it took 23–25 ms, and three monitors' (1920 × 1200 and two 1920 × 1080, three distinct stills) in 19.7 ms where they took 64.6–67.2 ms, before the 9 MB upload each that is now 0.6 MB. Its options (a) and (b), building the group of a node hidden at `opacity: 0` by its `enter` during the CPU first frame, or on a worker with the fade held until it is ready, were not taken: the first would draw or flatten nodes that are not shown, a change to what every hidden node costs, for what is now under a frame on one monitor, and the hand-off already holds the lock's clock so the frame that builds it never jumps. Three monitors still build one after another in that frame, about 20 ms; that is the known leftover. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/lock_exit.rs::an_exit_under_a_node_with_none_plays` (PNG `lock_exit_nested_mid`; on the old code the lock closed at once), `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::a_filter_blur_cut_by_its_surface_repeats_its_edge` (PNG `effects_filter_blur_cut`; the old code showed the magenta under it at red 185), `::large_blurs_are_kept_at_their_reduction` (three 2560 × 1600 surfaces, 1 MB each, no rebuild across repaints; the old code kept 16.4 MB each), `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_filter_blur_looks_the_same_on_either_backend` (lavapipe, and the Arc through gpu.sh: worst 1).

**2026-11-05 · lock-int (owner trial): the lock keeps its exit's end on screen until the unlock, and the unlock waits for that frame to show.** After the exit, the owner sometimes saw one dark frame on one monitor (a screen recording: mean luma 116 → 16 → 116 in one of six unlocks, the still, then nearly black, then the desktop). Cause, from the code and the owner's `STRAND_LOG=damage` log: when a lock's last exit ends, render unmounts what it kept drawn for it (the still, which has no pose) in the same refresh that closes the lock's spec, so the next paint of that surface draws the lock's `bg` alone (`$shadow`, near black; the log's `flatten=0.00` frame). strand-surface hears the close only at the main loop's next sync, so that frame was painted, sent to the GPU thread and presented before the unlock in every unlock of the log, on each monitor whose lock closed before the last one did (the 120 Hz eDP-1 most often, its frames coming twice as often); whether the compositor showed it before the unlock landed was the luck of a vblank, hence sporadic. Separately, the unlock never waited for the exit's last frame to be shown, so the compositor could also go from a frame from before the end to the desktop. Now render settles a lock that closes after its exit (`Renderer::lock_settled`): each of its surfaces draws one more frame, the exit's end (what had an `exit` gone, what had none kept drawn, the still), and then nothing, wanting no frame, until it goes or the lock opens again (`lock_frozen`; a new size is still drawn, and draws that end); what the lock kept stays mounted while a surface shows it, so a surface renewed then draws the end too. strand-surface, once every waited node has closed, sends the unlock when each content surface has no frame callback or presentation outstanding (`lock_frames_shown`: a CPU commit's, or the callback asked for the GPU thread's present; an unmapped, gone or renewed surface, or one whose last paint sent nothing, waits for nothing), still under `LOCK_EXIT_CAP` from the password, whose timer sends the unlock itself, and with the same token rules: asked again, `finished` and hotplug during the wait are those of the exit. The frame callback, not the GPU thread's `Presented` (which is the present call returning), is what says the compositor drew the frame. The cost is the frame's round trip, about a frame, on top of the exit. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/lock_exit.rs::a_closed_lock_keeps_its_exits_end_until_it_goes` (on the old code the frame after the close drew the lock's blue alone), lock VM `crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::an_exit_unlocks_once_its_last_frame_shows` (on the old code `Unlocked` came with the close, before the last frame's presentation), and lock VM `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::the_locks_last_frame_stays_until_the_unlock`, under a new fault, `lock_slow_close`, which hands render's close to strand-surface 400 ms late so that what the lock shows in that gap stays up for grim: every shot shows the still, where on the old render every shot in the hold was the lock's `bg` over the whole screen.

**2026-11-05 · lock-int review: the unlock waits for each monitor's own end frame, and the settled lock lasts until the lock session ends.** The review of the fix above found four holes. (1) `lock_frames_shown` judged "shown" when strand-surface heard the close: with one lock root on several monitors, a surface that had not yet painted since the close (the slower monitor, or one throttled at that moment) had nothing outstanding and passed, so the unlock could come before it drew the end. strand-surface now also asks the host whether each mapped content surface has drawn the exit's end (`SurfaceHost::lock_end_drawn`, true by default; the binary asks `Renderer::lock_end_drawn`) and looks again after each lock paint (an idle after the dispatch, once the commit is made) as well as each frame shown; the cap stays, and its warning names each surface still owed and why. Render marks every surface of a lock it settles dirty, so each owes and draws that frame; a preview that finds the scene as last painted counts the last frame as the end, since it is. (2) `finished` during that wait recreated the content with the same ids under the closed, settled root, which drew the old end (a still of the desktop) on a session still locked, its kept nodes still mounted. (4) A renewal with a refresh between `detach_surface` and `attach_surface` lost the settled state and the kept content (the rule "kept while a surface shows it"), so the new surface drew the lock's background alone. Both had one cause, settled state tied to surfaces: it now lasts until the lock opens again or the host calls `Renderer::lock_session_ended`, on `Unlocked` and `Finished`, which drops what was kept and redraws. (3) `renew_lock_content` returned `Some(new)` when the renewal itself ended the exit and unlocked, destroying `new`: it returns `None` then (`run/gpu.rs` already reads `None` as not renewed). The docs said "exactly one more frame": anything that invalidates a frozen surface (a new size, a new id, a backend or asset change, a failed commit) draws the end again, never anything else, and they now say so. Tests: `a_renewed_or_resized_frozen_lock_draws_its_end` (the reviewer's repro; on the old render the new surface drew the blue alone), `a_lock_on_two_surfaces_freezes_each_on_the_end`, `a_lock_finished_as_its_end_shows_lets_the_end_go` (host; without `lock_session_ended` the new lock drew the old end's green), lock VM `an_exit_on_two_outputs_waits_for_both_ends`, `a_lock_asked_for_again_while_its_end_shows_stays_locked` (no `Unlocked` 1.2 s on), `the_cap_unlocks_when_the_end_never_shows`, and `the_locks_last_frame_stays_until_the_unlock` now checks the card is gone and nothing changes in the hold, with a 150 ms exit and a 300 ms hold for half the cap spare, and runs presented by the GPU too (`..._on_the_gpu`).
