**2026-11-05 · lock-int (owner trial): before a lock's stills are taken, Strand settles its own surfaces, so the still is the desktop at rest.** The owner's launcher locks by folding the launcher into the island and calling `session.lock()` as it goes: the launcher's `exit { opacity: 0 }` (about 210 ms) and the island's icon fade start in the tick that asks for the lock, and the stills were taken synchronously in `before_lock`, so the lock opened on the folded card over the island with its icons hidden (an "empty island"), and played its way out to that still at the unlock. Three answers were weighed. Waiting for the exits to end (about 210 ms, more for a long one) puts the whole of the slowest animation in front of every lock; a config-side delay (lock after the panel has gone) is a rule each shell must know and get right, and adds a concept; settling removes the wait and the rule. So a lock asked for by its spec opening first asks the host to settle (`SurfaceHost::settle_for_lock`): render ends every running `exit` not under a lock (a closing surface's spec closes at once, handed over in the same sync, so it never paints at rest) and draws each other surface with a motion toward an end once more with every finite motion at its end, as `reduced_motion` does, while clocks, loops, a caret's blink and media run on; the lock's own surfaces are never touched, and open panels stay open. strand-surface then waits for those frames to show (frame callback or presentation, the GPU thread's included) and the closed surfaces to go (a GPU-held one once the thread let go), sends a `wl_display.sync`, and takes the stills when it comes back, at most `LOCK_SETTLE_CAP` (25 ms) after the spec opened. With nothing moving, or no `thumbnail screen` in the lock, nothing is settled and the lock is asked for in the same call as before; a lock asked for directly (the fail-closed restart lock, the relock after `finished`) never settles, so the security model, relock and hotplug are as they were. One log line says what was settled and how long it took. Measured in the lock VM: 2.1 ms on the CPU and 3.2 ms with the launcher presented by the GPU (lavapipe), one exit ended and one surface closed; a direct lock logs nothing and waits for nothing. Not settled, as they are not one node's motion toward an end: a palette or theme crossfade, a list's fling, and a surface still opening and not yet mapped (it is not in the still anyway). Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/lock_settle.rs` (the settle and its limits; nothing moving settles nothing), lock VM `crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::a_lock_waits_for_the_hosts_settled_frames` and `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::a_lock_from_the_launcher_shows_the_desktop_at_rest` (owner flow and a direct lock as control) and `::a_lock_from_a_gpu_presented_launcher_shows_the_desktop_at_rest`; on the code before, both strand tests failed with the still showing 0 icon and 256 glyph pixels.

**2026-11-06 · lock-int review of the settle: settled means committed and synced, not shown; a close mid-settle still locks; the marks end with the settle.** Two reviews of the settle above found three holes. (1) Render's marks were cleared only by a paint or a detach, so a surface that could not paint its settled frame before the cap (an output in DPMS off, a surface the compositor stopped calling back) kept its mark through the lock, and its first frame after the unlock snapped whatever moved then. However a settle ends (`LockSettleEnd::{Settled, Cap, Closed, Stopped}`), the manager now tells the host (`SurfaceHost::lock_settle_ended`), and the binary drops every mark (`Renderer::end_lock_settle`), as `Renderer::lock_session_ended` does too. (2) A surface that animates always owes a frame callback, so its settled frame painted only after that callback (up to a refresh), and the settle then waited for that frame's own callback too: 17 to 35 ms at 60 Hz, past the 25 ms cap in about half of all locks with an open surface moving. The settled frame now paints at once, the callback owed for the frame before notwithstanding (a commit without one is allowed; the frame before may just not be shown on its own), and a GPU-presented one goes at once where the WSI does not wait for callbacks (`wp_fifo_manager_v1`; without it Mesa's present would wait with no timeout, so it waits as any frame does, within the cap). Settled now means the settled frame committed (for a GPU-presented surface, the GPU thread's `Presented`, which the binary owes until it comes) and a `wl_display.sync` after it come back; its frame callback is not waited for. A compositor that holds a commit on its buffer's fence would apply it as soon as the GPU work is done, well inside a refresh and before the capture, which is of the compositor's next frame anyway, so the cap stays 25 ms rather than two refreshes of the slowest output. (3) A lock spec that closed while it settled was never asked for, where before a spec that opened always asked for the lock and only a token ended it: a close (or the spec going) mid-settle now ends the settle and asks for the lock all the same. Measured in the lock VM: an island still fading in when the lock came (a surface that stays open, mid-animation) settled in 3.5 to 7.2 ms (14.3 ms on the code that waited for the callbacks), the closing launcher in 2.3 ms on the CPU and 5.0 ms on the GPU, an animating panel in strand-surface's test in 3 to 10 ms (the cap on the code before). Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/lock_settle.rs::a_settle_mark_ends_with_the_settle` and `::the_lock_sessions_end_clears_a_settle_mark` (failed with the marks kept), `::a_nested_exit_and_a_finite_play_settle_on_an_open_panel`, `::an_animation_just_finished_settles_nothing`; lock VM `crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::a_lock_waits_for_the_hosts_settled_frames` (an animating panel, five rounds, each ending `Settled`, and the close mid-settle locking; ended at the cap on the code before) and `::a_lock_settle_ends_at_its_cap`; `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::a_lock_from_the_launcher_shows_the_island_faded_in` (three rounds: icons whole, one surface snapped, no cap), and the GPU launcher's test now checks the launcher was the GPU's until the lock was asked for, its release before the settle's end. Left: two outputs in the strand VM test (one output covers the settle; the stills per monitor are covered by lockmon's tests).

**2026-11-06 · lock-int (grain-over): `grain:` lies over a node's own pixels, as a pixmap of its own on a clock of its own.** In the lock VM, `thumbnail screen { filter: blur(36), brightness(0.6); grain: 0.03 }` over a sharp `thumbnail screen` showed the sharp still: the blurred one drew nothing but grain. The flattener drew one raster per node, either the source its props build (`grain:`) or its own (a thumbnail's frame, a graph, a spectrum, an `svg`, a Lottie), so grain replaced a raster node's pixels; it was drawn under an `image` or `icon` (hidden by an opaque one), dropped on an `effect` or `particles` (their props built the effect alone), and on a GPU frame it took a `shader`'s pass in its place (the lowering runs a node's pass for any raster item of that node). Now grain is always drawn over the node's own pixels, whatever its kind: over its background and raster source, and over a `shader`'s pass, a `canvas`'s drawing, an `image` or an `icon` (after their glow's content, so the grain does not glow), clipped to its shape, under its border, inner shadow, stroke, rim, a widget's parts, text and children (an `image` or `icon` is drawn over its own border, inner shadow, stroke and rim, and its grain with it; the review below sets these out, and the grain under a `filter:`); a plain box draws as before. Its pixmap is kept apart from the node's own (`RasterLayer::{Own, Grain}` in `RasterNodes`, each dropped when nothing draws it), so a 12 fps grain tick never draws a graph or a GIF again, and its raster item says it is grain, so a GPU frame draws it as an image over the pass. Grain keeps its 12 fps (m4-effects-paint-w2). Beside a clock of the node's own pixels it is a second clock from the same start rather than one clock at the faster rate: a single clock at 83 ms would show a GIF's 100 ms frame changes at 167 ms; each now ticks at its own times and the node wakes at whichever comes first. A node reading time keeps the same second clock (the review below). The cost, now said in design.md: a node with grain repaints its area 12 times a second unless `reduced_motion` is on, and holds a second pixmap of its size. A `merge`'s goo is still drawn over its grain (goo is laid under the children once they are drawn). Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::grain_lies_over_a_nodes_own_pixels` (`effects_grain_over.png`: a fed thumbnail, an image and an aurora with grain, each its own colour under the grain's grey with the grain varying, clipped to the thumbnail's corner), `crates/strand-render/tests/animated.rs::grain_over_a_gif_keeps_both_clocks` (frames at 110 and 210 ms at their own times, the grain moving at 84 ms between them, 18 changes of either clock in a second, each drawn, with at most two frames more), `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_shaders_grain_is_drawn_over_its_pass_on_a_gpu_frame` (one pass, the grain's image after it in the node's box); each failed on the code before.

**2026-11-06 · lock-int review of grain-over: under a `filter:` grain lies over what the filter draws; beside a node reading time it keeps its own clock; what lies over it, said exactly.** Reviews of the fix above found three things. (1) Grain was drawn inside the node's own `filter:` group, so the lock's `thumbnail screen { filter: blur(36), brightness(0.6); grain: 0.03 }` still showed no grain (per-pixel greys at 3 %, drawn at an eighth and blurred by 36, average to one flat grey), and each 12 fps tick changed the group's content, so its full-screen blur, which design.md says is drawn once (about 7 ms of CPU), was drawn again 12 times a second for as long as the lock stood. A filter draws the node and its subtree as one, so grain now lies over what the filter draws: it is counted with the node's own pixels (its record's hash and ink, so damage is unchanged) and drawn once the filter's group closes, clipped to the node's shape, under the node's opacity, transform and transition mask (drawn again over the grain alone, as the same mask), and inside its `mask:` and `blend:`, which become a group of their own around the filter's (`effects::split_filter`; a group applies its effects in order, so a filter then a mask draws as before). On such a node the grain lies over its children too, as they are inside what the filter draws; the other reading, grain kept inside the filter and the owner told to put it on a node above, would leave every `filter:` with `grain:` drawing grain no one sees at the cost of redrawing the filter on each tick. Under a 3-D tilt, which shares one GPU pass with the filter's own passes, the two stay one group and the grain stays inside it. (2) A node reading time had no grain clock of its own: its clock is refresh only when nothing else sets it, but a `graph`'s columns, a GIF's frames or `effect shimmer`'s cap set it, so `graph { opacity: wave(…); grain: 0.05 }` moved its grain once a column (about 3 times a second) and a timed GIF at 10 fps. Grain is now a second clock beside any clock of the node, time-reading or not; at refresh it costs nothing more, as the node wakes each frame anyway. (3) design.md's row said grain lies over "what its kind draws", but a text's glyphs, a widget's parts (a meter's fill, a slider's track and knob, an arc's ring), its stroke and rim are drawn later and lie over it: grain is a paint of the node's surface and of what fills its box (its background, a raster source, a shader's pass, a canvas, an image or icon), and the marks drawn on that surface lie over it, as its children do. The row now says so. Tests: `crates/strand-render/tests/effects.rs::grain_lies_over_what_a_filter_draws` (`effects_grain_over_filter.png`: an image under `blur(8), brightness(0.6)` shows its dimmed colour under grain that varies; beside it, under `mask: fade(bottom, 20)` as well, the grain fades out with the rest; three grain ticks later the grain has moved and no offscreen group was drawn again), `crates/strand-render/tests/animated.rs::grain_on_an_image_reading_time_keeps_its_own_clock` (a GIF with `rotate: t * 0deg` wakes for the grain's tick before its frames' 100 ms and the grain moves at 84 ms); each failed on the code before.

## lock-4k

**2026-11-06 · lock-4k: a thumbnail at its own size is copied, and a GPU stall is judged before the pump paints.** On the owner's new desk (two Dell U2720Q at 3840 × 2160, scale 1.5, beside a 1920 × 1080 and the laptop's 1920 × 1200; Hyprland, Arc B390) the lock showed Hyprland's "lockscreen app died" screen on the 4K monitors for about 1.9 s each time it locked. Strand's log: the four lock surfaces went to the GPU, then "the GPU thread answered nothing for 500 ms", and all four were renewed on the CPU; a renewal leaves an output with no lock surface until the new one's first frame, and Hyprland draws its dead screen on an output without one once the lock is older than its `misc:lockdead_screen_delay` (1 s). The GPU thread had not stalled. Measured with the owner's lock as an overlay panel on four headless outputs of the same sizes (`hyprland-nested.sh`, real Hyprland 0.57 on the Arc; `gpu.sh`'s sway showed the same paint times): each paint of a 4K surface held the main thread 445 to 524 ms, nearly all of it drawing the two `thumbnail screen` nodes (the still and its blurred copy), which sampled every pixel of a 3840 × 2160 frame bilinearly with four bounds-checked reads and an edge coverage each, about 200 ms apiece (under 60 ms at 1920 × 1200, which is why the laptop alone never showed it). `GpuHost::pump` paints its presented surfaces in turn and judged stalls after them, so the first 4K output's frame, answered within milliseconds, waited out the second's paint unread and was given up on. Two fixes. (1) `thumbnail`'s draw copies a frame placed at its own size on whole pixels (a screen's thumbnail on that screen, cropped by `cover` or not: every lock still), since bilinear sampling there returns each pixel itself, wholly covered; elsewhere each column's and row's taps are computed once rather than per pixel, with the same arithmetic, so the draw is byte for byte what it was (`media::thumbnail::tests::the_draw_is_the_per_pixel_draw_it_replaced`, against the old per-pixel draw kept in the test; it fails when the copy swaps a channel). On nested Hyprland a 4K paint with two live thumbnails went to 44 to 54 ms and its frames from 480 to 1054 ms apart to 17 to 130 ms, with no stall in three runs; a lock's stills are drawn once per surface, so the lock pays even less. (2) Stalls are judged at the start of the pump, on the replies just read and before it paints, so a long paint is never taken for the GPU thread's silence; a frame the pump sends is judged at the next pump, after its answer. The lock VM's new `main_busy` fault holds the main thread twice the bound right after a pump sent a presented lock's frame: `lock.rs::a_busy_main_thread_is_no_gpu_stall` fails with the judgement where it was (the surface renewed, as on the owner's desk) and passes with it moved, and the real stalls (`a_lock_whose_gpu_stalls_goes_on_on_the_cpu`, renewed 509 ms after the fault, and the exit's) are still given up on at the bound. Left as it is: the 500 ms bound (a working thread answered every request in under 260 ms here, its 4K `Attach` included), and Hyprland's dead screen after a renewal past the lock's first second, which only a real stall now causes.

**2026-11-06 · blur-ready: the first frame to show a blur pays for it on the main thread; the fix is general.** lock-4k left the lock's hand-off long because of each lock surface's first presented GPU frame (`gpu-frame cpu=` 57 to 79 ms at 4K optimised, about 1.6 s in the debug lock VM), and named the blurred still's rebuild as the next thing to look at. Verified from the code and the desk test in the lock VM: a node at opacity 0 is not drawn (`flatten/node.rs`, no opacity group, no filter layer, no raster item), so the lock's first CPU frame, which draws the copy under `filter: blur(36), brightness(0.6)` at its `enter`'s 0, builds neither that copy's 33 MB raster pixmap nor its group, and the first frame with the copy above 0 builds both on the main thread; on a promoted surface that is the first GPU frame, since the hand-off holds the clock one period on. lock-4k's "built again" was wrong: it is built for the first time, and nothing is built twice (one `Offscreen` per raster serves both backends, keyed by content, with opacity outside the key). None of this is the lock's own: any surface that first shows something under a filter or backdrop blur, or under a full-size colour matrix, pays the same in that frame, and any promoted surface showing a large image pays its upload's 33 MB clone on the GPU thread. Because of first-frame-lead the cost usually falls in a transition's first frame, so no earlier frame knows it is coming; a warm-up off the main thread would help only nodes held at 0 for a frame, the lock's case. The plan, general first and chosen by cost: the blur split over the raster's existing scoped helpers, byte-identical (it serves backdrop blurs on every frame of a slide-in, and glow, too); thumbnails drawn in the raster's BGRA order, one pixmap shared by the nodes fed one frame's pixels, none before a frame; `color_matrix` byte-identical but cheaper; strand-gpu's uploads swapped band by band into a bounded scratch instead of a clone. `tests/blur_ready.rs` holds the measurement and the guard: the lock's scene (a lock opened by the diff that mounts its content, two `thumbnail screen`s at 2560 × 1440 logical at scale 1.5, fed one 3840 × 2160 still, the copy fading in), whose counts of pixmaps and groups built per frame, CPU frame 2 (a reference PNG at 960 × 540 compared exactly, a hash at 4K) and the first GPU frame's uploads (hashes, which every device draws from) every later step keeps; the first GPU frame read back is compared with the CPU's within the GPU tolerance rather than with a PNG, since lavapipe's and the Arc's pixels differ. **2026-11-06 · blur-ready: a large blur and colour matrix run on the raster's helpers, byte for byte as before.** `blur_edge` runs in bands of output rows on `raster::share`, the scoped helpers a large paint's cells already use. Each band runs the blur as the whole of it ran (its rows' row passes into a ring, then each output row's column pass, tap by tap in kernel order), so each pixel's sums are the same, in the same order; the `r` rows above and below a band, which the bands beside it overwrite in place, come from a copy taken before the bands start, and each band passes them again. The output is the serial blur's byte for byte (`offscreen::tests::banded_blur_is_the_serial_blur`: every edge mode, sizes from 1 × 1 to the lock's 960 × 540 group, heights at and past the bands' threshold, sigmas 0.5 to 64; it fails when a band skips its halo's rows). It splits only when the work (pixels times taps) is at least 2^22, about a millisecond of a core's, ten times a helper's start, and into bands of at least 2r rows, at most `MAX_THREADS` (4); the helpers are the raster's, at most three in the process, joined before the blur returns, so an idle shell does zero work and the heap is each band's ring (about 1.3 MB at 960 × 540, σ 13.5) and the copied rows (about 0.9 MB), freed on return (`a_large_blur_runs_on_the_raster_lanes`, which also checks no helper outlives the call). It is the one blur filter groups, CPU backdrops and glow share. `color_matrix` keeps each pixel's float operations and changes how often they run: a straight channel's `c / 255 / a` comes from a table of the same expression, filled one alpha at a time as the pixels show it, a transparent pixel's result is worked out once, and a buffer of at least 2^18 pixels is split into bands on the same helpers (`color_matrix_is_the_reference_for_every_alpha`, every alpha with channels at, under and over it, five matrices, one thread and split; `a_full_screen_colour_matrix_runs_on_the_raster_lanes`). Measured with `blur_ready.rs` (`timing` profile, the container on the laptop, median of 5, ms): the lock's 4K group 33 → 16 (`blur_edge` at σ 13.5 on 960 × 540 25 → 11.6, `color_matrix` there 5.5 → 1.9), so the main thread's part of the 4K first GPU frame 44 to 46 → 27 to 29 and the CPU's frame 2 72 → 55; at 1920 × 1200, scale 1, the same group is 4.3 (the 6.8 design.md's "about 7 ms" was measured at); a full-screen 4K `color_matrix` 88 → 28, and a matrix-only 4K group 122 → 63 (most of what is left is drawing it at full size). The blur's split is about 2.2 times, not the 3 its work allows: the column pass streams its band's whole ring (1.3 MB) for each output row, and on the laptop's hybrid CPU the helpers can land on efficiency cores. **2026-11-06 · blur-ready: a thumbnail's pixmap is drawn in the raster's order, once for every node showing its frame.** Each `thumbnail` node kept its own full-size copy of the still it was fed: copied to RGBA (alpha raised to its largest channel), swapped back to the raster's BGRA by `RasterNodes`, and swapped again by strand-gpu's upload; the lock's blurred copy built a second 33 MB pixmap at 4K in the frame that first shows it, the same pixels as the sharp still's, and before any frame each thumbnail built a zeroed 33 MB pixmap and swapped it. Now `RasterSource::draw_bgra` draws in the raster's order (by default drawn and then swapped, so every other source is unchanged), and a thumbnail writes it directly, a captured pixel being its own bytes there. `RasterSource::content` names what a source's pixels are drawn from apart from its node (a thumbnail's frame, by the address of its pixels, and its fit; or no frame); nodes naming one content at one size and scale share one pixmap through a map of weak references, so a pixmap lives exactly as long as some node keeps it, and the frame's address is pinned (a `Weak` of its bytes) while a node keeps the pixmap, so no new frame at that address can take a stale pixmap; the pin is held by those nodes' kept pixmaps, not by the map, so it goes with the last node (see the pin-lifetime entry below), and an entry whose pixmap or frame is gone is dropped at the next draw, `retain` or `unused`. A group still keys its content by node, and pins the pixmaps it names, so no group is shared wrongly. Pixels are unchanged (`thumbnail::tests::bgra_draw_is_the_rgba_draw_swapped` across fits, sizes and fractional placements with pixels whose alpha is below a channel; `blur_ready.rs`'s PNG and hashes; `tests/thumbnail.rs::thumbnails_of_one_frame_share_one_pixmap` draws two shared and two own pixmaps the same; `offscreen::tests::a_shared_pixmap_is_freed_with_its_last_node`). The lock's first GPU frame loses the copy's pixmap (about 10 ms of the main thread at 4K: 45 → 18.6 ms with the filters' bands, at the `timing` profile, median of 5); its first CPU frame 21.6 → 18.8 and its CPU frame 2 55 → 45.6; each 4K monitor's lock keeps 33 MB less; `blur_ready.rs`'s counts per frame went from (2, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) pixmaps and groups to (1, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1). Not done: the plan's third part, drawing no pixmap at all before a thumbnail's first frame. A thumbnail's demand for frames is read from its record's bounds, which its raster item sets, so a thumbnail that pushed nothing before its frame would never ask for one; the blank pixmap stays, shared by the thumbnails of a size and no longer swapped, which leaves its allocation (about 2 ms at 4K, once per size).

A `Weak` of an `Arc<[u8]>` keeps the bytes' whole allocation after the last strong reference goes (the bytes live inside it), and the map was pruned only by a draw, `retain`, `unused` or a new pixmap, all in a paint or an apply. Pruning in the renderer's idle trim was not taken: the trim runs only at a wake that comes anyway (an idle shell is never woken for it), so it would shorten the leak, not end it. Now the pin is an `Arc` held by the kept pixmaps of the nodes sharing it (`RasterNodes`' `Kept`) and only weakly by the map: the frame's `Weak` is dropped with the last node that keeps the pixmap, whoever else still holds the pixmap, and a dead entry keeps a few dozen bytes, no frame. ## doc-formats

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: data from the web and from tools reads through the document path, with no HTTP client in Strand.** The owner asked for general building blocks so configs can use data from the web and from tools, not for a feed reader. Fetching stays outside Strand: `permit exec "curl"` through `from poll`, `from file`, `from listen` or an action with `-> T`. Four blocks are added, all on existing seams and with no new syntax: dates read from text, XML as a document format, `markup: html`, and `plain`/`links` on text. Scraping whole HTML pages stays out of scope: a full parser plus selectors would be a heavy dependency and new syntax, while `curl | htmlq` output already reads as text.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a `Date` filled from a document reads standard date text and Unix time.** Besides a record of year, month and day fields, a `Date` (a service field, a declared `type`'s field at any depth, a list item, a listen line, `-> Date`) reads text, trimmed, the first form that parses winning: digit text, where 9 to 11 digits are Unix seconds, 12 or more milliseconds, exactly 8 ISO basic `YYYYMMDD`, and fewer are refused (so `2026` never becomes 1970); RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 with a zone, also without seconds, with `+hhmm` or `+hh` (PostgreSQL prints `2026-11-07 21:30:00.123456+01`), or in the basic form `20261107T195510Z` (iCalendar, khal); RFC 2822, retried without a leading weekday when chrono refuses a full or a wrong one (`Mon, 08 Nov 2026`, a Sunday); a naive `YYYY-MM-DD[T ]HH:MM[:SS]`, the wall time as written (open-meteo gives its zone apart); and `YYYY-MM-DD` with hour and minute null. A number reads as its digits written out do (`date_from_number`), so USGS's 13-digit times are milliseconds and read as 2026, not year 58822, while `20261107`, which `date +%Y%m%d` prints and the document sniffing reads as a JSON number, is 7 November 2026 and not 1970-08-23, and `2026` or `0` is no date, the same as in quotes; a fraction or a negative number of 9 or more digits is Unix time (`date_from_unix`: |n| from 1e11 milliseconds, anything smaller seconds, which cannot be confused between 1973 and 5138). Anything else (ctime, `08:04 PM`, `05-AUG-10`) does not convert: the type's default and one report, or null for `Date?`, which the docs recommend. An instant moves to the local zone, as `File.modified` and notification times do, and is cut to the minute: `Date` stays minute-precision local wall time, with no `second` or zone field (no sample or shell needs one, and ordering, `format` and `add` work at minutes). The parser is `vm::clock::date_from_text` / `date_from_unix`, taking the zone as an argument (tests use a fixed one; `Zone::Local` is UTC on wasm, as the clock's is). It is reached from `instantiate::parse_text`, the one place text becomes a typed value, so `strand set`, `strand call` and the web shell accept date text too, plus one arm in the binary's `coerce` for numbers. No logic-side `date()` function: every place a date enters already goes through this path, and a function would be a second way to do one thing; `date_from_text` is public, so one costs a schema line if a real case appears. chrono's parsers are new to the web shell's module: it grows 34,002 bytes raw and 10,956 brotli (2,417,639 to 2,428,595 of the 2,500,000 budget, `scripts/wasm/build.sh` at 57830288 and after) (`dates_from_text_read_every_standard_form`, `dates_from_text_refuse_the_rest_and_never_panic`, `date_from_unix_reads_seconds_and_milliseconds_and_refuses_the_impossible`, `a_number_reads_as_its_digits`, `instants_move_to_the_zone_and_drop_seconds`, `parse_text_reads_a_date`, `a_date_field_reads_text_and_unix_time`, `an_action_reads_a_date_it_prints`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a `key=value` line's key starts with no digit.** `action now() -> Date ["date", "-Iseconds"]` printed `2026-11-07T21:05:09+01:00`, which the document sniffing read as one pair, key `2026-11-07T21`, value `05:09+01:00`, so the date never reached the `Date`; `12:30` from `date +%H:%M` was likewise a pair. A pair's key may no longer start with an ASCII digit, so a time or a date printed alone is text, read by every field as a scalar is. No real `key=value` or `key: value` source the services read (os-release, hostname, meminfo, `/proc` and sysfs `uevent` files) has a key starting with a digit (`documents_are_json_lines_or_text`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: XML is a document format, tried after JSON and before `key=value` lines, and bounded before roxmltree sees it.** A document is stripped of a UTF-8 BOM and trimmed; if it then starts with `<` it is tried as XML, and if that fails it is text, never pairs (`<title>a:b</title>` would otherwise split into a pair), with the reason logged once per changed document (`Document::NotXml`), so an HTML bot-check page served in place of a feed is never a silent empty list. roxmltree 0.21.1, already linked, recurses once per nesting level (the process aborted at about 3,000 levels on a 2 MiB stack, from roughly 12 KB of input) and checks duplicate attributes in quadratic time (90k attributes took 9.5 s), so a linear pre-scan (`custom::xml`, skipping comments, CDATA, PIs and quoted values, reading a DTD's internal subset token for token as roxmltree does, and refusing a construct it cannot follow; see the review paragraph below) refuses a document nested deeper than 128 (serde_json's own limit; real inputs reach 12), an element with more than 64 attributes (real ones have about 8), a DTD declaring a parameter entity, an external entity or an entity whose value holds `&`, `%` or `<`, and declared entities whose references expand past the document cap. DTDs are otherwise allowed, since nmap, D-Bus introspection and fontconfig carry them; nothing outside the document is ever fetched, and roxmltree's `nodes_limit` is one million. No dependency was added (`a_doctype_is_read_and_its_entities_bounded`, `xml_is_bounded`, `xml_survives_mutation`, `xml_that_is_not_well_formed_is_text_and_says_why`, `one_line_xml_is_not_pairs_and_html_stays_text`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: how an XML element becomes data.** The root element is the document, as a JSON top-level object is; its name is not a path segment (a rule letting a path start with it would be one more, ambiguous when the root has a child of its own name). An element with neither attributes nor child elements is its text: CDATA and entities decoded, both ends trimmed, inner line breaks kept, an empty element "". Any other is a record whose type is the marker `<element>` (no identifier can be it, so the binary applies the element rules to XML only), holding its attributes as `@name`, then its child elements and non-blank text runs (`#text`) in document order, repeated names kept in place rather than grouped: grouping would lose the order that text read across child elements (D-Bus `doc:para`, Atom `type="xhtml"`) needs, and a text field named `""` would be unreadable in watch and replay JSON. Names keep the prefix the document writes (`dc:creator`, read from the source span, since the same namespace may be bound twice); default-namespace names are bare; comments, PIs and namespace declarations are not fields. Reports and replay write such a record as JSON with its repeated names grouped into one array at the first one's place (`xml_elements_become_records_text_and_order`, `element_records_write_grouped_json`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: one name lookup for key paths and declared types.** A name `n` finds the matches of the first step that has any: child elements named exactly `n`; the attribute `@n`; child elements `p:n` with any prefix; attributes `@p:n`; and, for the name `text`, the element's own text. So RSS's `link` never finds `atom:link`, `creator` finds `dc:creator`, `href` finds `@href`, and OPML's `text` attribute beats the text alias. A child beats an attribute of its name, agreeing with the exact stored name; `= "@name"` reaches the attribute. On JSON objects a declared type's field takes an exact name, then a `p:n` key; a JSON key path stays exact (`json_path`, with its own search below the top level), as it was before XML, so `title` as a service field's key does not find `og:title` while a `type`'s `title` field does (a recorded difference: loosening JSON key paths would change what existing configs read). A string key (`= "dc:creator"`, `= "@state"`, `= "#text"`) is one exact segment, as it already parsed; m5-docs' "a key path cannot name the chip itself" stays true of identifier paths, and grammar.md now says what a string key is. In a key path the first segment is searched for depth first (16 levels, as JSON's) when the root lacks it, so `= item` finds RSS's items under `channel` and RSS 1.0's beside it, and the first element found holding it gives all its matches, not every element of that name in the document (a GPX track paused once has two `<trkseg>`s: `= trkpt` reads the first's points, `[Seg]` reads both); each later segment reads the first match of the one before, a number picks that match, and the last segment's matches are the value, several of them a list. A prefixed name shadowed by an unprefixed sibling (fedora's `slash:comments` beside `comments`) cannot be named inside a `type`: a recorded limit, not new syntax (`xml_names_match_exact_then_by_local_part`, `xml_key_paths_find_items_anywhere`, `type_fields_match_by_local_name`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: the declared type decides list or single, and text or record, for every document.** A list type over one value is a list of it if it converts, and does not convert otherwise (reported, not a silent `[]`); a missing key is `[]`. A single type over a list reads its first item, not the first that converts, which would hide a mismatch. This loosens JSON too: `{"level": [1]}` read as an `int` was a mismatch and is now 1, deliberately, so a format never changes how a type reads its data (`a_value_that_does_not_convert_is_reported_once` now uses an object for its second bad value). An XML element read as text, a number, a bool, an enum, a path or a `Date` is its text content, its own and its descendants' in document order, whitespace collapsed where it has child elements, the trimmed runs joined by a space except before closing and after opening punctuation; one with no text at all does not convert (Atom's `<link href rel/>` read as `text`), or reads null for `T?`; a JSON object is never text. So mixed content and Atom `type="xhtml"` read as text, losing their formatting, as the goal's wording says and so that `markup: none` never shows raw tags. `length`, `angle` and `duration` read plain number text (px, deg, seconds), since XML has no numbers. Blank text read as an optional type other than text is null with no report. A value inside a field's that held something and does not convert (a list's item, left out; a record's field, its default) is now reported once with its path, `` `news.posts`: `item[0].pubDate` holds "Sat Nov  7 20:45:15 2026", which is not a `Date?` ``, where it used to vanish silently, which dates and XML would have made common; a field whose own value converts resolves a report of that value first. A `from listen` line's nested mismatch is logged once until another. `to_value` for `any` needed no grouping: a record of no known type is null there, an element as a JSON object is (`a_list_type_wraps_one_value_and_a_single_type_takes_the_first`, `an_element_reads_as_its_text`, `number_types_read_number_text`, `blank_optional_values_are_null`, `a_nested_field_that_does_not_convert_is_reported`, `an_rss_file_fills_a_typed_list_with_dates`, `an_atom_poll_reads_entries_with_links_and_dates`, `a_listen_line_of_xml_is_a_document`, `a_json_api_s_rfc3339_dates_read_as_dates`, `rdf_ecb_opml_and_gpx_read_into_declared_types`, `a_page_that_is_not_xml_is_reported`, `a_commands_xml_is_read_as_its_declared_type`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a document is at most 4 MiB, refused whole past it, and Latin-1 is read as windows-1252.** The cap was 1 MiB, which a long feed with full content or an nmap scan of a subnet passes, so it is 4 MiB (`MAX_DOCUMENT`, also an action's output and a listen line). A file over it used to be read cut at the cap, which for JSON or XML is a different document or none; it is now refused whole: its fields keep their last values and the log says its size once per size (`an_oversized_file_is_refused_not_cut`, `a_document_just_under_the_cap_is_read`, `a_file_over_the_cap_keeps_its_value_and_latin1_reads`), as a command printing too much already was. Bytes that are not UTF-8 under an XML declaration naming ISO-8859-1, Latin-1, windows-1252 or US-ASCII are read as windows-1252, the WHATWG reading of all three, since feeds that declare Latin-1 carry 1252's quotes and euro; valid UTF-8 is never re-read, whatever it declares, and any other encoding is lossy UTF-8 as before, so no encoding crate is added (`a_latin1_feed_decodes`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: no `feed` service; recipes instead.** A builtin `feed` service (a URL in, items out) was weighed and dropped: it would add a concept, an HTTP client and a fixed item type to the toolkit, while `curl` in a `from poll` service, XML documents and `Date` fields cover RSS 1.0, RSS 2.0 and Atom with a `type` the config owns, and the same rules read a JSON API, a scan or a currency table. The site's "Data from the web and from tools" page gives those recipes, and its types are the ones the services tests read (`POST` and `ENTRY` in `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs`). Scraping HTML stays out of scope: a page that is not XML is text, said once, and a tool that extracts what is wanted can print it as JSON. A builtin `Feed` document record (RSS 2.0, RSS 1.0 and Atom normalised into one shape, beside `File` and `Date`) was weighed on the same grounds and dropped: RSS 2.0 and RSS 1.0 read with one declared type (`= item`; `date` and `creator` found by local name) and Atom with two (`Entry`, `Link`), while a record would add a whole-document key rule, two records in the wasm-built schema and feed policy frozen into Strand (which `rel` link, which date, category text or `@term`) that the config's own `find` and `??` say better; nothing here stops adding it later, normalised in `coerce` from the element data, if many configs come to carry the same mapping.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: the markup converter lives in strand-scene, one implementation for render and logic.** `strand_scene::markup::parse(text, level, limit)` serves both `markup:` levels and the `plain`/`links` text methods. strand-scene is the one crate both the compiler and the renderer already depend on, and it builds for wasm, which follows the `keys` precedent; the compiler gains no strand-render or strand-text dependency, and strand-web links the code once. It returns the shown text, styled runs (bold, italic, underline, strike, mono, link) and the links' hrefs as written; render maps the runs to its text spans. Render passes the text engine's 64 KiB `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` as the limit, so parsing stops once that much is shown; logic passes none, because a search must see the whole text. basic moved here unchanged (its tests with it), except for the shared entity decoder below. Measured (`scripts/wasm/build.sh`): the live examples' module grows from 2,417,639 to 2,438,969 bytes brotli (+21,330; +48,501 raw), within the 2,500,000 budget, for the converter, the 2,125-name table and the strike and family spans; the full table was kept. Render parses on each flatten of the node, with no cache: in a release build on the owner's laptop a 204 KB GitHub release note (`markup: html`, about 28 KB shown) costs 0.77 ms per flatten and a 48 KB planet entry 0.31 ms, under the 1 ms a frame may pay before a per-node cache earns its keep, so none was added; basic always paid the same per-flatten cost. `TextSpan` gains `strikethrough` and a per-span `family` and `GlyphRun` a `strike` rect from parley's strikeout metrics; code is shown in `$font.mono`'s family, then the generic monospace (the pixel tests' single vendored font has no monospace face, so `layout_markup_html.png` shows code in it, and strand-text's `strikethrough_and_mono_spans_shape` proves the override with DejaVu Sans Mono). Hostile input is bounded the way basic's always was: one forward pass, a remembered "no `>` after here" so a `<` with no tag end never rescans, an unterminated quoted attribute value turning quote-awareness off for the rest of the text (so it is scanned once), dropped elements found with one forward search for their close tag, styles nested at most 32 deep and lists indented at most 8 spaces (`malformed_html_never_fails_and_stays_linear` counts the bytes the scans look at and holds them under 8 per input byte for 1 MiB of `<`, 100k nested `<b>`, unclosed scripts, comments and quotes, and every prefix of the fixtures).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: `markup: html`, a third level for HTML fragments.** `markup: html` reads the HTML in feed summaries, release notes, calendar descriptions and mail-style notification bodies, leniently and in one linear pass, with no tree, CSS or images. Blocks: a blank line around p, h1-h6, the outermost ul/ol/dl, blockquote, pre, table, figure and hr; a line break for br, div, li, tr, dt, dd, caption and the sectioning elements (section, article, header, footer, aside, main, nav, figcaption, address, details, summary); break runs collapse to at most one blank line, two `<br>`s in a row make one, and both ends are trimmed. Lists: `• ` for ul and `N. ` for ol (honouring `start` and `value`, numbers of at most 20 digits), with 2 spaces per nesting level up to 8. Tables: one line per row, cells joined by ` · ` (an empty cell adds none). dt is bold and dd indented 2; an unclosed dt or th ends at the next cell, term or row. Styles: bold (b, strong, h1-h6, th, dt), italic (i, em, cite, dfn, var), underline (u, ins), strikethrough (s, strike, del), monospace (code, kbd, samp, tt, pre) and links (`a` with an `href`; an anchor without one is plain text), not clickable; headings are bold only, since spans have no size. A close tag closes its innermost open tag and anything inside it, a stray one is ignored, and anything open closes at the end. img shows its alt text. script, style, head, title, template, noscript, svg, math, iframe, object, video, audio, canvas and select are dropped with their contents, up to their close tag or, unclosed, the end. Comments (conditional ones too), downlevel-revealed `<![if …]>` markers, doctypes and processing instructions are dropped; CDATA is its text. Every other tag (span, font, small, sup, `o:p`, custom elements) is dropped and its text kept. Outside pre, whitespace runs become one space and spaces beside a break go; in pre everything is kept but a first newline. A `<` not followed by a letter, `/`, `!` or `?`, or with no `>` after it, is text. basic keeps its tags and its rule that unknown tags stay text, so `Vec<T>` in a notification body still shows; html is a separate level, not a widened basic, and the docs say which to pick. Mastodon's `class="invisible"` spans show their text, since there is no CSS. Markdown (GitHub's `body`) is not HTML; the docs say to ask for `body_html`.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: both markup levels share one entity decoder.** This amends the 2026-10-06 basic decision ("What `markup: basic` takes for a tag"), which decoded only the XML five and `&#39;`: apps that send markup send HTML entities, so `&mdash;` and `&#8217;` now decode in notification bodies too. The decoder covers every WHATWG named reference that ends in `;` (2,125, from a generated sorted table, `scripts/gen-html-entities.py`, searched by binary search) and numeric references of at most 8 digits, decimal or hex, with 0, surrogates and values past U+10FFFF giving U+FFFD and 0x80-0x9F mapped through windows-1252 (`&#150;` is a dash, as feeds rely on). `&nbsp;` (and any reference to U+00A0) is a plain space, which html never collapses but drops beside a break like any space, so what `plain()` returns matches `contains("foo bar")`. The legacy names without `;` are not decoded, because `?a=1&copy=2` in a URL would become ©; unknown, unterminated and over-long references stay literal, and expansion never recurses (a reference yields at most two characters). `layout_markup.png` is unchanged.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: `plain(markup)` and `links(markup)` on text.** `t.plain(html)` returns the text `markup: html` shows, without its styles, so logic can search, shorten or count it (`note.plain(html).lower().contains("nvidia")`). `t.links(html)` returns the hrefs in order, as written, because logic has no base URL to resolve a relative one against. Both take the property's own `Markup` enum, so `n.body.plain(basic)` serves notification search too, and `plain(none)` is the text unchanged (and `links(none)` empty). The argument is required: a default of `html` would silently drop `<T>` from a basic body, and writing `plain(html)` mirrors `markup: html`. A free `strip_html()` was rejected because it adds an html-only concept beside the existing levels; `links` was kept because it costs nothing (the parser sees every href) and serves calendar join links, release notes and notification bodies alike. Both call `strand_scene::markup::parse` with no limit, the same reading render shapes (`plain_matches_what_markup_shows`), so what a search finds is what the text shows. A null receiver lifts as for every text method.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: the two streams meet in the site's news list.** The page's sources put RSS 2.0, RSS 1.0 and Atom items into one declared `Story` type with `map`, join the lists with `+` (decisions.md flex) and sort them newest first with `sort_by(s => s.when).reverse()`, since a `Date` orders field by field from its year; each item's summary is the feed's HTML, shown by a `text` with `markup: html; max_lines: 3`, and `plain(html)` searches release notes in logic (`sources.nvidia`). Neither stream could build this alone, so it landed with the merge, with one end-to-end test over the RSS and Atom fixtures: the order across both feeds, `plain(html)` and `links(html)` of a document's field, the search, and the summaries reaching the scene as written with `markup: html` (`a_news_list_from_two_feeds_shows_and_searches_html_summaries`). The `Live` harness in `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs` now keeps the scene its ticks build, for that check. Merged, the live examples' module (`scripts/wasm/build.sh`, its lint first) is 2,449,764 bytes brotli and 8,576,387 raw, against 2,417,639 and 8,493,873 at 57830288: +32,125 brotli and +82,514 raw for both streams together (dates +10,956, markup +21,330 brotli, measured apart), leaving 50,236 bytes of the 2,500,000 budget. The first review round (numbers read as their digits, `+hh` offsets, the `Date` schema text) brings it to 2,450,619 brotli and 8,576,469 raw (+855 and +82).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: the pre-scan reads a DTD as roxmltree does, and refuses what it cannot follow.** Review found two ways past the bounds. The scan skipped quoted strings inside `<!ATTLIST`, `<!ELEMENT` and `<!NOTATION`, while roxmltree's `consume_decl` ends them at the first `>`, quotes or not; and on a construct it could not close the scan stopped and returned `Ok`, trusting roxmltree to stop there too. So `<!ATTLIST r a CDATA '>` with no partner quote hid 20,000 nested elements from the depth count (roxmltree went on and overflowed the stack, aborting the process), and a quote partnered two declarations later hid an `<!ENTITY>` between them from the expansion count. The scan now tokenises the internal subset exactly as roxmltree's `parse_doctype` does (white space, `<!ENTITY`, comments, PIs, the three declarations to their first `>`, `]` then `>`, anything else an error), reads an entity declaration to its closing `>` as roxmltree does, and refuses a document at any construct it cannot follow rather than handing it on, since such a document is not well-formed and roxmltree refuses it anyway. An entity declared twice counts as the larger of its values: roxmltree expands the first (as XML says), and the map kept the last, so `<!ENTITY e "<2 MiB>"><!ENTITY e "">` counted nothing for each `&e;` (`the_scan_reads_a_dtd_as_roxmltree_does`, `a_doctype_is_read_and_its_entities_bounded`). The not-XML reason is logged once until a document is something else, not once per reason: roxmltree's reasons carry a position, so a `from listen` of `dmesg -w -r`, whose `<6>[ 12.3] …` lines start with `<`, logged every line.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a `text` field reads markup as written.** Reading XML turned markup that sources print into element data: a file holding an HTML fragment (`<div><h2>Hi</h2><p>…</p></div>`) read as `body: text` was `""` with no report, since the root `div` has no `body`; a status script's `<span foreground="#e06c75">CPU 92%</span>`, which bar scripts print for Pango, was `""` too; and `<b>CPU</b>`, an element of text alone, answered every key as `CPU`, losing its bold. Before XML all three were text documents, which answer every key with themselves. A field typed `text` now reads an XML document as written when the document is one element of text alone (for `text?` too, since that element answers every key anyway), and, for `text` but not `text?`, when the document holds nothing at the field's key; `text?` keeps null for a missing key, as with JSON, so a feed's optional fields still read null, and every other type reads the element tree (`<value>42</value>` as an `int` is 42). The type decides, as it does everywhere else in reading documents, so no key or syntax was added for it; the choice between `text` and `text?` already says "absent means something". The cost is that a feed's required `text` field whose key is missing shows the feed's XML rather than `""`, which is at least visible. The service side never sees the language's types, so `custom::FieldSpec` carries `text: TextField` (`No`, `Optional`, `Required`), set from the declared type by `spec_of`, and a field whose type changes between text and anything else restarts its service on reload (`a_text_field_reads_markup_as_written`, `markup_in_a_document_reads_as_written_for_text`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a record type with a `text` field reads text.** An element with neither attributes nor child elements is its text (`Data::Text`), and a record type over text did not convert, so whether an element read as `type Guid { isPermaLink: bool?; text: text }` depended on whether it happened to carry an attribute: RSS's bare `<guid>` (the common case) beside `<guid isPermaLink="false">`, `<category>` without `domain`, Atom's `<title>` without `type`, and fontconfig's `<dir>` without `prefix` (three of whose four `<dir>`s were left out of a `[Dir]`) did not convert. Text read as a record whose type has a field named `text` is now that record with `text` holding it and the other fields absent (null, or their default), as the same element with an attribute reads; a record without such a field still does not read text. It applies to JSON strings and text documents too, since the type decides for every format (`text_alone_reads_into_a_record_with_a_text_field`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a field's report replaces one of the other kind, and says what happened to the value.** A field reports its own value not converting once, and a value inside it once, until the field converts wholly. A report of one kind open silenced the other, so a feed whose `item[0].pubDate` was reported and that later served an HTML page in its place kept showing the stale date message, never the field's. A report of the other kind now resolves the open one and is reported; a second bad value of the same kind still is not news. A nested report ends by what happened: a list's item "is left out", a record's field "reads as the type's default" (`a_page_that_is_not_xml_is_reported`, `a_value_that_does_not_convert_is_reported_once`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: an element's text joins its runs with a heuristic, documented rather than changed.** Text runs are stored trimmed (a `#text` field reads clean), so whether white space bordered a run is lost, and element text joins runs with a space except before closing and after opening punctuation: `H<sub>2</sub>O` reads `H 2 O` and `<b>W</b>ord` `W ord`. Keeping the border white space would put it into every `#text` a config reads, for word-internal markup that the samples (feeds' `type="xhtml"` content, D-Bus `doc:para`) rarely hold; spec.md 5.6 now states the rule. A feed's HTML read through `markup: html` or `plain(html)` is not affected: it is text, not elements.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: date digits are read by their count, and a date past chrono's range in a zone is no date.** This amends "a `Date` filled from a document reads standard date text and Unix time". Review found two faults in it. First, the move into the local zone used chrono's `naive_local`, which panics when an instant on chrono's first or last day is moved past it by the offset; the RFC 3339 fallbacks take a signed year of any width (`+262142-12-31T23:30Z`), and a 16-digit number read as milliseconds reached the same days, so a polled value or `strand set` could end the logic thread. `in_zone` now adds the offset with `checked_add_offset` and an instant whose wall time falls outside is no date. Second, any 12 or more digits were milliseconds, so three common forms became wrong dates without a report: `date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S` and the Wayback CDX timestamp (14 digits, year ~2612), a 12-digit `+%Y%m%d%H%M` (1976), and journald's `__REALTIME_TIMESTAMP` microseconds (16 digits, year ~58,800). The same reasoning that made `20261107` a date and `2026` none decides them: the count of integer digits says what the digits are, 8 `YYYYMMDD`, 12 `YYYYMMDDHHMM`, 14 `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS` (wall time as written, unsigned, no fraction), 9 to 11 seconds, 13 milliseconds, 16 microseconds, 19 nanoseconds, and any other count is no date (the default and a report). A magnitude rule cannot tell `20261107195510` from milliseconds, and a plausibility window would hide the mismatch rather than report it. With these counts no number reaches chrono's edge any more (11 digits of seconds end in 5138), so the range check guards text alone. Two near forms were added because the site claims ISO 8601 and the samples hold them: the basic local `YYYYMMDDTHHMM[SS]` iCalendar writes under a TZID, and a trailing ` UTC` read as `Z` (`date -u '+%F %T %Z'`, Go's RFC 1123 pubDates) (`an_instant_at_the_edge_of_the_range_is_no_date_in_a_zone`, `a_number_reads_as_its_digits`, `dates_from_text_read_every_standard_form`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a `text` field reads a document as written only when it holds none of the fields and has no prolog.** This amends "a `text` field reads markup as written". The missing-key rule ran per field, so it also ran on `from listen` lines and the `line(doc)` event: an XML line updating one field (`<s cpu="7"/>`) overwrote a required `text` field with the raw line, where the same JSON line leaves it alone as the listen merge promises, and a feed lacking one `text` key (`subtitle`) showed its whole source. A document that holds the key of any of the service's fields is now data, and a `text` field whose key it lacks is absent there (`""` for a file or a poll, unchanged for a listen line); only a document holding none of them, which is what a markup fragment is to a service reading it, is read as written. A document with anything before its root element (an XML declaration, a DOCTYPE, a comment) is data too and never read as written, so a SOAP-style `<?xml …?><string>EUR 1.08</string>` gives `text` its content: a fragment meant for `markup:` never carries a prolog. Applying the rule only to whole-document reads was weighed and refused: it fixes the listen merge but not the feed showing its source. A typo in a single-field service's key over a feed still shows the feed, which is visible rather than silent (`a_document_holding_a_field_is_data_not_markup`, `a_listen_line_of_xml_updates_only_its_fields`, `markup_in_a_document_reads_as_written_for_text`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a list of records takes one object or element only when it holds one of their fields.** This amends "the declared type decides list or single". A record converts from any record, missing fields taking their defaults, so the wrap rule turned any JSON object or element read as `[T]` into one item of defaults, with no report: GitHub's rate-limit answer `{"message": …}` read as `[Release]` showed one empty release, and an action's `-> [T]` returned it rather than an error. Before the wrap rule, a JSON object read as a list did not convert. A single record now wraps only when the item record type (a `Date` aside, which reads its own forms) has a field the lookup finds in it; otherwise the field does not convert and is reported, as the paragraph's "not a silent `[]`" intended (`a_record_without_the_item_s_fields_is_no_list_of_it`). This holds where the object itself is read as `[T]`: an action's `-> [T]`, or a key that finds it. A service field whose key the error object lacks, such as the recipe's `releases`, is a missing key, `[]` with no report as before, which the site says beside its advice to poll with `curl -f` (review round 3).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: an empty element is an empty list or a record of defaults; a recursive `text` field does not read text; a blank `path?` is null.** An element with neither attributes nor children is its text, so an empty one (`<trkseg>` holding a line break, nmap's `<ports/>`) was blank text, which no record and no list of records read: valid GPX and nmap output gave a mismatch report and the default. Blank text read as a list of anything but `text` is now `[]`, and read as a record other than `Date` (which has no default) the record of its fields' defaults, as an element with none of its fields is. The arm that reads text into a record with a `text` field wrapped the text and read the same record again; when that field's type was the record itself (`type Node { text: Node? }`, allowed since types may recurse) it never ended and overflowed the stack. That arm now applies only when the `text` field's type, without `?` and lists, is not a record. Blank text read as `path?` was exempt from "blank is null" alongside `text?`, which spec 5.6 and the site did not say; it is now null like every optional type but `text?`, since a blank path names nothing (`an_empty_element_is_an_empty_record_or_list`, `a_recursive_text_field_does_not_read_text`, `blank_optional_values_are_null`).

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: the XML scan bounds namespaces and entity declarations, and a `text` field named `text` keeps a fragment's markup.** Review round 3 found two more places where roxmltree's work is not linear. Each element that declares a namespace copies every namespace in scope and checks each copy against those already copied, and each entity reference is looked up in a list of every declaration. The depth and attribute limits still allowed about 8,000 prefixes in scope, and the expansion budget counted empty entities as nothing, so a few hundred kilobytes kept the services thread busy for minutes. The scan now refuses more than `MAX_NAMESPACES` (64) namespaces in scope (an OpenDocument root has about 35), more than `MAX_NAMESPACE_COPIES` (2^20) copies in all (an Atom feed with XHTML entries makes about a thousand), and more than `MAX_ENTITIES` (256) entity declarations, repeats included (real internal subsets declare a handful) (`xml_is_bounded`). Also, the root's own text read by a field named `text` no longer counts as a field the document holds: `{ text: text }` over a bar script's `<span foreground="#e06c75">CPU 92%</span>` had read `CPU 92%` and lost the colour, where before this branch the document was text (`a_text_field_reads_markup_as_written`). Attributes still count, since `<s cpu="5" label="CPU"/>` is data. The docs now say that an action's `-> [T]` over XML reads the root as one item, so a feed's entries need a type that holds them, and the end-to-end tests use the site's exact `Release` and `RateDay` types.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: a replay's edit names a repeated element's n-th by its index, and lines of text are no one item of a list of numbers.** Review round 4 found two places where the branch's rules met older code. A glitch report writes an XML element's repeated names as one JSON array (`Data::write_json`), but the recorder's per-field diff walked the element's record name by name, so an edit inside the third `Cube` of the ECB's rates was written `Cube.@rate`: the replay found an array there and dropped the patch, and an edit of an RSS item's second `<category>` replaced the array with one string. `record.rs::diff` now counts an element's names and writes the n-th of a repeated one as `name.n`, the path the JSON has (`an_elements_repeated_names_are_edited_by_their_index`). And the new rule that a list type over one value is a list of it met the older reading of a number with a unit, which takes the first word: a command printing a port per line, read as `[int]`, became `[22]` with the other lines lost and no report, where on main it did not convert. Text of several lines now converts as a list's one item only for an item that keeps it whole (`text`, `path`, a record reading it as its `text` field); for a number, a bool or an enum it does not convert and is reported (`a_list_type_wraps_one_value_and_a_single_type_takes_the_first`). Splitting the lines into items would add a format, so a per-line list stays a JSON array the command prints. Also, the site said a script's Pango `<span foreground=…>` keeps its colour under `markup: html` or `markup: basic`; neither draws a `span`'s attributes (html drops them, basic shows the tags), so the page now says `markup: html` and that a colour belongs in the config, chosen from data the script prints.

**2026-11-07 · doc-formats: values on one line are no one item of a list of numbers either.** The check of round 4's fix found its guard stopped only at line breaks: `pidof`'s `1234 5678`, or `22\t80\t443`, read as `[int]` still became one item holding the first number, since a number with a unit reads its first word. A list of a primitive other than `text` or `path` now refuses, over text or over an element's text, text of several values: several lines, or a word after the first that is itself a number. A number and its unit (`45 °C`, `16303392 kB`) stays one item, and a single number over the same text still reads the first, as on main (`/proc/loadavg` read as a `float`). Test: `a_list_type_wraps_one_value_and_a_single_type_takes_the_first`.

## service-ready

**2026-11-07 · service-ready: every service has `ready`, a change one flush after its boot values.** A config could not tell a service's first answer from its defaults: `on change` takes the boot report as its baseline (decisions.md:2436-2440), and only some services had an `available` or `present` standing in for "has answered". So a handler that should make the world match a value from the start, a loading placeholder, or a reaction to a daemon's restart had no general spelling. Every service, builtin, plugin or declared, now has a read-only `ready: bool`: a run is up and has called `Cx::ready`. It is false before that, after `Cx::unready`, and while no run is up (failed and backing off, or stopped). No schema declares it: the checker types `svc.ready` (`schema::READY`) and the VM reads it from the new `ServiceHost::ready` (default true), so none of the 27 hand-written schemas or the Store structs changed and `StoreHost`'s field index stays the derive's; the reference prints one "every service" row. On the logic side it is a `Signal<bool>` per `Client`, separate from the run's boot-hold flag (`wait_ready` and `ended()` keep theirs). It turns true as an ordinary write, by the first pump after the runtime's tick counter has moved past the tick the run's `Ready` arrived in: the boot values' rebaseline is spent at that flush, so the write is a change `on change svc.ready` sees, even when the boot read lands inside `wait_ready`'s hold (several pumps, no flush between). `Ready` wakes the loop once for that pump; nothing polls. It turns false at once on `Unready`, when the run ends (an error, a disconnected channel, a panic) and when it is stopped. `on change` still never runs at boot: a handler opts in by naming `svc.ready` (`on change outputs.all, outputs.ready after 1500ms { if outputs.ready { … } }`). It means "reported", not "settled", so the documented idioms debounce. `available` keeps its meaning (the backend exists): it is part of the boot report, so reusing it would make existing handlers fire at boot. Rejected: a `ready` event (bindings could not read it), an `initially` modifier on `on change` (new syntax), and folding into `available`. A declared field or action named `ready` is `check::reserved_field`, and a service schema declaring one is refused; neither the builtin schemas nor the owner's config use the name.

**2026-11-07 · service-ready: `Cx::unready`, called by a service that clears what it showed.** outputs' failure path (a lost compositor connection) cleared `all`; with `ready` true a reader took the empty list for a change, and a file written from `outputs.all` would have written an empty monitors file. Now it calls `cx.unready()` first: `ready` turns false and the clearing patch is a boot value again (rebaselined), so no reader sees the empty list while ready, and `on change outputs.all` does not fire for it. A handler naming both the list and `ready` is rebaselined in that flush and so does not run for the false transition; one naming only `ready` does (spec.md 8.4). A `from dbus` declaration is unready while its daemon does not own the name (its values null), and ready again once a new owner has been read; with no owner at its start it still ends the first frame's hold (`ready()` then `unready()`), so a missing daemon never delays the shell. `from file`, `from dir`, `from poll` and `from listen` keep their first-read `ready()`.

**2026-11-07 · service-ready: the mock's keyed boot report is a reload write, as the real host's.** `SchemaHost::set_initial` set a keyed list with a plain `replace_all`, so `on change` fired for it in the mock while the real host (the derive's `How::Initial`, then `StoreHost`'s mirror) rebaselines with `replace_all_reloaded`. Its only caller (`strand export`, plain `system.*` fields) did not notice; it now uses `replace_all_reloaded` (`reload.rs::a_keyed_boot_report_is_a_baseline`). The mock's `ready` is a settable cell per service, true from the start so `strand export`'s files never wait (`SchemaHost::set_ready`).

**2026-11-07 · service-ready pre-step: no builtin says ready before its values settle.** The owner's island carries a 1.5 s `armed` guard (`wake_up`, island.strand:82, 279-280) on `on change audio.sink.volume, audio.sink.muted`, `audio.source.muted`, `brightness.level`, `brightness.keyboard` and `media.title`. Each of those services calls `ready` only after its whole first state: audio publishes its first state once its PipeWire syncs are back and the session manager's `default` metadata is read (`ready_to_publish`, audio/thread.rs), brightness reads both lights before its one update, and media reads every player present at its start (bounded) before its first update. So `ready` needs no weakening and no service needed fixing. The guard was written with the island's first version (shell repo a1667cb), before `on change` skipped late boot reports; what it can still catch is a real change made by another program at login (WirePlumber restoring a volume, a brightness daemon), which no readiness can tell from a user's change. The documented reconcile idioms debounce for the same reason.

**2026-11-07 · service-ready review round 1: `outputs` is unready when its output manager goes while the connection stays.** Only the connection-failure path called `cx.unready()`; a `finished` manager or a removed global (a compositor shutting down removes its globals first) went through `drop_manager`, whose next publish sent `all = []` as a change with `ready` still true, so a `file` reading `outputs.all` could write an empty monitors file, the case `Cx::unready` was added for. The serve loop's publishing is now `Client::publish`: a lost manager is `Cleared` (unready, then the clear), and nothing is shown ready again until another manager is bound and answers its first `done`. A compositor that withdraws the manager for good leaves `outputs` unready, so a file reading it waits. The spec's wording that every service whose source goes turns unready first was narrowed to what does: `outputs` and declared `from dbus` services; the builtin D-Bus services stay ready when their daemon goes and show what they read again as a change (spec 12, services.md). Test: `crates/strand-services/src/outputs.rs::tests::a_lost_manager_clears_its_outputs_unready`.

**2026-11-07 · service-ready review round 3: a service with no run is ready from the start, and the docs say so.** The builtins the shell fills itself rather than a run, served by the `SchemaHost` fallback (`screens`, whose list main sends, `clock`, `calendar`), have `ready` true from boot, while services.md's "Every service" row, spec 5.6 and 12 and site/concepts/services.md promised false before the first report; monitor-profiles round 2 had left this open. Giving `screens` a real ready cell would make every `file` that reads it wait on main's first monitor report, and on hosts that never send one (the mock, the eval sandbox) wait for ever, a larger change than this round's. So the docs are narrowed instead: those services are named as ready from the start, and `on change screens.ready` never runs (services.md is generated from crates/strand-dev's text).

## live-files

**2026-11-07 · live-files: a `file`'s `text:` reads the enclosing scope (amends m5-tools, "the `file` element").** m5-tools gave `text:` the template scope only, while the path, `template:`, `run:` and `when` were already ordinary expressions; so a config could pick among literal texts but not put a setting, a service or `outputs.all` into the content, and keeping another program's config in step (kitty's font size, a status file, a compositor's monitor lines) needed a shell action, with the content in the process list and no ownership check. Now `text:` compiles as a template hole when `Template::compile_expr` accepts it (it reads only the theme), byte for byte as before, `.light()`/`.dark()` and the channels included; otherwise it is checked and lowered as an ordinary chunk (`FilePart::Value`) and its value written by spec 9.8's Values rule (text as is, numbers shortest, a colour as `hex(c)`, a token at the current table's value, a list or record an error). The test is which errors the template compiler gives: only `template::not_theme` means "reads the scope". `.light()`/`.dark()` in such a text are `file::other_mode` (the VM has no other-mode table). Template files and `strand export --template` keep the theme-only scope, so export stays offline and pure (`m5/export.rs::an_exported_template_reads_the_theme_only`). Chosen over a mixed IR with a "value from scope" hole (one evaluator per text, so a lambda never meets template-only functions halfway) and over making `text:` always ordinary (which would take `.light()` from `text:`, dropping a feature). The HIR now keeps the real expression, so `check::secret_flow`'s existing `file` sink warns on a password in `text:` (a warning, like every sink). The colour channels stay template-only: the plan's "channels in ordinary expressions too" was not needed by anything here and would add methods the VM can only answer through the token table. (Corrected in review round 2:) `join` in such a text writes a token by its current value, as a template's `join` does, through `VmHooks::token` like `hex`; it had written the token's inner form (`Ref("fg")`), so adding one scope read to a theme text that joined a token corrupted the file (`outputs.rs::a_token_joined_in_a_scope_text_is_its_value`).

**2026-11-07 · live-files: `text: null` writes nothing.** A top-level `file` cannot be gated by `if` and a `when` holds props only, so a null `text:` (only one that reads the scope; a bare `null` literal included) is how a config says "leave it": nothing is written or run, no notice, the path stops being a target so the writer lets go of bytes it was still retrying there (`OutputContent::Leave`). A null inside a template hole stays `template::null`.

**2026-11-07 · live-files: a `file` waits for the services it reads.** Each `file` gets its own service frame in lowering (merged into the enclosing frame, so a top-level `file` holds what it reads, as before by accident of the frame it sat in), patched like every scope's uses, `let`s and `fn`s followed (`reads::compute` folds called `fn` bodies into the chunk). The content memo reads `ServiceHost::ready` for each, tracked, first: while one is false the memo is `Content::Waiting` and nothing is written, even with `??`, since the values are defaults. This generalises the pending wallpaper and closes the boot hazard a `when outputs.all…` already had (writing the "no monitors" branch over a good file before `outputs` reported). `outputs` calling `Cx::unready` before clearing its heads (service-ready) is what keeps a compositor exit from writing an empty monitors file. A waiting file whose service has no run up (failed, backing off) is a standing notice naming it; one starting is no news. A service with no run up waits with that notice rather than writing its defaults. (Corrected in review round 1:) a declared `from dbus` service whose daemon is absent has a run that is up but not ready, so a file reading it waits with no notice; a builtin whose backend is absent (`battery` without UPower) is ready with its defaults, and a file reading it is written (spec 9.7, Pending). (Corrected in review round 2:) a waiting file keeps its path as one of the writer's targets, so a paced write made while the service was ready still lands when it turns unready (a logout 0.3 s after a second layout had left monitors.lua one layout behind); before, only a written file was a target and `Job::Keep` dropped it (`outputs.rs::a_waiting_file_keeps_its_target`).

**2026-11-07 · live-files: the writer paces paths and holds a looping `run:`.** Every changed tick used to write; a status file following a fast-changing service could write many times a second. Now a path is written at most once per 500 ms: the first write at once, the newest content of the window when it ends (identical bytes do not count as a write); a `run:` due for that path waits for the paced write, so three quick changes still run once. The loop guard is for a `run:` whose program changes what the text reads (a compositor reload re-enabling a panel that `outputs.all.filter(o => o.enabled)` maps): a write that comes while the file's `run:` runs or within 1 s of it ending is a round; three rounds in a row hold the `run:` with a standing notice until the file is quiet for 1 s, then it runs once for the last content (a slider dragged past three rounds is caught up), and a round straight after that catch-up run holds it again, let go without a run. A true loop so costs at most four runs per outside change. Writes themselves are never held. (Corrected in review round 2:) the catch-up run that ends a hold takes the notice away, since the `run:` is no longer held; it had stood until the next write that was not held (`run::outputs::tests::a_catch_up_run_takes_the_loop_notice_away`). A longer debounce composes from `on change x after T { snap = x }`.

**2026-11-07 · live-files: `hex` and `argb` are ordinary builtins.** They existed only in the template compiler, so `outputs.all.map(o => hex(…))` in a scope text, or a colour picker's label, could not format a colour. They are now schema functions (`lift`, null in null out) on a colour, or on a token read through the new `VmHooks::token` (the current token table, tracked; while the program mounts, before the table's memo exists, a table made for that read). The template keeps its own `hex`/`argb` nodes; both share `template::render`'s formatting, so the bytes agree. No check for animation-clock reads in a `file` was added: a `file` draws nothing, and a time-bound value reaching `text:` is already an error naming it at render.

**2026-11-07 · live-files review round 1: a text that changes on its own is let go by the loop guard, and the loop notice stands while held.** A write within 1 s of the file's own run ending counted as a round whatever caused it, so a `file` following a source that ticks about once a second (a player's position) with a `run:` was held after three ticks and, since every later tick came while held and pushed the hold back, never ran again while the music played; and each held write's `Outcome::Written` took the loop notice away at once. The writer now tells the two apart by what a hold does: a true loop stops when its `run:` is held (nothing changes the text), while a text that changes on its own writes again. A write that comes while held and more than 1 s after the last run ended lets the hold go at once, and the file's writes are no rounds until it is quiet for 2 s (`RunState::own`, `OWN_QUIET`); a held write reports nothing, so the notice stands until a write lands unheld. A narrower window was not taken: pacing puts a real loop's writes about 300 ms after its run ends and a once-a-second ticker's about 800 ms after, so any window either misses slow loops or catches fast tickers. A loop on top of a text that also changes on its own is then bounded by pacing alone (two runs a second). Test: `crates/strand/src/run/outputs.rs::tests::a_text_that_changes_on_its_own_is_not_held` (writes every 250 ms: the notice is the last word while held, and five or more runs; the old writer ran three times and showed `Written`).

**2026-11-07 · live-files review round 3: a waiting file's notice stays while it waits.** Since round 2 a waiting file is still a writer target, so a write paced from before its service went down (or a held `run:`'s catch-up) lands after the content turned `Waiting`, and its `Outcome::Written` took the file's notices away as any landed write does, including the "waits for `svc`, which has no run up" notice, which is posted once, when the content turns `Waiting`. The file then waited with no notice in the overlay or `strand watch`. `Files` now keeps each waiting file's notice (`set_waiting`, cleared when the content is anything but `Waiting`), and a write that lands for a file still waiting posts it again. Test: `crates/strand/src/run/outputs.rs::tests::a_write_landing_while_waiting_keeps_the_notice` (the bookkeeping; the overlay path itself needs a running shell).

## output-id

**2026-11-07 · output-id: `Output.id` is the monitor's `Screen.id`.** A saved monitor layout must name a monitor by what survives a move to another port, and `outputs.all` had only the connector `name` (which moves) and make, model, description and serial, while `screens:` and `Screen.id` name monitors by strand-surface's `MonitorId` (make, model and description, the connector wlroots appends dropped, ` #2` for a second identical one).
