The earlier paragraph's "never get one" for sway, niri and labwc is corrected there: an apply any of them leaves unanswered for 100 ms (a slow modeset) gets the surface as well, which is harmless. Test, failing without the fix (1.49 s of CPU in a 1.5 s wait): `crates/strand-services/tests/outputs.rs::an_apply_with_no_frame_surface_to_make_waits_without_spinning`.

## settings-shape

**2026-11-08 · settings-shape: a new record of records is written as sections.** settings-tables writes a new record among section-written siblings as a section shaped like them, but with nothing to follow (no file yet, the dictionary's first entry) it wrote the value as encoded: the monitor-profiles page's first **Save this profile** gave `[profiles]` and one inline line of about 400 characters per set of monitors. The page shows `[profiles."…"]` with `[[….mons]]` tables and tells a Hyprland builder to save the best guess once and edit its section, so a fresh builder had no section to edit. Now a value written with nothing of its kind to follow (`settings.rs::natural`: a new field, a replaced one, an entry of a table with no record siblings) is a `[section]` when it is a record that holds a record or a list of records, its lists of records `[[…]]` tables, its records that hold records sections under it; a dictionary's `[name]` header is left out when every entry is a section, and a section of nothing but tables has its first table right under its header, as on the pages. A record of plain values stays one inline line, which reads well (`size = { w = 5, h = 4 }`), and an entry next to inline ones is inline, so a file written inline keeps its form. Rejected: writing every record as a section (a plain record is clearer inline, and every existing test of a plain record's write would change form). Test, failing without the fix: `crates/strand-core/tests/settings.rs::a_new_record_of_records_is_written_as_sections`.

**2026-11-08 · settings-shape final round: a file of comments alone keeps them above the first write.** A `monitors.toml` a builder starts with only a header comment, saved into from the monitor-profiles page, had the new `[profiles."…"]` and `[[….mons]]` tables written above that comment, which ended up as the file's last line. toml_edit keeps a document with no keys or tables as trailing text, printed after anything inserted, and settings-tables follow-up's rule that a header stays above what follows covered a header over a table, not over nothing. `apply_edits` now takes such a file's text out before the edits (`head_of`) and puts it above the first thing printed after them, a root value or else the first table, a blank line apart unless it already ends with one (`put_head`); with nothing written it goes back at the end as it was. Test, failing without the fix: `crates/strand-core/tests/settings.rs::a_header_with_nothing_under_it_stays_above_the_first_write`.

## output-id-order

**2026-11-08 · output-id-order: identical monitors are numbered by their connectors' names, and no id ends in a separator.** Found building the owner's monitors shell on nested Hyprland 0.57 (strand-issues 2026-11-08). Identical monitors (the same make, model and description) were numbered ` #2`, ` #3` in the order they came while Strand ran (output-id review round 3: an output kept its id while connected, a new one took the lowest number free) and in the order of their names after a restart, so three of Hyprland's headless outputs made as eDP-1, then DP-6, then DP-2 had eDP-1 plain while running and DP-2 plain after a restart, and a profile keyed by those ids put each monitor where another was. An id that depends on history cannot be the same after a restart, which has none. The rule now: the identical monitors connected, on or off, are numbered in the order of their connectors' names (`outputs::by_name`, digits by their number: `DP-2` before `DP-10`), the first plain, then ` #2`, ` #3`. An id is a function of which monitors are connected, so a restart gives the same ids, and applying a configuration, which connects and disconnects nothing, still renames nothing (round 3's profile loop cannot come back: turning one of two identical monitors off or on is no change to the set). The cost, taken knowingly: plugging in an identical monitor on a port named before another's, or unplugging one, renumbers the others of that identity while Strand runs (no rule both independent of history and free of renames exists: one monitor alone must be plain, so a second one makes one of the two ` #2`). One of two identical monitors unplugged and plugged in again on the same port comes back to the ids from before, as a restart would give; plugged in on another port, the two are numbered by their ports' names, which can swap them (DP-1 `X` and DP-2 `X #2`, DP-1's monitor back on DP-5: DP-2 is `X` and DP-5 `X #2`), the set of ids the same but not which monitor has which. Considered and rejected: keeping round 3's rule and persisting ids across restarts (state kept outside the config for a naming problem, and wrong as soon as the monitors move while Strand is stopped). `Screen.id` follows, as round 3 has it, so strand-surface numbers the same way: `Monitors::renumbering` gives `Screen.id` the `outputs` list's ids when the list names every monitor of an identity shown, else numbers them by name (`connector_order`, a copy of `by_name`; `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::output_id::both_order_connectors_alike` holds the two equal) among those shown and the connectors the list gives that identity (a monitor off has no `wl_output`; one just plugged in may not be in the list yet). A monitor shown whose id changes is unplugged and plugged in again under the new id, as one whose description changed always was, so its surfaces are made for the new id; the list is read at each plug and unplug and at each `State::poll`, so the list arriving (the `outputs` service started, a monitor turned off) renumbers too. A list gone empty at a poll (no run of `outputs` up, which happens 5 s after its last reader goes) renames nothing, so a page that reads `outputs` only while open does not remake the bars of an identical monitor each time it closes; the next plug or unplug numbers its own identity without it (review round 2, below). Round 4's `outputs::shown`, which let a run's new heads take the ids shown, is gone: with ids a function of the set, no run has anything to inherit. Separately, the id joined its parts with `" | "` even when one was empty, so Hyprland's headless outputs (no description) were `Unknown | Unknown | ` with a trailing space, and a description `make model serial` with no serial ends in a space, which the id kept; a profile written by hand, or read back from a file an editor trimmed, no longer matched. Each part is now trimmed and an empty description is left out with its separator (`Unknown | Unknown`), on both sides; every id with a description and no trailing space is byte for byte as it was (the owner's saved `LG Display | 0x07C7 | LG Display 0x07C7` and `Ancor Communications Inc | ASUS VS239 | Ancor Communications Inc ASUS VS239 L3LMTF263862` are checked). Tests, each failing without the fix: `crates/strand-services/src/outputs.rs::tests::identical_monitors_have_the_same_ids_after_a_restart`, `::an_identical_monitor_unplugged_and_replugged_is_numbered_by_name`, `::identical_heads_are_numbered_by_name`, `::an_id_has_no_trailing_separator`, `crates/strand-surface/src/monitor.rs::tests::identical_monitors_are_numbered_by_name_whatever_their_order`, `::identical_monitors_take_the_outputs_numbers`, `::an_id_has_no_trailing_separator`, and on nested Hyprland 0.57 `crates/strand/tests/compositor_matrix.rs::identical_outputs_are_numbered_by_name` (a headless output made on `AAA-1` while `strand run` runs is plain and NESTED-1, NESTED-2 become ` #2`, ` #3`, `Output.id` and `Screen.id` alike; a fresh run gives the same; removed, the others are as at the start). The monitor-profiles how-to also says now that some machines name the built-in panel `LVDS-…` or `DSI-…`, which its `o.name.starts_with("eDP")` does not find: no Strand feature for it, by the owner's decision.

**2026-11-08 · output-id-order review round 2: with no `outputs` list, a plug or unplug renumbers its own identity alone.** A list gone empty at a poll renamed nothing, but the next plug or unplug read the empty list and numbered every identity without it, so after the `outputs` run stopped, plugging in or unplugging any monitor, even one unlike the others, renamed DP-2 from `X #2` (beside DP-1, identical and off) to `X`: its id depended on whether an unrelated plug had happened since. Now a plug or unplug with no list renames only the monitors of the identity that came, went or was described anew (`Monitors::renumbering_after`; the manager passes a monitor's identity before an unplug or a new description as `left`), numbered by name among those shown; with the list it renumbers every identity, as a poll does. What stays, documented in architecture.md and `Screen.id`'s schema doc: with no run of `outputs` up, nothing says a monitor that is off is still connected, so it does not count. A run of Strand started with DP-1 off and no `outputs` reader shows DP-2 as `X`, where `Output.id` (once a run is up) says `X #2`, and turning one of two identical monitors off then renames the other. No config is affected that reads `outputs` the whole time (the monitor-profiles recipe reads `outputs.all` at top level); making `Screen.id` count monitors that are off without the service would need strand-surface to bind the output manager itself, a second manager in the process beside the `outputs` service's, which outputs-apply took care to avoid on Hyprland 0.57; not worth it for a config that does not read `outputs`. Test, failing without the fix: `crates/strand-surface/src/monitor.rs::tests::without_the_list_a_plug_renumbers_its_own_identity_alone`.

## ws-shown

**2026-11-08 · ws-shown: a screen shows one workspace.** Found on nested Hyprland 0.57 (strand-issues 2026-11-08): docked with the lid shut, Hyprland moves the panel's workspace to the monitor that stays on, which already shows its own, and `workspaces.all` had both `active` on that screen. Hyprland's IPC is right after the move (`j/monitors` names the one shown), but its `ext-workspace-v1` keeps the moved workspace active, and `merge` took `active` from the protocol for every workspace it joined. The protocol stays preferred, as the merge's rule has it, except where it has two or more shown on one screen: there the adapter's `active` says which, and where the adapter names none of them the first stays (`wm::one_shown_per_screen`). A screen the protocol has one shown on keeps the protocol's answer, so a protocol event ahead of the adapter still shows first. sway (no `ext-workspace-v1` in 1.9; its `visible` is right) and niri (one output in the matrix; its IPC's `is_active` is per output) were not affected, and the matrix test runs on sway too. Tests, failing without the fix: `crates/strand-services/src/wm/mod.rs::tests::a_screen_shows_one_workspace`, and on nested Hyprland 0.57 and sway `crates/strand/tests/compositor_matrix.rs::one_workspace_is_shown_per_screen_after_a_screen_goes_off` (a workspace kept by a window shown on the second output, which is turned off with the compositor's own command as a lid switch does, then with `outputs.apply`, and on again each time: the store reads as shown what the compositor shows, one per screen).

**2026-11-08 · ws-shown review round 2: with the adapter behind, the workspace it places on the screen stays.** Where the protocol shows two workspaces on one screen, the adapter's `active` says which; where it said neither, the first in the adapter's order stayed, in the lid-shut shape the moved workspace, the wrong one, until the adapter caught up. The adapter's answer now counts only on that screen (an adapter behind the move may still show the moved workspace on the screen turned off), and with none shown there, the one it places on that screen stays, the one shown there before the move; the first only when it places none or both there. Test, failing without the fix: `crates/strand-services/src/wm/mod.rs::tests::a_screen_shows_one_workspace` (the adapter behind cases). The two matrix tests that change the shared compositor (`identical_outputs_are_numbered_by_name` makes `AAA-1`, `one_workspace_is_shown_per_screen_after_a_screen_goes_off` turns a monitor off) now put it back when they fail (`OnPanic`), so one failure does not fail the matrix tests after it.

## dbus-action-run

**2026-11-08 · dbus-action-run: a `from dbus` action reads as its run, `bolt.enroll.error` its last failure.** A `from dbus` method action's failure went only to the log, so a page enrolling a Thunderbolt device with bolt's `EnrollDevice` could not say why bolt refused it (found building the owner's monitors shell). A declared command action already reads as its run (lockmon, action-error), so a D-Bus action read without a call now reads the same way, the same `ActionRun` record, no new type or syntax: `bolt.enroll.running` while a call waits for its answer (a count, as an action with a result may have several), `bolt.enroll.started` when the oldest still waiting was made, and `bolt.enroll.error` the daemon's error name and message (`org.freedesktop.bolt.Error.Exists: …`, the name kept because a daemon's message alone is often not enough to tell its errors apart), or ``"`org.freedesktop.bolt` is not running"`` or ``"`…` has no method `EnrollDevice`"`` when the call was never made. As for a command, the failure is cleared by a new call and by an answer without an error. The state is the service's (`Custom::runs`, keyed by the action's index, set by `run_dbus` when it takes a call and when the answer comes) and reaches the logic thread as the service's fields do, one memo per action in `CustomHost`, so a reload that restarts the service starts its runs afresh; a call still waiting when the service's run ends otherwise (the review's fix below) is not counted on either. So the clear on a new call lands when the service takes the call, not at the handler's call as a command action's does; a refusal that comes back before the logic thread's next flush is then heard as one change, the same window a command action has for a command that fails before the flush. `stop()` is a load error on this run (`check::unknown_field`, its help saying why): a method call cannot be taken back once sent, and dropping the wait while the daemon still acts would break the rule `call_method` keeps, that a call is never reported refused while the daemon may still act. Left for later: a glitch report does not carry the run. The recorder keeps a declared service's `values` only (`declared_change`), and a command action's `ACTION_FAILED` names a program, so a replay shows a D-Bus action's run as never called; recording `runs` needs the eval side to feed them back, which the bolt page does not need to show why bolt refused. Rejected: a service-level `bolt.failed(action, why)` event as `session.failed` has, which would add a second spelling for what a command action calls `.error`. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/flex.rs::a_dbus_actions_run_is_read_through_its_name`, `crates/strand-services/tests/custom.rs::a_dbus_actions_run_says_why_its_call_failed`, `crates/strand/tests/services.rs::a_config_services_action_failure_is_read_as_its_error`.

**2026-11-08 · dbus-action-run (review): a call whose run ended is lost, and one the service could not take is the run's error.** The review found two ways the run could mislead. A call's wait is a task of the run that made it, so when that run ends while bolt still waits on polkit (the 5 s stop after the Thunderbolt popup, its last visible reader, hides; a failed run retried; a reload's restart), the task goes with it, but the store the next run starts from still counted the call, and `bolt.enroll.running` stayed true for good. `run_dbus` now begins by zeroing every run (`lose_calls`), and an action that was waiting gets ``"the service stopped before `org.freedesktop.bolt` answered; whether the call took is unknown"`` as its error, since the method may have acted. Keeping the run alive while a call waits was rejected: a stop is the client's, by readers, and one body holding it up would be the first exception to that rule. The other: a call the service could not take at all (its body failed and backs off, its bus turned off, or its run ended before reading the call) never reached `run_dbus`, so `.error` kept whatever it held. The custom store gets the `refused` event every service's refusal goes through (`Service::refused`, as `network.failed` is), which `CustomHost`'s observer makes that action's error until a run takes its next call; `CustomHost::action` now refuses through `Client::act_or_refuse`, the path `DynService::action` takes, so the call is the action's failure and no longer a fault of the handler that made it (spec.md 12), and `strand call` still hears it. The event is the store's, not syntax: the rejected `bolt.failed` above stays rejected. Tests: `crates/strand-services/tests/custom.rs::a_dbus_actions_run_says_why_its_call_failed` (a slow call, then a restart), `::a_dbus_action_the_service_cannot_take_is_refused`, `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::tests::custom_services::a_dbus_action_the_service_cannot_take_is_its_error`.

## check-settings

**2026-11-08 · check-settings: `strand check` reads the settings files, an unreadable or broken file an error, a bad value a warning.** `strand check` type-checked `state monitors from "monitors.toml" { … }` but never opened the file, so a profile with a typo'd key or a wrong type was found only by the running shell (found building the owner's monitors shell). `check::settings::check` now reads each file a settings declaration names, in a component or surface too, resolved as instantiate's `Storage::resolve` does (`~/…` from `$HOME`, absolute as is, else under the checked config directory, through any symlink), parses it with toml_edit's span-keeping `Document`, and decodes each declared field with the shell's own `persist::decode_item`, so check and shell cannot disagree on what loads. The severities follow what the shell does with each: a file that cannot be read (`check::settings_unreadable`) or is not TOML (`check::settings_syntax`) is an error, because the shell takes nothing from it and never writes it, so every setting in it is silently the last good value; a field whose value does not decode (`check::settings_value`) is a warning with the shell's own message (`profiles: "a + b": mons[0]: unknown field "scael"`), because the shell keeps that field's last good value and loads the others; a top-level key no declaration of the file has (`check::settings_unknown_key`, with a did-you-mean) is a warning too, the shell never reading it. Making a bad value an error was rejected: the shell runs with it, as it does with check's other warnings, and a value a user is still editing should not fail a script that checks the config. A missing file is no problem, since the shell starts from the defaults and makes the file on its first write. Each report is labelled at the innermost key, value or table header the decoder stopped at (`blame`, walking the item as `decode_item` does), so `[profiles."a + b"]` with `[[profiles."a + b".mons]]` tables shows the line of the bad key; the declaration is a second label, so `strand check monitors.strand` reports it too. The TOML files join check's source map so the renderer shows their lines. Two declarations of one file are read once, a key unknown only when no declaration of the file has it. The runtime overlay and the last-good snapshot are not read: they are the running shell's state, not the config. The language server did not run it at first (its source map is one entry per `.strand` document); see the review below. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/src/check/settings.rs::tests::a_good_or_missing_file_is_quiet`, `::a_typod_key_is_a_warning_on_its_line`, `::a_wrong_type_is_a_warning_on_its_line`, `::a_dictionary_of_records_with_tables_is_read`, `::syntax_errors_and_unknown_keys`, `crates/strand/src/check.rs::tests::settings_files_are_read_as_the_shell_reads_them`.

**2026-11-08 · check-settings (review): the editor shows a settings file's problems at its declaration, and a file checked alone outside the config is said to stand alone.** The language server now runs `check::settings::check` on a copy of its source map, the TOML files added there only, and shows each problem at the declaration that reads the file, the field's (a bad value) or the `from "…"` path's (a broken file, an unknown key), its message naming the TOML file and line (`` `…/monitors.toml:6` ``); quick fixes inside the TOML file are dropped, and each file read is stamped, so an edit to it outside the editor is seen at the next analysis. Publishing to the TOML file's own URI was rejected: every other request treats the source map's files as `.strand` documents. `strand check pages/mon.strand` on a file outside the default config directory checks it with its own directory as the config, as it always has for the asset, shader and path checks, so a settings path relative to the config is looked for beside the file and, missing there, reports nothing; finding the config root by walking up was rejected (a directory of many configs would be taken whole), and site/start/running.md now says to check such a config by its directory. Tests: `crates/strand-dev/tests/lsp.rs::a_settings_files_problems_are_shown_at_its_declaration`.

**2026-11-08 · check-settings (final review): every problem in a field is reported, and the editor reads a settings file that appears.** `decode_item` stops at a field's first failure, so `on = "yes"` beside a typo'd `widht` in one monitor was reported once, the typo first and the wrong type only after it was fixed: a check per problem. `blame`, which found where the first failure was, became `faults`, which walks the item as the decoder does and gives every failing leaf its own `check::settings_value` warning at its own line: each key a record does not have, each field, dictionary value and list element that does not read, and each dictionary key that does not read (worded by decoding that entry alone, so the message is the shell's). What fails only as a whole, two dictionary keys that read as one, is reported at the value with the decoder's own reason. The messages keep the shell's chaining (`"a + b": mons[0]: on: expected bool`), and the shell is unchanged: it still drops the whole field at the first failure, which is what each warning says. The language server stamped only the settings files it read, so a file that was missing when the config was analysed (the shell makes it on its first write) was watched only when it was in a directory the config is read from, whose own stamp changed; one elsewhere (`~/.local/state/…`) showed its problems only after another edit; `check::settings::paths` now gives every declared file's resolved path, and the server stamps each, a missing one as missing, so its appearance makes the next request rebuild and republish. Watching `**/*.toml` through the client was rejected: settings files can live outside the workspace (`~/…`), and a request already re-reads what changed. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/src/check/settings.rs::tests::every_problem_in_a_field_is_reported`, `crates/strand-dev/tests/lsp.rs::a_settings_file_made_later_is_read_when_it_appears`.

## proc-run

**2026-11-08 · proc-run: an action without a result is a job, and its run has its output.** Following a program's output (an updater's log, a backup's progress, a download's bar, why it failed) needed a model, and the owner approved the plan's (spec.md 5.7, 5.8). Every program Strand reads goes through one reader, `strand_services::proc`, with two lifetimes: a watch (`from listen`, unchanged: it runs while read and restarts when it dies) and a job (an action without a result: it runs because it was called, outlives its window, a reload and strand, and is not restarted; its end, with its status, is the news). The job's run gains `code` (`int?`, the status as a shell's `$?`, 128 + n for a signal), `lines` (`[Line]`: `n`, `text`, `stderr`, `open`; the last 1000 lines, at most 256 KiB) and, in `error`, why it failed; an optional block of fields reads its stdout lines as a `from listen` block does, with `on act.line(doc)` hearing them while a handler is mounted, never starting the run. `lines`, `code`, `error` and the fields reset when a run starts, never when one ends; a run's end is one flush in a fixed order (last line events and merge, `lines`, `code`, `error`, `running` false), so `on change act.running` sees everything and upkeep's `after 800ms` wait goes. An action with a result keeps no `lines` or `code` (several calls run at once, so one log would mix them): reading them is `check::no_run_output`. Rejected: `from listen` with parameters started on demand (a second service lifetime and a `start` method, breaking "sources fixed at load"; a pacman run would get SIGTERM 5 s after its window closed and be restarted when it ended); a streaming `-> stream T` (an `Async` is a load: superseded, dropped when unkept, 10 s, dying with strand, the opposite of a job); a `job` declaration (it would duplicate `running`, `started`, `error`, `stop()`, the queue, the permit, the listing and the recording actions already have); an event alone, `on act.output(line, stream)` (lines printed before a window opened would be lost, and every author would rebuild a capped log, O(N) a line and rate-guarded). The owner chose that strand keeps `lines` (question 4): it holds what was printed before a window opened, shows the open line, survives a reload and costs at most 256 KiB per chatty action.

## proc-keeper

**2026-11-08 · proc-keeper: a job's pipes are held past strand's exit by a keeper process.** Reading a job's stdout and stderr puts strand on the far end of its pipes, so when strand exits, crashes or is restarted (`pkill -f '^strand run'`) the job's next write raises SIGPIPE: measured, pacman exits 141 (mid-transaction, the worst outcome on the table), `yes` and coreutils die, Python exits 120. Before this, stdout was `/dev/null` and stderr strand's fd 2, so the risk did not exist. The owner chose the keeper (question 1): strand starts `/proc/self/exe __keep` (a hidden subcommand dispatched first in `main`, its children restored as every spawn site's are) the first time a command action runs, joined by a socketpair; strand sends it a duplicate of each run's pipe read ends (`SCM_RIGHTS` through `rustix`) and releases them once it has read them to their end; when the socket ends the keeper reads every pipe it still holds to its end, drops the bytes and exits when none is left. A job therefore never dies of, or blocks on, strand going away. Rejected: a memfd (no end of file, unbounded while strand is gone), ignoring SIGPIPE in the child (breaks `yes | head` and undoes child-signals), PDEATHSIG (kills jobs with the shell), and capturing only while strand lives with `tee -p` as the documented remedy (the weaker promise). `-> T`, poll and listen commands need no keeper: they already end with strand. The keeper is also the hook for stdin and for re-attaching after a restart, both left out (proc-out).

## proc-lines

**2026-11-08 · proc-lines: output is framed as a terminal shows it, and line events are lossless, bounded and external input.** One framer serves listen, poll, `-> T`, jobs and `run:` (spec.md 5.8): `\n` and `\r\n` end a line; a bare `\r` starts the line again (git's hundred progress updates in 3 ms are one line redrawn); `\b` removes a character; CSI, OSC, two-byte escapes and other controls but `\t` are removed; invalid UTF-8 is U+FFFD per line; a line over 4 MiB is skipped for fields and events and cut to 2000 characters in `lines`; leading spaces are kept in `lines` while documents stay trimmed. A line not yet ended is the open line, shown and never committed by a pause: a quiet timer would split wget's `Connecting… connected.` in two. No pty: it turns pacman into a screen (cursor moves, `\r\n`, streams merged), sends SIGHUP to jobs when strand goes and turns prompts on; buffering when piped is the program's to fix (`stdbuf -oL`, `--line-buffered`, `python3 -u`), documented with the remedies. `line` events are lossless and bounded by backpressure, replacing "lossless and unbounded": while more than 4096 lines or 4 MiB wait for handlers strand stops reading that command's stdout, so it waits as on a slow terminal, while stderr keeps draining. A command's `line` events are queued as input (`rt.input_events`, not `rt.events`, services/custom.rs:955), so a handler appending lines is not throttled by the 30 writes/s guard (spec.md 8.7); a loop through a program is already bounded by process start-up and one run at a time. This changes existing `from listen` handlers, for the better; the stream tests the throttling first, since it may explain lines missing from upkeep's log.

**2026-11-08 · proc-lines: a program's lines run as input but wait for a closed panel.** proc-runtime (7) put `line` events on `rt.input_events`, so a frozen listener (a closed bar, panel, osd or window, or a fault-frozen component) dropped them as it drops a click; review proved a panel closed for 0.8 s lost all 37 lines its handler should have heard, where before the branch the same handler caught up on reopen. That broke spec.md 5.1's "a service event that comes while the surface is closed … is delivered when it opens (the latest 256 per handler)" and 5.6's "sees every line"; the plan wanted these events exempt from the 30 writes/s guard only. strand-core's queue now keeps the two apart: `input` (its handlers run as input, uncounted) and `drop_frozen` (a frozen listener's events are dropped), `rt.input_events` setting both and the new `rt.external_events` the first alone, for data from outside the graph that a handler keeps. A command's `line` queue (a `from listen` service's and an action block's, one `LineSink`) is external. Tests: `crates/strand-core/tests/feedback.rs::external_events_run_as_input_and_wait_for_a_frozen_listener`, `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::custom_services::a_closed_panels_line_handler_catches_up_when_it_opens`.

## proc-streams

**2026-11-08 · proc-streams: stdout and stderr stay two pipes, each line tagged, their order across them approximate.** The owner chose this (question 2) over one merged pipe. Two pipes keep the one fact strand knows for certain, the stream a line came on (`Line.stderr`), and keep stderr's chatter out of data fields: a text line answers every key, so with one pipe ffmpeg's banner would fill `progress: text?` and curl's bar a data field. The tag is never a severity: curl, git, wget, ffmpeg, `tail -F`, pactl and systemd-run write normal output to stderr, and `pacman -Qkk` writes warnings to stdout and exits 0. The cost is order: no kernel ordering exists across two pipes, so lines are in the order strand read them (a `bash -x` probe read `done` before `+ echo done`); where exact order matters, a helper writes `2>&1` and its lines carry no tag. Fields (a listen service's and a job's block) read stdout alone. The stderr of polls and listen commands, which went to `/dev/null`, is piped, drained and kept for their diagnostics; a successful run's stderr goes to the debug log, so spec.md's old "stderr is strand's own log" (false on the owner's session, where strand's fd 2 is `/dev/null`) is gone.

## proc-format

**2026-11-08 · proc-format: a structured document naming no field is read as written by a required `text` field.** Fed through the reader, 388 of the last 400 lines of the owner's `/var/log/pacman.log` were read as `key: value` pairs and lost a `{ line: text }` field: `[2026-11-08T16:04:17-0700] [ALPM] transaction completed` splits at its first `:`, and the key `[2026-11-08T16` passes every key test; so did every `error:`, `fatal:`, `curl: (7)` and `http://` line. The rule spec.md 5.6 already gave XML (read as written by `text`, not `text?`, when the document holds nothing at the key of any of the source's fields) is made general, per document, to JSON objects and `key=value`/`key: value` lines; the source's fields are a service's, an action block's or a `-> T` record's. A `text` or `text?` field reads a JSON number, bool or array as written (`1.10` was `1.1`), a string as its value and `null` as nothing; the plan named `text` only, and `text?` is included because the conversion of a value present is the same for both, only absence differs. So a line can lose its text only when the author named a field after that line's key, which the config shows (`{ error: text?; line: text }` reads `error: x` as data). Rejected: a format keyword per source (`as text`, `as json`), which would duplicate what field names declare and could disagree with them; deciding once from the first line (yay prints `:: …` text before pacman, a helper's JSONL can carry a stray text line, and a run whose first line is `error:` would read as pairs throughout); reading pairs as text answering every field (would fill `text?` and number fields, against spec.md's XML rule). Multi-line framing (JSON over lines, blank-line records) is left out (proc-out).

## proc-reason

**2026-11-08 · proc-reason: why a command failed is the end of what it printed, head and tail, in `.error`.** "Error" is three questions with three signals: did it fail (the exit status, with `ok`; strand decides), why (stderr, framed and bounded; strand keeps it), and is this line an error (the program's own field, prefix or phrase; the config decides). For the second, `run:`'s 4 KiB tail (outputs.rs) is made general: stderr, framed, blank lines dropped, whole up to 4 KiB, else its first 1 KiB and last 3 KiB at line boundaries joined by a `…` line (the head keeps git's `fatal:` and pacman's `error: failed to commit` ahead of a hundred conflict lines, which the last six lines alone would lose), else stdout's last 1 KiB, with 100 ms of grace after exit. It follows the existing headline after `": "`, the format `run:` already used, in an action's `error`, a call's `.error`, poll and listen diagnostics, a job's `strand watch` notice and the `run:` notice; with nothing printed the text is exactly as before. No separate `reason` member: `.error` is where record.strand, upkeep and every recipe already look, so they improve with no edit. A failing `-> T` stays at info (a calculator failing on every key must not warn), a job's failure at warning, a successful run's stderr at debug. No severities and no regex: every marker surveyed (`error:`, `==> ERROR:`, `fatal:`, `E: `, `exists in filesystem`, journald's `PRIORITY`, restic's `message_type`) is a field, a prefix or a phrase, which `starts_with`, `contains` and typed fields read; a regex would be a string mini-language (design.md) and new code in the binary. The one gap, numbers inside progress text (`45% (1740/3867)`), gets a plain function, `numbers(t) -> [float]`, beside `number(t)`: every run of digits with an optional fraction, no sign, exponent or grouping (`5-6` is `[5, 6]`, `1,234` is `[1, 234]`), null in, `[]` out.

**2026-11-08 · proc-reason: a failing command is named past `stdbuf` and `env`.** The headline named argv[0], so every command written the way buffered-output.md teaches failed as `` `stdbuf` failed (exit status: 23): rsync: … `` and long-job.md's promised `` `rsync` failed … `` was wrong as written. The headline now names the program `permit exec` checks: the see-through rule moved from strand-compiler into strand-core (`strand_core::command`, pure and wasm-clean, the one crate the checker and both runtimes already depend on), so the check and the headline cannot drift apart. The runtime applies it to the concrete argv rather than lowering an index into `ExecAction` and the services' `Source`: a source has no parameters, so the two readings agree, and for an action whose parameter fills a wrapper's place the concrete reading still names what runs; this keeps every interface as it was. "could not start `x`" keeps argv[0], since that is the program strand failed to start (`stdbuf` itself missing). The rule covers an action's run and notice, a `-> T` call's `.error`, a poll's and a listen command's diagnostic, and a `file`'s `run:` notice. Tests: `crates/strand-core/src/command.rs::tests::the_program_is_past_stdbuf_and_env`, `crates/strand/src/run/exec.rs::tests::a_run_failing_says_why`, `crates/strand/src/run/outputs.rs::tests::a_failing_run_says_why`, `crates/strand-services/tests/custom.rs::a_failing_poll_says_why`, `::a_listen_command_that_ends_says_why`.

## proc-list

**2026-11-08 · proc-list: a list parameter is one argument per item.** A command action's parameter may be a list of a passable type (`[text]`, `[path]`, `[int]`, `[float]`, `[bool]`, `[Enum]`), spread in place, each item one argument as `text` shows it, never split; an empty list adds none; each `[path]` item's `~/` is expanded as a `path` parameter's is. A list of lists or of records stays `check::type_mismatch`, its help pointing at `json(v)`. `strand check` and hover show it as `{pkgs…}`. `--` before a list of names is documentation only: a table of which programs take `--` would be per-program knowledge. A list right after a shell's `-c` is `check::shell_script` as any parameter is, its help giving the safe form, `["sh", "-c", "pacman -Qi -- \"$@\"", "sh", pkgs]`. `from dbus` already took `[text]` and `file run:` already spread a `[text]`; `check::action_coalesced`'s "pass everything in one call" now has the feature it names. Each item is an argument, so each is a secrets sink; a list is a literal of the program for the recording's taint rule only when every item is.

## proc-ok

**2026-11-08 · proc-ok: `ok 0, N…` lists the statuses that are no failure, and `code` holds the status.** The owner chose both (question 3). Without them `-> T` throws away a "none" answer and a poll keeps stale values, forcing `sh -c` wrappers, the "shell scripts as the data layer" design.md criticises, for checkupdates (2), grep (1), diff (1), rsync (24), restic (3) and borg (1); prior art is systemd's `SuccessExitStatus=`. `ok` follows the command on its line (after a poll's `every`), before a block; it is allowed on command actions, with or without a result, and polled commands, and is `check::ok_not_here` on `from listen` (its end always means a restart), `from dbus` actions and polled files. 0 must be written (`ok 2` is `check::ok_without_zero`, help `ok 0, 2`) so the clause reads correctly alone. A listed status is success (`-> T` reads its output, a poll updates, `error` null, no notice) while `code` still holds it, so `backup.code == 3` can say "some files skipped"; an ok'd non-zero run's stderr is logged at info, and a signal is never ok. Guidance, from the design that argued against `ok`: use it only where a status is unambiguous; pacman's 1 means both "no orphans" (`-Qdtq`) and "no such package" (`-Qi nosuch`), so `ok 0, 1` would hide the second, and the guide keeps a one-line `sh` for that case. The plan left two things open, decided here: a status outside 0 to 255 is a load error, `check::ok_status` (no program can end with it, so writing one is a mistake), and `ok` is a contextual keyword, so no name `ok` breaks.

**2026-11-08 · proc-ok: a command that printed nothing reads `[]` as any list, `[text]` included.** spec.md 5.7 and the exit-statuses page say that a listed status's empty output is `[]` or null, and the plan's own example was checkupdates' 2, "none, so `[]`"; but doc-formats had left blank text read as a list of `text` one blank item, so `-> [text]` answered `[""]` and a shell writing `updates().len == 0` for "up to date" never saw it. doc-formats gave no reason for keeping text out of its blank rule (it was written for empty XML elements, which it made `[]` for every other item type), and a list holding one empty text is no reading of "nothing": blank text read as a list is now `[]` for every item type, an empty element read as `[text]` too. The plan's `-> [text]` and `{ names: [text] }` examples still read several lines as one item (proc-output above), so grammar.md, its fixture and `check::ok_not_here`'s help now write `-> text` and `{ names: text }`, as spec.md 5.7 already did. Tests: `crates/strand/src/run/exec.rs::tests::an_ok_status_is_not_a_failure`, `crates/strand/src/services/custom.rs::tests::an_empty_element_is_an_empty_record_or_list`.

## proc-permit

**2026-11-08 · proc-permit: `permit exec` sees through `stdbuf` and `env NAME=value`.** The buffering fix (`stdbuf -oL`) and the locale fix (`env LC_ALL=C`) would otherwise push authors to `permit exec "stdbuf"` or `"env"`, which permit any program. The owner chose the see-through, limited to exact forms (question 5): when a command's first item is `stdbuf` followed only by `-i`, `-o` or `-e` options, or `env` followed only by `NAME=value` items, the program checked against `permit exec`, and by `check::shell_script`, is the one after them (`first_program`, check/collect.rs; check/actions.rs). The plan left the forms' detail open, decided here by what keeps the rule exact: every item seen through is a text literal (a parameter there stops it, since its value could be a program); `stdbuf`'s options are `-i`, `-o` and `-e` with the mode attached (`-oL`) or as the next item (`-o`, `L`), or `--input=`, `--output=`, `--error=`; `NAME` is a letter or `_` then letters, digits or `_`; the two forms may follow each other (`stdbuf -oL env LC_ALL=C pacman` checks `pacman`), since each runs the item after it as its program and nothing else. Anything else (`env -i pacman`, `env -u X pacman`, `stdbuf --help`) is not seen through, and the program checked is `env` or `stdbuf`.

**2026-11-08 · proc-permit: the see-through takes `stdbuf` and `env` by their own names alone, and `env` only the variables that cannot change the program.** Review found the first form reopened what spec.md 5.6 closes (a program run by its path needs its own permit): `program_at` matched the wrappers by basename at any path, so with `permit exec "pacman"` alone `["/tmp/evil/env", "pacman"]` and `["./stdbuf", "-oL", "pacman"]` loaded, though what runs is the binary named `env` or `stdbuf`; and it took any `NAME=value`, so `["env", "PATH=/tmp/evil", "pacman"]` ran `/tmp/evil/pacman` and `["env", "LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so", "pacman"]` loaded any code into it. The claim above that each wrapper "runs the item after it as its program and nothing else" held only for the system's wrappers with harmless variables. Now a wrapper is seen through only as the bare word (found on `PATH`, as a bare `pacman` is) or as `/usr/bin/…` or `/bin/…`; any other path is checked as itself. `env`'s items are kept to a list rather than a denylist, since the variables that load code are many and per program (`LD_*`, `PATH`, `PYTHONPATH`, `PERL5LIB`, `BASH_ENV`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `GCONV_PATH`…): `LANG`, `LANGUAGE`, `LC_…`, `TZ`, `TERM`, `NO_COLOR`, `COLUMNS` and `PYTHONUNBUFFERED`, the locale, time zone, terminal and buffering fixes the plan names, each of which selects data, never a program or a library. Any other variable stops the seeing through, so the permit must name `env`, which says plainly that anything may run. Test: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::the_see_through_permits_only_name_value_and_buffer_options` (the reviewer's cases, string form included).

## proc-out

**2026-11-08 · proc-out: what following programs' output leaves out, on purpose.** A regex or `match` function (every marker surveyed is a field, a prefix or a phrase; a string mini-language and new `.text`). Strand classifying lines as error, warning or progress (stream is not severity; severity is the program's convention). A pty, terminal emulation, colour as markup (a screen, not lines; SIGHUP on close; prompts switched on; a future `terminal` element covers it, Kitty does for upkeep). Writing to stdin or answering prompts (a protocol and a security story, pkexec mid-transaction; stdin stays `/dev/null` so prompts fail fast; the keeper is the hook if it comes). A format keyword per source (proc-format). Multi-line framing: JSON over lines (`pw-dump --monitor`), blank-line records (`udevadm --property`), logfmt's several pairs per line (no config needs it; each program has a one-line structured form). `from listen` with parameters or started on demand (that is a job: an action with a block). A streaming `-> T` (an `Async` stays a load). Several runs of one action at once, keyed (one at a time makes `lines` one log and `code` one status; two jobs are two actions; revisit for a download manager). `lines` on listen services (a watch's lines are data for handlers, and `lines` would collide with services' own fields of that name; `([x] + xs).take(N)` in a handler is one line; revisit when a second log follower appears). Syntax for environment, working directory or stdin (`env NAME=v`, seen through by the check, and `-C`/`--cwd` flags cover it). Re-attaching to jobs after strand restarts (`running` reads false and the keeper drains the output; possible later through the keeper). Re-running a `-> T` load without a dummy argument (a real gap about loads, not output; its own decision, `calc.reload()`). Timestamps per line (`n` orders lines; a program that stamps its lines gives the time as a field). Exact interleaving of stdout and stderr (proc-streams).

## proc-interface

**2026-11-08 · proc-interface: the compiler and the runtime meet at `ExecAction`, `RunUpdate` and the `Line` record, so the language and runtime streams change disjoint crates.** Following programs' output is built in two streams (language: strand-compiler, strand-dev, site; runtime: strand-services, strand, strand-eval), so the interface lands first, lowered but not yet parsed. `hir::ArgvPart::Spread(i)` is a list parameter's items, which the VM expands into `ExecRequest::argv` (one argument each, none for an empty list, each `[path]` item's `~/` expanded; `ExecAction::paths` lists `[path]` parameters too), so the host never sees a list. `ExecAction` gains `ok: Vec<i32>` (`[0]` unless written) and `fields: Option<ActionFields>` (the block's record and its `CustomField`s), and `hir::SourceSpec::Poll` gains `ok`. How a block reaches the config was open in the plan ("action blocks feed `LineSink` under the action's name"), decided here: the host serves a block exactly as it serves a `from listen` service named after the action, so the language stream lowers `backup.percent_done` and `on backup.line(doc)` as reads and events of the service `backup`, and the runtime stream makes its custom-service host answer for that name, fed by the run's stdout lines; global names are unique, so it never collides with a service, and reading it never starts a command (the entry runs nothing itself). Rejected: carrying block values through `Instance` as the run's are (the conversion of a document into the declared record lives with the custom services, which would have to be split), and a synthesized `CustomService` with a new source kind (every source consumer would learn a kind that runs nothing). A run's output reaches the program as one `RunUpdate` per flush through `Instance::update_action_run` (`reset`, then `keep_from` and `lines` by number, then `code`, `error`, `running`: the end order), beside the old `set_action_run` and `set_action_error`, which stay for the replay harness and tests. `ActionRun` reads `running`, `started`, `error`, `code`, `lines` in that order (a D-Bus method's run `code` null, `lines` empty), and `Line` is a schema record keyed by `n` (`record Line key n`), so a `for` over `rec.lines` keeps each line's node; the plan's `lines: [Line] key n` is written as the record's key, the form schema files have. `lines` changing bumps one tracked counter, and the list value is built once per change and kept, so a read of `rec.running` while lines arrive re-reads a cached list. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/mod.rs::tests::a_list_parameter_is_one_argument_per_item`, `crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/runs.rs::tests::lines_apply_by_number`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/flex.rs::a_runs_lines_and_code_follow_the_hosts_updates`.

## proc-runtime

**2026-11-08 · proc-runtime: where the runtime stream's build reads the plan more narrowly or more widely than its words, and why.** (1) The `poll(2)` `Reader` is the readers of the threads that own a process (a job's, a `-> T` call's, a `run:`'s); a `from listen` or polled command lives on the services' async runtime, which reads its pipes with tokio, so it shares the `Framer` and the `Tail` and not the `Reader`: one framing and one reason rule, two ways of waiting. (2) The framer removes every string escape (OSC, DCS, SOS, PM, APC, until BEL or `ESC \`) and ESC with intermediates (`ESC ( B`, which `tput sgr0` prints), not only OSC and two-byte ESC: each would otherwise leave a stray letter in a line. (3) A `text` field reads a JSON number, bool or array as written when it is the whole document (`1.10`); a value at a key reads as serde writes it (`[1,2]`), which differs only in spacing, since the parsed document keeps no source spans. (4) A listen line keeps the Latin-1 fallback `decode_document` has (a line that is not UTF-8 throughout); a job's line replaces bad bytes with U+FFFD per line, as a terminal shows them. (5) The keeper's protocol is one `SOCK_SEQPACKET` datagram of 9 bytes per message, and a release means "read these to their end, then close them": a job's thread ends at its program's end plus the grace, never waiting on a pipe a background child holds. (6) A `-> T` call still reads to its stdout's end (a child holding stdout times out, as before), its stderr read alongside and for the grace after it exits; its output is framed before it is read as `T`. (7) Program `line` events go on an input queue (`rt.input_events`), so a frozen listener (a faulted or parked component) drops them as it drops input; a parked item's services are released anyway. The rate guard's exemption also needs the handler spawned as input (`spawn_input`), which `instantiate/mount.rs` does not yet do: `a_line_handler_appending_every_frame_is_not_throttled` is ignored until the language stream changes it. (8) The host serves a block before the program mounts (`CustomHost::declare_blocks` at boot and before each reload, `prune_blocks` after a committed one), as a `from listen` entry whose source runs nothing (`Source::Fed`), filled by `client.seed` and its `line` events emitted on the entry's queue; a reset is every field null. The job's thread looks the block up as it reads, so a reload that declared it afresh is read from its next line. (9) A job's stderr lines are logged at debug as they are read, before its status is known, so a run that fails logs them too; that adds lines, never loses one. (10) The glitch report needs no new record kinds (strand-core's flight format stays as it is): a job's line is an `EVENT` record named `action <name>` (`{"line": {n, text, stderr, open}}`, or `{"~skipped": k}` past 32 ended lines a frame), as a result call's answer is a `FETCH` named `action <name>`; the end the plan calls `ACTION_END` is the existing `ACTION` end record, whose exit is the code. The replay steps are `line action <name> [stderr] [open] "<text>"` and `end action <name> [code N] [failed "<why>"]`. A run's taint also counts the command's own written words (`"-c"`, a script) as the config's, which `is_text_literal` (chunk constants) does not hold. A block's fields and `line` events are recorded under the action's name as a declared service's are; replaying them waits on the language stream lowering `act.field` and `on act.line` (the sandbox serves no block until then). Tests: `crates/strand-services/src/proc.rs::tests`, `crates/strand-services/tests/custom.rs::a_flood_of_lines_waits_for_its_handler_and_loses_none`, `crates/strand/src/run/exec.rs::tests::a_run_outlives_strand_without_sigpipe`, `::a_reload_keeps_reading`, `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::custom_services::an_action_block_is_served_under_the_actions_name`, `crates/strand/src/run/record.rs::tests::run_lines_are_recorded_bounded_and_held_back`, `eval/tests/replay.rs::a_recorded_jobs_lines_are_replayed`.

## proc-language

**2026-11-08 · proc-language: the language of programs' output, and the readings the plan left open.** The parser takes `ok INT (, INT)*` after any source and after any action's command, and a block of fields (fields alone; a `permit` there is `syntax::expected`) after any action; `ok` is a keyword only on that line before a number or a `-`, so `ok -1`, `ok 2.5` and `ok 2s` are one `syntax::expected` each. The checker deduplicates and sorts the statuses with 0 among them. A block on a `from dbus` method's action is `check::misplaced` (it prints no lines), as `ok` there is `check::ok_not_here`. A block field may not be named `ready` either (`check::reserved_field`, with the run's six): the block is served as a service of the action's name (proc-interface), and every service answers `ready` itself. For the same reason an action with a block named after a builtin service (`action audio() […] { … }`) is `check::redeclared`, since its reads would reach the builtin. A block's field reads lower as reads of that service (`hir::ExprKind::Service(name)`), and the instance announces each block to the host through a new `ServiceHost::declare_block` (default: nothing; `SchemaHost` mounts its cells, so tests, `strand export` and the eval harness read blocks too), with `stop` for a block a reload removed; the strand crate's host may implement it or register blocks its own way. `lines` or `code` read on a `from dbus` method's run is `check::unknown_field` (the spec's load error), on a `-> T` action `check::no_run_output`, a warning. The `stdbuf`/`env` see-through (proc-permit) holds for every command `permit exec` checks: an action's, a polled or listen command's (a string command split into words first) and a `file`'s `run:`; `stdbuf` needs at least one option, as `stdbuf` itself does, while `env` may have none; the program after them is a written-out item not starting with `-`; and a permit naming any program of the chain allows the command, so `permit exec "stdbuf"` or `"env"` still allows anything after it, as before, and no config that loaded stops loading. `strand check`'s listing and an action's hover show `ok 0, 3` after the command when more than 0 is listed (`ActionDecl::shown`), and the hover adds the result type and the block's fields. `numbers(t)` takes `text?` (null in, `[]` out); a `.` with no digit after it ends a number (`3.` is 3). The spec's `rec.error?.split("\n").first` is a nullable read (`split` through `?.` is `[text]?`), corrected to `rec.error?.split("\n")?.first`. Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::action_blocks_ok_and_list_parameters_check`, `::each_proc_output_check_has_its_code`, `::proc_output_checks_help_with_the_fix`, `::the_see_through_permits_only_name_value_and_buffer_options`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/vm.rs::a_list_parameter_is_one_argument_per_item`, `::numbers_reads_progress_text`, `::an_action_block_is_read_as_the_service_named_after_it`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/fmt.rs::ok_clauses_and_action_blocks_format`, `crates/strand-dev/tests/lsp.rs::an_actions_hover_and_completion_show_its_output`, `crates/strand-dev/tests/tree_sitter.rs::highlights_capture_every_keyword_in_grammar_md`.

## proc-output

**2026-11-08 · proc-output: the integration of the language and runtime streams, and what proving the five use cases with real programs changed.** The two streams met at four places, each now wired. (1) A command's `line` events were already queued as input (`rt.input_events`), but `mount.rs` spawned every service event's handler with `spawn_for`, so a handler keeping each line was still throttled by the 30 writes/s guard; the queue now says what it is (`EventQueue::is_input`, strand-core), and a handler of an input queue runs with `spawn_input`, so the host decides and no event name is special-cased in the compiler (`services/mod.rs::a_line_handler_appending_every_frame_is_not_throttled`, un-ignored; it fails without the change). (2) Blocks: the runtime serves an action's block through `CustomHost::declare_blocks`/`prune_blocks` around each mount, so the strand crate's host keeps `ServiceHost::declare_block`'s default; `SchemaHost`'s implementation serves blocks in the replay sandbox, and the harness's `set`/`emit` steps and the replay plan's known services now count an action with a block as the service of its name (`eval/tests/replay.rs::a_recorded_blocks_fields_and_lines_are_replayed`, `eval/tests/smoke.rs::a_blocks_fields_and_lines_are_what_its_steps_say`); end to end, `run/tests.rs::an_action_line_handler_hears_every_line` (2000 lines at once, every one heard in order, the end after the last). (3) `ok` was enforced by the runtime from `ExecAction.ok` and `SourceSpec::Poll.ok` already. (4) `strand check`'s listing says a list is one argument per item; the claims the language stream proved as text now name the runtime's tests. Two changes came from running the plan's use cases headless with stand-ins that print as pacman, restic and journalctl do and with real curl and `tail -F`. A `from listen` command that ends with nothing on stderr no longer gives the last 1 KiB of its stdout as why: its stdout is the data it fed for as long as it ran, so a restart's diagnostic was the journal's last entries; the headline is all there (`tests/custom.rs::a_listen_command_that_ends_says_why`), and spec.md 5.8 says so. And the plan's `-> [text]` over checkupdates and `{ names: [text] }` over `pacman -Qdtq` assumed a program's lines read as a list, which doc-formats decided against ("a per-line list stays a JSON array the command prints"): two lines are one item, and blank text read as `[text]` is `[""]`. The rule stands; spec.md 5.6–5.7 and the exit-statuses page now use `-> text`, `{ list: text }` and `grep -c` read as an `int`, and the page says how to print a list. Whether a list of `text` should read a program's lines one per item is left to the owner.

## proc-review

**2026-11-08 · proc-review-2: what the second review of programs' output changed, and why.** (1) A run is read while it stops. `stop()`'s escalation slept between SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL with nobody reading the pipes, so a program that printed while asked (a progress loop, `rsync -v`) blocked on its full pipe, never ran its SIGINT cleanup and was SIGTERMed (143, not 130), its last lines lost; `stop_group` now reads the pipes between its looks at the leader, for a job and for a call with a result (`exec.rs::a_chatty_run_is_read_while_it_stops`, a Python loop whose `KeyboardInterrupt` handler prints and exits 130). (2) A `file`'s `run:` hands its pipes to the keeper as a job does. Piping its stdout (for the reason's "else stdout's last 1 KiB") meant a daemon it started in the background (`pkill mako; mako &`) died of SIGPIPE at its first line once strand stopped reading, `STDERR_GRACE` after the run; on main stdout was `/dev/null` and stderr already had the same flaw. Putting stdout back on `/dev/null` would fix only stdout and drop a reason the spec promises, so the run's pipes go to the keeper, which reads them on after release; the keeper now hands out run ids (`Keeper::next_run`) because jobs and `run:`s share it (`outputs.rs::a_daemon_a_run_starts_outlives_its_reading`). The plan's "the keeper is not needed for … `run:`" was written when `run:` piped stderr alone; this extends it, it adds no concept. (3) A failing poll is the same failure while its headline is: its reason may differ every run (curl's "timed out after N milliseconds"), so comparing the whole text reported every interval; the first report still carries the reason, and a new headline is news (`tests/custom.rs::a_poll_failing_with_a_changing_reason_is_reported_once`). (4) When the see-through stops, `check::no_permit`'s help names the item that stopped it (`PATH=/x`, `--help`, a parameter) and warns that permitting the wrapper would allow any program, instead of suggesting `permit exec "env"`, the exact outcome owner question 5 was meant to prevent; one function in strand-core (`command::not_seen_through`) serves actions, sources and `run:` (`checker.rs::the_see_through_permits_only_name_value_and_buffer_options`). (5) Docs: a closed surface catches up on the latest 256 lines, so "none is lost" holds only while a handler hears them; pacman prints its conflicting files on stdout, so they are in `lines`, not `.error`; `code` is 130 only when SIGINT ends the program (`rsync` exits 20); and the long-job recipe no longer interpolates (Strand has none) or counts restic's errors from `lines`, which keeps only the last 1000 while restic prints up to 60 status lines a second.

**2026-11-08 · proc-review-3: a job's thread has the stack its parse needs, a replayed `lines` keeps the live bound, and the exit-statuses recipe reads `.error` apart from the value.** (1) A job's thread was given the 64 KiB a thread that only starts and waits needs; it now also parses each stdout line of an action with a block (`svc::read_line`: serde_json, or roxmltree to `xml::MAX_DEPTH`), and a line nested 32 levels overflowed it, which aborts the whole process, bar and lock with it. A job's thread now reserves 1 MiB (`exec::JOB_STACK`; a reservation, only the pages a parse touches are mapped; 256 KiB already passes 127 levels in a debug build), and a call with a result keeps 64 KiB since its parse runs on the logic thread (`exec.rs::a_block_reads_lines_nested_as_deep_as_the_parsers_take`, 127-deep JSON objects, XML elements and JSON arrays). Parsing off the thread was the alternative; it would move a block's field merge away from the lines it came with and break the end order for nothing a larger reservation does not give. (2) The eval sandbox numbered a replayed job's lines but never dropped any, so a recording of a chatty job replayed more than the 1000 lines (256 KiB) the shell kept, and a view counting or listing `rec.lines` replayed differently from what it drew. The sandbox's run now keeps the ring's bound in the ring's way (added lines push the oldest out, an open line dropped is open no longer, a redraw never trims) and sends the front as `keep_from`. The bounds moved to strand-services-schema, which both strand-services and the eval crate depend on (`POLLED` is the precedent), so the two cannot drift; `strand_services::proc` re-exports them (`eval/tests/smoke.rs::a_replayed_jobs_lines_keep_the_live_bound`). (3) The exit-statuses recipe wrote `updates() ?? ""`, which reads a failed call (null) as the same `""` the ok'd status gives, so the page about telling "none" from failure taught the conflation `ok` exists to prevent; it now reads the call's `.error` before its value, for grep's count too, and says why `?? ""` alone hides the failure. Its advice for a list was a helper piping checkupdates into jq, whose status is jq's, so checkupdates' failure and its "none" both arrived as 0; the page now splits the text in the config (`(news ?? "").split("\n").filter(l => l != "")`), which keeps `ok` and `.error`, and says a helper needs `pipefail` and then owns the status.

**2026-11-09 · lines-list: a program's text output read as a list is a list of its lines.** This overrides the 2026-11-07 doc-formats sentence "Splitting the lines into items would add a format, so a per-line list stays a JSON array the command prints" and the 2026-11-08 proc-output "The rule stands". The earlier sentence was a review agent's call, never put to the owner; proc-output left the question to the owner, who approved this reading through an independent advisor on 2026-11-09. The line is already Strand's unit of program text everywhere: the framer (spec.md 5.8), `rec.lines`, `line` events, `from listen`'s one document per line, the `key=value` detection, and list parameters spreading one argv item per item. Reading a list from those lines removes a concept (a list of `text` that is secretly one item), and the old reading failed silently: `{ names: [text] }` over `pacman -Qdtq` printing fifty orphans had `names.len == 1`. The whole-document check runs first and is unchanged, so JSON (a pretty-printed array spanning lines) and XML keep their reading; only a document that is text, or `key=value` lines holding none of the service's fields' keys (the condition under which a `text` field already reads such pairs as written), splits. It applies to an action's `-> [T]` and `-> [T]?`, to a field typed `[T]` or `[T]?` with no key path (a key naming the field itself is none) of a `from poll` command or file, and to a `from file` field, which reads the same document a polled file does (the brief named `from poll` files; leaving `from file` out would make one file read two ways by its source keyword). A line is what the framer gives (`\n` or `\r\n` ends one, a bare `\r` redraws it, controls removed, a file's lines too); blank and whitespace-only lines are no item, so a trailing newline adds none and nothing printed is still `[]` (null for `[T]?`, as before: a blank document is not split); each item is trimmed. A value item (`text`, `path`, a number, `bool`, enum, `length`, `duration`, colour, `Date`) is the line read by the single-value rule, so `45 °C` per line is 45 each. A record item is the line read as a `from listen` line is (`svc::read_line`): JSON lines are a record each, a `key=value` line a record of its pairs, and a required `text` field reads a line naming none of the fields as written, so a record with any required `text` field takes every line; a line that fills no field is its text, which a record without a `text` field does not read. A line that does not convert is left out and reported once with its index (`names[2]`), the rule items inside a document already had; for a field that report is the field's nested report, for an action an info log line naming the action. Spaces, tabs and commas separate nothing: one value per line. To keep `pidof`'s `1234 5678` refused as `[int]` (it would otherwise read 1234 by the number-and-unit rule), an item holding several values (`several_values`) is no item of a list of numbers, now checked per item (`list_of`), which also covers a JSON array's string items and repeated XML elements (`["22 80"]` read as `[int]` had been `[22]`); and an action's output of lines none of which converts is no list (its `.error`), where a field reads `[]` with the nested report, so neither is a silent `[]`. The report and the error add the help "`[int]` reads one value per line: print one per line (`pgrep`), or read `-> text` and `.split(" ")`" (for a field, "declare the field `text`"). Text starting with `<` that is not XML (an HTML page served in place of a feed) splits into values but never into records: read as a list of records it is reported as before, not read as a record a line (`a_page_that_is_not_xml_is_reported` caught a page read as two bogus posts when key paths still split). Text of several values inside a document (a JSON string, an element's text, a `from listen` line) keeps the doc-formats rule. A single type over several lines is unchanged: `text` the whole, a number the first (`/proc/loadavg`). `from listen` fields are unchanged: one line is one document, one item. The service side learns a field's list shape through `FieldSpec::lines` (`custom::Lines`: `No`, `Values`, or `Records` with the item record's fields), set by the binary from the declared type, as `FieldSpec::text` already was; a reload that changes it restarts the service. grammar.md, its fixture, spec.md 5.6's poll example and `check::ok_not_here`'s help return to `-> [text]` and `{ names: [text] }`; the exit-statuses page reads `updates()` as `[text]` directly and keeps its `pipefail` paragraph. Tests: `crates/strand/src/services/custom.rs::tests::a_list_reads_a_text_outputs_lines`, `::a_list_type_wraps_one_value_and_a_single_type_takes_the_first`, `crates/strand-services/src/custom.rs::tests::a_text_document_read_as_a_list_is_its_lines`, `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::custom_services::a_polled_commands_lines_fill_a_list_field`, `crates/strand/src/run/exec.rs::tests::a_list_result_reads_a_programs_lines`.
